35_marg2563: Aleph: teaching, namely that man may know himself and God. The people of the Jews did not have it, and therefore rightly lay under their enemies.
35_marg2564: How doth the city sit solitary. He declares that the overthrow of the wretched city and the ruin of the heavenly people did not only happen under the Chaldeans, but was to be fulfilled more fully under Titus and Vespasian; for before the last captivity she is not rightly said to sit alone, unless perhaps to heighten the grief. We read that the Chaldeans left the poor tillers of the land, over whom Godolias was ordered to rule. Nor is the city wholly destroyed, but its wasting is put off until after the death of Christ, so that not a stone is left upon a stone in it. But when they returned from the captivity the rod of fury grew, because through the warnings and corrections of the prophets they did not return to God, but were always ungrateful for God’s benefits. Whence Moses: “I know thy obstinacy and thy most stiff neck; thou hast always been contentious against God”; and Stephen in the Acts of the Apostles: “You stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart.” Therefore, often worn down by scourges, oppressed by enemies, afflicted with every evil, even so they did not believe, but provoked God most high. And so, the ten tribes being already carried captive into Assyria, the two which remained, following the house of David and worshipping God in hope, as their malice grew little by little, are first carried captive into Chaldea; whence the city is mourned here: How doth the city sit solitary, etc.
35_marg2565: Historically. How doth the city sit solitary. Jerusalem, stripped of her people, full of shame, humbled among her enemies, once full of people and glorious among the enemies, is become as a widow, the mistress of the Gentiles: forsaken by her kings, made desolate of her priests, her temple profaned and the glory of her vessels cast out, forsaken by the help of God. Mistress of the Gentiles, as she had before overthrown and subdued them.
35_marg2566: In the moral sense. The soul sits alone as a widow, stripped of the goods of the virtues, which has put itself under the lord of the Chaldeans and has despised the bridegroom of her youth. The Chaldeans who take her captive are interpreted: these are the demons, who call the soul back from the throne of the heavenly country and take her captive into their power. Whence: “Go into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans”; because, being the daughter of God, thou wouldst not stand in the light of the virtues, go, thy name being changed, into the darkness of blindness. Whence Jeremias, groaning, cried out: How doth the city sit solitary, namely the soul, once like a city full of people with the virtues and the prayers of the saints, now desolate; which before was strong in divine works among throngs of companions, now sits squalid among enemies, with no fellowship of the saints, no communion of the sacraments, no sharing with the bridegroom, but brought under tribute to the vices. Whence it is also said: “My father has left me bound to many creditors, whom I do not satisfy though I labour daily.” Many are the tributes of sins to which the soul is bound, until she returns to freedom through penance. Whence: “Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth.” Whence the voice of the mourner follows: Weeping she hath wept in the night.
35_marg2567: Allegorically. How doth the city sit solitary. More tearfully is the Church to be mourned, widowed by the bridegroom’s absence as her faults demand. How doth the city of God sit solitary, made desolate of the help of the angels. For if the bridegroom were with her she would not be mourned, because “the children of the bridegroom cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them”, but they rejoice with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice. But when they perceive the mother, that is, the Church, widowed of the bridegroom, not only the children but all the friends too are wont to weep; whence Jeremias wept before all and for all, not for the ruin of stones but of men. How doth the city sit solitary shows the posture of one weeping; whence Job too is told to have sat on the dunghill, that the feeling of one grieving might be expressed, and he himself is interpreted “grieving”. Of this captivity it is said: “Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat”, we, namely, who would not sit on the throne of the kingdom and stand on the highest summit of heaven, rightly sit and grieve upon the rivers of temptations. Whence Isaias: “Come down, sit in the dust, O daughter of Babylon, sit on the ground; there is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans.” So our Jerusalem, when she has come into the confusion of sins, has no throne of dignity, but is soiled in earthly vices. Whence Jeremias laments not only that she sits soiled with earthly works, but that she is alone and as a widow. Not truly a widow; for even if she is despised by the bridegroom for a time, yet the rights of betrothal are kept, so that if she wishes to return through penance she may receive the bridegroom when she has made satisfaction, and the garment of immortality, clothed again in which she will lie under no one’s tribute. Whence Paul: “Owe no man any thing, but to love one another.”

35_marg2568: Paschasius. Historically, etc. Who she is that weeps the letter Beth shows, which is interpreted “house”: she, namely, who went into Egypt with Jacob and came out by the Lord’s mercy, according to that: “When Israel went out of Egypt”, etc. But again, as her sins demanded, she is carried captive into Babylon; whence weeping she hath wept in the night, because by day no rest is given them, that at least they may be comforted by their own tears, and at evening wash the eyes which before they lifted up to idols. And what is worse, of all her friends who flattered her before, there is none to comfort her. Her tears are on her cheeks, that they may be the more confounded among the enemies and filled with their own reproaches. For the people was led into captivity because of idolatry and was harshly afflicted by the enemies; but more harshly under Titus and Vespasian, the people whom God’s patience bore long, but who, impenitent, treasured up wrath for themselves in the day of fury.
35_marg2569: Weeping she hath wept. The fourth topic of complaint, by which base and lowly things undeservedly suffered are set forth; it is used very often here.
35_marg2570: In the moral sense. The soul weeps, namely in the blindness of sins, of which it is said: “Let that night be solitary, and not worthy of praise.” But she does not weep by her own choice, but by the Lord’s mercy; whence the prophet, lamenting in the person of the Lord, says: How doth the city sit solitary. For unless the Lord, moved by mercy, had seen her sitting alone, she would not have wept for herself at all. “The Lord looked on Peter, and he wept bitterly.” Her tears are on her cheeks. The cheek of the soul is the conscience; the face is shaped in the cheeks, as each one’s quality is shown in the conscience. And the conscience which knows its sins ought always to be watered with a fountain of tears; whence David: “My sin is always before me.” Otherwise: There is none to comfort her, the true comforter, namely the Holy Spirit, being lost, especially when all her friends, that is, the affections of wicked love, become her enemies, since in the day of judgement, according to the Apostle, the thoughts will rise up accusing or defending the wretched soul, and the demons, the worst persuaders, who now flatter to deceive.
35_marg2571: Allegorically. Weeping she hath wept in the night. The Church of Christ weeps in the night, that is, amid the adversities of this life, because, though she is predestined to glory, yet she dwells amid the darknesses of ignorance and the perils of blindness. She weeps without for what she endures; she weeps within for the miseries of her blindness. But weeping she weeps, because first she is pricked within, and so outwardly she is baptized with her own tears, which are brought forth from the fountain of the heart; whose abundance the prophet implies when he says: weeping she hath wept. In this way the outer man no less than the inner is washed to be made new; whence it follows: her tears are on her cheeks, those who know how to bewail their own and others’ sins, not to cover them, of whom it is said in the Canticle: “Thy cheeks are as a piece of a pomegranate, besides that which lieth hid within.” For in these the Church’s beauty is shown, and by their preaching we are brought over into the body of the Church; who, as they labour more than the rest in the body of Christ, so they groan and weep more for those whom they see dwelling in sins and in the blindness of error. The Church weeps in the night because she is not ignorant of the darkness of her sins; she bears tears on her cheeks, by which she renews her beauty daily. For Mary profits Martha as she labours, while weeping she weeps at the Lord’s feet. The bride weeps, removed from the bridegroom’s embrace, and in the valley, that is, in the night of this ignorance, weeping she weeps for longing of the country, namely the heavenly one, and for her own sins and others’ in this world; she weeps in those who are dead to the world. She weeps in the virgins, in the widows, in all who confess themselves pilgrims and strangers upon the earth. There is none to comfort her among all them that were dear to her, the saints namely, or the angels, unless she receives the comfort of the Spirit; whence all her friends have despised her, because God despised her. And are become her enemies, to whom God is an enemy, from whose justice they cannot disagree.
35_marg2572: There is none to comfort her, etc. This properly belongs to the last captivity, for from then on they had neither princes nor priests. But in Babylon they had comforters, Daniel, Ezechiel and many others.

35_marg2574: Historically. Juda hath removed her dwelling place because of the multitude of her sins: they were carried captive, namely, not only as far as Babylon, but from there, like runaway slaves, because of the affliction of bondage they moved on to other nations; but even there they found no rest. Whence it follows: All her persecutors have taken her in the midst of straits, who pursued the runaways and afflicted more cruelly those already in straits. For rightly those who had fled the Lord’s light yoke are pressed down by hard affliction, and those who held cheap the freedom promised in Christ rightly labour in the affliction of bondage. Juda hath removed from some enemies to others, fleeing the cruelty of their masters. Like Cain the slayer of his brother, the Jews dwelt among the nations, wandering and fugitives, finding no rest, carrying about the shame of their confusion, because they did not fear to kill Christ their brother.
35_marg2575: For by the fullness of her sins Juda removed into captivity, which by heaping them up she provoked God’s vengeance upon herself. For otherwise God would not hand over his beloved and glorious nation into the shame of captivity, who says he cannot yet hand over the Amorrhites, because the sins of the Amorrhites are not yet complete.
35_marg2576: Juda hath removed her dwelling place. The soul, namely, which ought to praise God and lay open its sins by accusing itself, afflicted by the bondage of the vices, moves from vice to vice and finds no rest; whence the Apostle: “I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind.” But there is no way of escape, except that which he himself points out: “the grace of God by Jesus Christ.” But the wretched soul is at length caught by her persecutors in the midst of straits, wearied in the manner of women with child; whence: “Woe to them that are with child, and that give suck in those days.”
35_marg2577: Allegorically. Juda hath removed her dwelling place, that is, the Church of Christ, having lost her freedom, has often removed into bondage to the nations and into the affliction of the vices, and has found no rest, but fleeing from place to place she is caught by her persecutors and afflicted with heavier straits. For often our Jerusalem is thus taken captive and afflicted in history, and wanders captive among enemies, as the earthly Jerusalem prefigured in history.

35_marg2581: Historically. The ways of Sion. Having first set out the whole, he passes to the several kinds of persons, so that while the whole is divided into its kinds and the kinds are joined again into the whole, the mourning may be multiplied more fully. And because the Lamentations are composed in metre, they are sometimes adorned with the figures of worldly eloquence, and are set out by metaphor with rhetorical propriety. Whence it is said here: The ways of Sion mourn, etc.; not that ways feel or mourn, but, brought to desolation, they stir up mourning in those who pass by, because there are none that come to the solemn feast. Like it is what Moses says: “Hear, O ye heavens, the things I speak”, etc. Isaias too calls heaven and earth to witness, that all the elements may know that God is justly angry and has been provoked to wrath.
35_marg2582: The ways of Sion, namely the virtues that lead to the heavenly Jerusalem, mourn, because there are none that come to the solemn feast of the soul from whom the bridegroom has been taken, when the soul slips from the citadel of lofty intention to outward actions. Her solemn feast is the inward contemplation of the heavenly life; but there are none that come to the solemn feast, namely the affections of the former life do not come to the solemnities of contemplation, the soul’s or God’s, because the gates of the senses are broken down. For there are gates of death, and there are gates of justice, of which it is said: “Open ye to me the gates of justice”, etc., and in Isaias: “Open ye the gates, and let the just nation enter in.” But because “death is come up through our windows”, the virginity of the soul is in affliction and the royal priesthood groans, while in place of the virtues we are filled with the bitterness of the vices. Let us therefore go out of the gates of death and build again the gates of life, asking which is the gate of the Lord, that we may walk in it.
35_marg2583: The ways of Sion. As often as the Church, for her sins, is filled within or without with the bitterness of the Lord’s fury, rightly the ways mourn, the gates lie broken down, the priests namely groan, the virgins are in affliction, so that the whole boarding of the house, signified by the number four, is seen to be shaken. Whence Jeremias says elsewhere too: “Stand ye on the ways, and see, and ask for the ways of the Lord”, etc. The ways are the prophets, the patriarchs and others through whom one comes to Christ, who is the true way. For as lights are called so from Christ the light, so ways can be called so from him; whence Abraham is called the first way of believing. These are the ways of Sion, that is, of the heavenly city; these mourn and groan because there are none that come to the solemn feast of the heavenly country, because the gates are broken down; for those who are over the office neither enter themselves nor let others enter. The priests sigh because, namely, the ways mourn; the virgins are in affliction because the gates are broken down. And rightly are priests coupled with virgins, because the priesthood is strong in virginity and virginity needs the guidance of priests; when these ranks are consumed, the crowd of those who follow dies with them. Whence it follows generally: And she is oppressed with bitterness; because if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it.

35_marg2584: Her adversaries are become, etc. These things were foretold in Deuteronomy and so fulfilled: because they would not obey God, who had made the nations subject to them, they were rightly made subject to the nations.
35_marg2585: Historically. Her adversaries are become her lords, because the Lord hath spoken through Moses in Deuteronomy, saying: “The Lord will deliver thee to fall before thy enemies, and thou mayest be scattered through all the kingdoms of the earth; thy sons and thy daughters shall be given to another people”; and a little after: “The stranger that liveth with thee shall rise up over thee, and shall be higher; he shall be as the head, and thou shalt be the tail.” But the Lord spoke these things because of Jerusalem’s iniquity, not to make her sin by foretelling it, but to call her back from sin by warning. But because she would not obey God, the prophet laments that all these things have happened by God’s just judgement; therefore the letter He is set first, which is interpreted “these”, as if to say: because of these are the judgements which God foretold long ago through Moses.
35_marg2586: In the moral sense. Her adversaries are become, namely the demons ruling, of whom it is said: “If the spirit of him that hath power ascend upon thee, leave not thy place.” For if the wretched soul had been on guard against the enemies who counsel evil, she would not have let them be her lords. They are enriched against us, namely as the habit of the vices grows strong and increases, so that we cannot flee except by the help of God. But the Lord too is angry, who because of our iniquity hath spoken this vengeance; “who speaketh once, and repeateth not the selfsame thing the second time.” Yet we must not despair or cease from mourning, because only the children, that is, the faint-hearted, not the strong, are taken captive. Before the face of the oppressor: entangled, namely, in many snares, from which yet they are loosed by God’s mercy. For the stronger enemies press on, sometimes as lords defiling the very intention of a good work, sometimes entangling the resisting soul by longer habit of pleasures, according to that of Solomon: “He that nourisheth his servant delicately from his childhood, afterwards shall find him stubborn.” From these we are freed with the more difficulty, the higher and richer they are as they rule.
35_marg2587: Allegorically. Her adversaries are become, namely the heretics, or the pagans, or bad Catholics; they are enriched with eloquence in disputing, though there is a dearth of understanding; whence it is said: “I will send upon them not a famine of bread, nor a thirst of water, but of hearing the word of God.” When this is taken away, the enemies of the Church are raised up as lords and are enriched with the wealth of the Scriptures, for the multitude of our iniquities. Then indeed “dumb dogs, not able to bark”, they cannot defend the faith or give due teaching to those under them; whence the children, who have not perfection of teaching or of life, are led into captivity, having no rulers or defenders, before the face of the oppressor, the enemy namely, visible or invisible, bound by the chains of sins.

35_marg2588: And from the daughter of Sion, etc. The fifth topic, by which we set the several hardships before the eyes; this is to be noted almost everywhere.
35_marg2589: Historically. And from the daughter of Sion, etc. To this sentence Vau is set first, which is interpreted “and”, as if to say: and these things which were set out above are added in vengeance by the just judgement of God. For Jerusalem, besieged, had lost all the comeliness of her beauty outwardly and of her gladness inwardly: her riches taken away, the temple and priesthood profaned, she herself laboured with famine and pestilence, and there was none to help, because her princes are become like rams that find no pastures, their strength dissolved, with fearful heart thinking not of defence but of flight.
35_marg2590: And from the daughter of Sion. The soul, namely, enticed by evil ways, which has lost her beauty, that is, the adornment of the virtues; nor do the princes of the mind help, namely the rational motions, or the defences of the Scriptures, by which she ought to have beaten back her persecutors; but rather, the strength of the virtues being wearied, bound by the bonds of sins, she is driven into the pit of eternal confusion.
35_marg2591: And … is departed. The Church, namely, of which it is said in the Canticle: “Behold thou art fair, O my love.” Beauty departs from her when the faith is corrupted by the madness of the heretics, the faith of which it is said: “Thou hast put on praise and beauty.” Her princes are become, namely the pastors and rulers in the Scriptures, like rams that find not the pastures of life. They are gone away without the strength of the divine word, wherever error drives them, before the face of the pursuer; so that they who neglect to drive the Lord’s flock to the pastures of life go themselves bound to the pastures of death, without the strength of the virtues. For the beauty of the Church is in all the faithful, but most in the priests and those who serve the altar, and in the virgins, who were mentioned above as in affliction.

35_marg2592: Historically. Jerusalem hath remembered. She does not remember her desirable things for comfort, but to multiply her grief, when her people falls in the enemy’s hand; whence Zain is set first, which is interpreted “these”. For this is the perfect vengeance: that she should grieve for the good things lost and, conscious of her prevarication, endure the evils that come upon her; as if to say, this is the divine and perfect vengeance which the giver of the law foretold, namely when she should fall into the hands of the enemies and none should help. Moreover, the enemies have seen her, etc., as we today mock the sabbaths of the Jews when they are recited, because they killed him in whom they ought to have had the true sabbath. And this is the just requital of sins: to fall into the hands of the enemies, to remember continually the days not only of affliction but of prevarication, and from remembrance to gape after the use of desirable things; so that from the affliction a new grief may grow, from the prevarication the sorrow of confusion, from the things lost an incurable longing may burn, from the office of her religion reproach may sting.
35_marg2593: Hath remembered. The soul, though late, remembers her desirable things when she sees herself straitened on every side and her affections rushing into the hands of the devil; and when she, who thought she stood more securely, is struck by divine vengeance, then the deeds of her prevarication come running together, then she remembers her worst affliction, she who had wandered through many vices; not for comfort but to heighten the pain, according to what the wicked will say in hell: “We have erred from the way of truth, and the light of justice hath not shined unto us, and the sun of understanding rose not upon us. We wearied ourselves in the way of iniquity and destruction, and have walked through hard ways. What hath pride profited us? or what advantage hath the boasting of riches brought us? All those things are passed away like a shadow; we are consumed in our wickedness.” The enemies have seen her, etc. The evil spirits draw the leisure of our free time to unlawful thoughts, and so they mock; which canons, monks and all who are free for the ministries of God must greatly beware of, lest their sabbaths not only be reproached by the inward judge but also mocked by the enemies. And if our sabbaths are mocked for our vain thoughts, what is to be thought of those who, when they ought to be free for the Lord, do not fear even to commit shameful deeds? If therefore we wish to be free for God, let us be free for him alone in heart and body; whence: “Be still and see that I am God.”
35_marg2594: Hath remembered. For the Church often sees her people falling into the hands of the enemies, that is, of the demons: one falls through avarice, another through lust, another through the delight of the flesh. For all these and the like the Church continually laments; she remembers all her desirable things, that is, those which are promised us in heaven, from which we both slip away and she is a pilgrim. Our sabbaths too, that is, the feasts, are no less violated by us than they are mocked by the enemies; whence: “Where is their God?” and elsewhere: “My tears have been my bread day and night, whilst it is said to me daily: Where is thy God?”
35_marg2595: Often, handed over for our sins to pagans or heretics or vices, we remember our prevarication; and then the demons mock our sabbaths, when they see us keeping holiday from good things; whence: “They that trouble me will rejoice when I am moved.”

35_marg2596: Heth. Hath grievously sinned. He shows that the cause of so great misery is a single sin, which being kept, all are kept, and being gone, all are let go: this is unbelief; whence: “Hear, ye rebellious and unbelieving.” For out of unbelief they always provoked God, worshipped idols, would not believe in Christ; whence: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin.” Therefore is she become unstable, and not a stone is left upon a stone in her. All that honoured her: the scribes, namely, and Pharisees, who for gain’s sake called the sinning people blessed, and in turn the erring people called them blessed and pillars in the house of the Lord; but now they despise one another, because they trusted flatteries. Sighing, turned backward expresses the bearing of captives, who, as they are led away, look back at their native soil, weeping and groaning.
35_marg2597: Hath grievously sinned. As if to say, the soul is snatched through divers vices for the sin of unbelief, which did not fix her steps upon the rock of the virtues; whence the angels or holy men who before honoured her despise her, so that at last she may groan for her sin and return to God and hear the voice of one warning behind her back; whence Isaias: “Thy ears shall hear the word of one admonishing thee behind thy back.” Whence Mary, turned backward, found Jesus, whom before she sought and did not find. So Jerusalem too, who is mourned here for the sin of unbelief, if she acknowledges and believes, turned backward and groaning in the law, finds him whom she thought dead. But those who are unbelieving and do not look backward even to this day are unstable like Cain, and bear the sign of their confusion, and go towards Babylon, that is, towards confusion.
35_marg2598: Jerusalem hath grievously sinned. The Church, defiled in her members by some heresy, sins the sin of unbelief. And so she wanders unstable, grounded in no solidity of faith, she who before was grounded upon the firm rock. And the peoples who honoured them with various affection, seeing their heresy cast down and trodden underfoot by the Catholics, despise and detest them. But they themselves sigh.

35_marg2600: He bewails her threefold: because she sinned against God, because she did not repent, because after the scourges she would not return to God; whence: because she hath not remembered her end.
35_marg2601: Historically. Her filthiness is on her feet. As if Jerusalem has become unstable and, wearied by a long way, bears filth on her feet; which he bewails more of the inner man than of the outer. The feet of the Synagogue are the teachers of the law, who ought to have led her by the way which is Christ. But these feet are defiled with the filth of crimes. And she hath not remembered her end, that is, Christ, who is “the end of the law unto justice to every one that believeth”. Therefore she is wonderfully cast down; whence Jerusalem cries out in her own voice: behold, O Lord, etc. For from the beginning until here the prophet has lamented; but from here on she herself, humbled and confessing her sin, laments her punishments; which the letter Teth signifies, which is interpreted “good”; whence: “It is good for me, O Lord, that thou hast humbled me.” And she, humbled, no longer waits for the prophet, but with groaning and tears cries out: behold, O Lord. In the manner of rhetoric she makes a complaint with indignation, to move the judge against the enemy and herself to receive mercy; whence she adds: because my enemy is lifted up, namely against thee; she does not lay it to thy justice but to his pride; as if: Behold first my affliction, that thou mayest have mercy, not my crimes. Behold the things for which thou shouldst be angry. Then, because the enemy is lifted up, that thou mayest take vengeance.
35_marg2602: In the moral sense: her filthiness. The soul has filth on her feet, the filth namely of the vices, she who has lost the brightness of the heavenly life and of her former conversation; whence: “Arise, Jerusalem, shake thyself from the dust.” For the soul which is intent on earthly deeds must have filth on her feet, that is, on her affections; whence: “Our soul is humbled down to the dust.” From these the feet must be washed daily, lest there happen what follows: she hath forgotten her end, she is wonderfully cast down, not having, etc. But let the soul say, let the Church say: Behold, O Lord, my affliction; not my sin, that thou mayest condemn, but my affliction, that thou mayest set free; because the enemy is lifted up, that is, laying it to thee, insulting thee, as if thou couldst not set us free; whence David: “Many say to my soul: There is no salvation for him in his God.”
35_marg2603: Her filthiness. The Church bears filth on her feet, because in the misery of this life there is no one who walks without the squalor of the vices, at least on the feet by which the earth is touched. Hence the Lord washed the feet of the disciples and bade us wash one another’s, and said to the apostles: “Shake off the dust from your feet.” And he washed their feet for this, that they might be both beautiful and clean, and so run through the whole world to preach; of whom it is said: “How beautiful are thy steps in shoes, O prince’s daughter!” and elsewhere: “your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace.” But filth on the feet is a reprobate life in the preachers, because they do not remember their end, that is, the judgement to come; whence they are wonderfully cast down in the sight of God, not having the Spirit the comforter, they who ought to comfort others. Turned, therefore, and humbled, let them cry: behold, O Lord, etc.

35_marg2606: Historically. His hand. The Chaldean put out his hands to the holy of holies, into which it was not lawful for any but the priests alone to enter, and once a year and with blood; he carried off the vessels of beauty and profaned the sanctuary. The cause of this is given: because the Lord saw the Gentiles enter into his sanctuary, that is, the Jews living like Gentiles and polluting the sanctuary, which he himself had forbidden; whence it follows: of whom thou gavest commandment, etc. And elsewhere: “He delivered their strength into captivity, and my beauty into the hands of my enemy.”
35_marg2607: His hand. The devil boldly puts out his hand to the soul’s desirable things and carries off the adornments of the virtues, faith, hope, charity, discretion, etc.; which the just judge permits to be done, because he saw the Gentiles, namely wicked suggestions and thoughts and pleasures, enter into the sanctuary of the soul, which ought to have shut the door and prayed to the Father in the chamber. Then chastity is corrupted, abstinence overthrown, and the chief of the cooks tries to overthrow all the walls of the soul, that is, the virtues; and so he leaves the soul stripped of her goods as a vineyard, without a comforter.
35_marg2608: His hand, etc. The old enemy puts out his hand to the Church’s desirable things in her members, defiling faith, cutting off baptism, corrupting doctrine, handling the body and blood of the Lord unworthily, and laying waste the precious vessels, that is, the sheep of Christ, like a wolf. And the cause of so great an evil is given: because the Gentiles, namely those who love the flesh, as it were keeping the foreskin and not having the circumcision of Christ, are made ministers of the altar.

35_marg2609: Historically. All her people. How great a famine the Jews suffered the histories do not pass over, and Josephus especially makes it plain; whence here: all her people sigh, they seek bread to relieve the soul, that is, the bodily life; see, O Lord. Note what it profited the prophet when he lamented for Jerusalem, who did not lament herself; who yet above is brought in lamenting as it were in her nobler members, but now, as if the breath of life had been received, all the people is shown lamenting: see, O Lord, etc. For as a hen warms her eggs and gives them life, so spiritual men warm those under them little by little, by warning or by lamenting, that they may bring them to life along with themselves.
35_marg2610: All her people sigh, they seek bread, the bread of the word of God, the bread that came down from heaven. In the distress of famine the Church seeks this bread from the teachers and does not find it, because they have given all their precious things for food, namely heavenly things for earthly, eternal for perishing, to relieve the soul; because they can relieve it, kindled by countless longings, but not fill it. Hence too the people sigh and seek the bread of God, because the wicked are afflicted and tormented because an abundance of life is not had delightfully as they would wish.
35_marg2611: They have given all their precious things for food. The unhappy soul gives all her precious things for food when she bends the virtues of the mind to passing delight, and strives to relieve herself while she contrives to satisfy divers vices and longings. Whence her people is lamented as sighing and seeking bread, because, though she has given all her precious things for food, the affection of lust is not filled by sight, taste and the other senses. Whence, if perhaps some virtue returns and the soul, refreshed by the Spirit of God, grows strong, rightly with the multitude of the elect she cries out lamenting: see, O Lord, etc.; as if she said: I am become vile to myself, lowly in my own eyes, because the hand of the Lord hath touched me; for Caph is interpreted “hand”. And when the hand of the Lord, by punishing or by relieving punishments or by instructing, has touched the soul or the negligent Church, soon, coming back to herself and groaning, she says: see, O Lord, etc.; as if: consider thy work, how vile it is. The soul which before, delighted with the vices, gloried, being touched by the hand of the Lord, confesses herself vile, she who had been made in the image of her creator.
35_marg2612: The Church is made vile when, as the number of the wicked grows, she seeks not the highest and heavenly things but the lowest and earthly.

35_marg2613: Discipline, or contrition. For what the prophet mourns is discipline for others and contrition of heart, that they may mourn in like manner.
35_marg2614: Historically. O all ye that pass by. It is the mark of the wretched to reckon their own sorrow the greater the less they have tried to understand another’s, and the more they feel their own sorrow the less they allow another’s to be equalled to it. But more truly the remnant that is saved laments such things with contrition of heart, when the sanctuary is destroyed, the temple profaned, the altars overthrown, the light of the candlesticks put out, the books burned, priests and Levites taken captive, virgins and wives defiled by the enemy’s lust, all holy things polluted. For these things and the like the remnant that has been saved not undeservedly mourns, when they see their nation losing earthly goods no less than heavenly. For so God made a vintage of her by just judgement, as he spoke in the law and the prophets.
35_marg2615: O all ye that pass by. The soul weighed down with vices, not wholly blinded, seeing others hastening with longing to the country and walking by the way of virtue, cries out with great grief: O all ye that pass by the way; as if: see with what perils I am troubled, with what tribulations afflicted, to what sufferings I am subject; for the Lord hath made a vintage of me, that is, by just judgement he has taken away the goods of the virtues with which he adorned me as a bride, in the day of his fury, provoked by my evils. You therefore that pass by the way, that is, who despise the present life, tending to the true way which is Christ, see if there be any sorrow like to my sorrow: I have lost heavenly things, I have treasured up wrath for myself in the day of judgement, and weighed down with my evils I cannot hasten with you to the joys of heaven.
35_marg2616: O all ye. Our Sion, whose conversation is in heaven, set in heaven looks on her members on earth and from on high sees what they suffer daily; whence in pity she cries out: O all ye that pass by the way, the saints namely, of whom David says: “Going they went and wept”, etc. These go by the way which is Christ, following his footsteps, turning aside neither to the right hand nor to the left. For, called to the paschal banquet and keeping the paschal vows, they eat the lamb in haste according to the law. The Church sees these walking by the royal way to the country, and, hindered by many cares for her children, she groans and cries: O all ye that pass by the way; not to draw them back from the way, but to warn them to suffer with her: attend with the mind and see with the gaze of charity if there be any sorrow like to my sorrow. “A woman, when she is in labour, hath sorrow”; whence the Apostle: “My little children, of whom I am in labour again.” For the Church, who brings forth and begets and nourishes and suckles, is saddened for all; whence: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” So too the Church suckles the tender, calls back those turned away, waits for the slow, chastens the headlong that they may look ahead, lest the enemy find any outside the camp while she herself hastens to the country in ordered ranks; whence: “Who is she that goeth up by the desert, as the morning rising?” To those, therefore, going up or passing by it is said by the more excellent members: O all ye that pass by; because there are some things which I grieve for on their account, others which I endure from those within or without; I am kept from the country, I linger in exile. Attend therefore: though unwearied devotion carries us towards the prize, see my sorrow. I wished to bring up my children and to bring them out of the misery of exile and lead them to the joys of heaven; but many go astray, many provoke, many languish, few are they who care to come. “I became all things to all men, that I might save all”; I mourn for all and burn for all. See therefore if there be any sorrow like to my sorrow; stretch therefore the eye of the mind to the last day of judgement, and see that the Lord hath made a vintage, that is, will make a vintage of me in the day of his fury, of which it is said: “Rebuke me not, O Lord, in thy indignation”; as the Lord spoke, in the day of his fury, when he will render to every man according to his works.

35_marg2618: Historically. From above he hath sent, etc.: vengeance from on high, of which it is said in Job: “The fire of God fell from heaven”, etc. He hath sent fire, namely the powers of the air, into my bones, that is, to afflict the strong within and without, and so to teach those who would not listen to God when he spoke gently; whence he adds: and hath chastised me. He hath spread a net for my feet, that I might not go after my wills and vain longings to the end of life; he hath turned me to go through straits and tribulations. He hath made me desolate: the Jews are made desolate until the end of the world, and wasted with sorrow.
35_marg2619: From above he hath sent. When the soul is corrected by the Lord for her sins, coming back to herself she is pricked to her health, and bears witness that fire has come from the Lord into her bones, that is, into the marrow of her thoughts; whence she is chastised and taught by God; and because she feels the nets of God’s teaching spread before her feet, she is turned back, she abstains from unlawful things, she turns the riot of pleasure and lust into tears; and wasted with sorrow she laments the more strongly, and receives no comfort of the present life, the more truly she sees that she has gone astray in them through vain longings.
35_marg2620: From above he hath sent fire. Those who have believed, from the Jews or the Gentiles, and have been made one Church, rightly say: from above he hath sent fire, that is, the Holy Spirit, by whom the strengths of the virtues are made firm and the Church is taught by God not to serve idols any more nor seek the delights of the world; which the letter Mem signifies, which is interpreted “out of the very gifts”, namely of the Holy Spirit, by which the Church, giving thanks, says that she is taught to love chastely and fear chastely, and by which she blushes for the vices she had served. He hath spread a net, namely of preaching, that I might not go after the vanities of errors and lusts. He hath turned me back, that I might go after him and not perish. This net was entrusted to the apostles, to draw fishes out of the sea of this world. For my feet; whence: “I have restrained my feet from every evil way.” He hath made me desolate of the present goods which before were my comforts. Wasted with sorrow all the day long, namely with sorrow for present tribulations and love of the goods to come.

35_marg2621: Historically: Hath watched, etc. For the yoke of iniquity to sleep is to rest secure and unpunished in the sluggishness of wickedness; but it watches in the hand of the Lord; whence Jeremias: “I see a rod watching”; to whom the Lord: “I will watch over my word to perform it.” For while we are sluggish our sins lie hidden, but in the hand of the Lord they watch, while they accuse us for the vengeance of just requital; whence: “The voice of thy brother’s blood crieth to me from the earth.” They are folded together, as a weight to press down, and put upon my neck: in place of a golden collar she is bound round with the cord of iniquity; whence each one is bound fast with the cords of his own sins. So she is given into the hands of sinners, and she will not be able to rise until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in; which Nun signifies, which is interpreted “everlasting”. For her everlasting yoke is perpetual captivity.
35_marg2622: In the moral sense. Hath watched. The yoke of the soul which submits itself to vices and crimes watches in the hand of the Lord, unless by repenting daily she sets it before her eyes; whence: “My sin is always before me.” For David wished to watch and wash away his sins with weeping, lest their yoke should watch in the hands of the Lord; whence: “Turn away thy face from my sins”; as if: I do not wish them to watch in thy hand, but that I may watch against my sins and cleanse them with weeping, lest thou put my iniquities, folded together, upon my neck, and deliver me into a hand out of which I shall not be able to rise.
35_marg2623: Allegorically. Hath watched. When the Church is subjected to temptations of whatever kind, the yoke of her iniquity watches in the hand of the Lord, and she is subjected to enemies visible as well as invisible, having lost the necklaces which the bridegroom had given her for adornment; whence, groaning, she says: they are folded together and put upon my neck; whence Isaias says that because the daughters of Sion walked with stretched-out necks, all their ornaments were to be taken away, and among the rest the collars and necklaces. Collars hanging on the breast show understanding to the mind. Necklaces signify all the ornaments; these lost, churchmen walk with womanish affection with stretched-out necks and speak with winks of the eyes, clapping with their hands and feet that they may walk with measured step, following the glory of the world. Rightly therefore is she pressed down by the yoke of iniquities who is stripped of such great ornaments of the virtues; whence the iniquities folded together with an unbreakable cord are lamented, and put upon her neck, by which some members are strangled, as we read that Judas hanged himself with a noose; whence she adds: my strength is weakened; because the wicked are handed over to eternal destruction, “where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched”. For as the verse above, which is headed Mem, that is, “out of the very things”, namely those the Lord sent from heaven, turned her to penance, so out of the yoke of her iniquities Nun, which is interpreted “everlasting”, drove her into destruction, that by God’s just judgement, according to her impenitent heart, she may incur everlasting punishment. Not that the Church, predestined to life, is handed over to these punishments; but what happens to her members she reckons to herself and laments.
35_marg2624: My strength is weakened, etc. The sixth topic of complaint: that she, when she was expecting good from the Lord, fell into the greatest miseries.

35_marg2625: Historically. Hath taken away all my mighty men. These things happened more fully in the last captivity, under whose oppression neither prophets nor priests remained. For in the Babylonian captivity they had Daniel and Ezechiel and many comforters; but in this all the mighty men were taken away; which Samech signifies, which is interpreted “help”. Whence Isaias: “I will take away from Jerusalem the valiant and the strong, the whole strength of bread and the whole strength of water, the prince and the captain over fifty, and the skilful in eloquent speech”, etc. Hence we read that the angels themselves cried out in the gates of Jerusalem: “Let us go out from these seats.”
35_marg2626: Hath taken away, etc. The senses of the virtues, which the soul feels to be captive in her; whence the Lord brings against her the time of vengeance when he takes away the divine help; and that being taken away, the enemy leads her captive into the confusion of error, and while he makes her forget the teaching of the preachers, he destroys the chosen strivings of the mind, that he may the more easily possess her, stripped of the virtues, as in a strange land, lest by remembering sound doctrine and amending her life she return to her former state.
35_marg2627: Hath taken away, etc. The spiritual Jerusalem, as often as she is shaken by tribulations of whatever kind, as often as by persecutions, or is attacked by heretic enemies, rightly laments, saying: The Lord hath taken away all my mighty men. For often in the whole world few mighty men have remained who would defend the cause of the faith with sound doctrine. He hath called against me the time, as sins demanded. The Lord brings the time of vengeance to destroy her chosen men, because there is none to defend or set himself as a wall for the house of Israel.

35_marg2628: Historically. The Lord hath trodden the winepress, etc. The winepress signifies vengeance and the punishments of sins; whence Isaias: “Why then is thy apparel red?” etc.; he brings in the Lord answering the angels who ask: “I have trodden the winepress alone”, etc., that namely in which punishments are trodden out for the wicked and rewards for the good. This the Lord alone trod, because he had no helper; for neither angel nor archangel took a human body, that dying for us he might tread down and crush the strength of our adversary. This winepress the Lord trod in his passion for the virgin daughter of Juda, that he might pour out rewards for believers, and for the unbelieving and those who crucified him the punishments of perpetual captivity and eternal damnation. The prophet, therefore, seeing the hardness of the Jews, laments that the Lord hath trodden the winepress for the daughter of Juda; for what the Lord suffered for her remedy she turned for herself into the torment of the last captivity and of eternal damnation; whence he brings in the person of the Synagogue herself weeping: Therefore do I weep, etc. The comforter is far, etc. This we often prove if we look at the faithlessness and hardness of the Jews. And it is said by metaphor: the Lord hath trodden the winepress, etc. By metaphor: the Lord brought his vineyard out of Egypt and planted it in the land of promise, and it remained long barren and unfruitful, according to that: “I looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it hath brought forth wild grapes.” Therefore the Lord trod the winepress: the wine he kept for himself; the husks of the swine he pressed with perpetual captivity.

35_marg2629: The Lord hath trodden the winepress. The Lord treads the winepress for the barren soul, empty of virtues and works, when he afflicts her as barren and idle with a fitting punishment; whence she says: Therefore do I weep, etc.; because she feels she has lost the comforter and, impenitent, is rushing to where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, where a great weeping of the soul is described, that she may know that after the vain gladness of this world all comfort will fail her. There the children will be lost, because the fruit of evil works will be scattered; the enemy alone will prevail.
35_marg2630: The Lord hath trodden the winepress, etc. When, namely, by his passion he made the powers of the air subject to the Church. And she is truly the virgin daughter of Juda, because “the law shall come forth from Sion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem”; for her the Lord trod the winepress, that is, the yoke of oppression, that she might be free. But because, as the Lord trod, there had been much dregs, therefore the prophet says lamenting: my eyes run down with water. And so Ain is put between, which is interpreted “fountain” or “eye”. For when the press of the cross pressed, a fountain flowed from the side of Christ; whence: “And immediately there came out blood and water.” By this fountain the bride is bought and washed, to be joined to the bridegroom’s embraces; with this she is dowered, that she may rejoice, that she may cleave to the bridegroom alone, love him alone who loved her so much. And because Ain is also interpreted “eye”, not undeservedly from this fountain the eye, made drunk, runs down with the water of tears; whence: “My eyes have sent forth springs of water”, etc. The comforter is far, etc. As often as the Church is afflicted with tribulations, as often as she is left desolate of the help of God, she runs back to tears as to her accustomed weapons; but when, as the teacher warns outwardly, the Paraclete is not present to instruct and teach within, therefore her children become desolate and the enemy prevails. Whoever of the teachers, therefore, sees the Church entrusted to him turned too little, let him draw from the fountain of love to bring forth tears, until he brings back the comforter, the Paraclete who turns her; otherwise, as the enemy prevails, her children become desolate, those namely not yet weaned, not yet brought to the perfect man.

35_interl11385: the earthly, or the Church, or the soul
35_interl11393: vainglory, while we credit good things to ourselves, and by that very vanity, as with menstrual blood, we defile whatever we touch
35_marg2631: Sion hath spread forth, etc. It signifies the pain as of one in labour; whence elsewhere: “As he that swimmeth spreadeth forth his hands to swim”, so Sion too in her straits; and Isaias says: “Anguish hath taken hold of me, as the anguish of a woman in labour.” It is the anguish of the heart, which is expressed in the spreading of the hands more than in the crying of the mouth; whence Phe is written first, which is interpreted “of the mouth”; because when Sion spreads forth her hands in her straits, she signifies that she cannot express with her mouth what she suffers in her heart, since she is without a comforter. Whence: “Depart from me, I will weep bitterly: labour not to comfort me”, etc. The Lord hath commanded against Jacob: by the just judgement of God both the Chaldeans and the Romans were brought on; for nation does not rise against nation except at the Lord’s command. As a menstruous woman: as a woman is abominable while she suffers her courses, so are the Jews held everywhere on earth.
35_marg2632: Hath spread forth, etc. The soul which had been a mirror of God and a supplanter of vices, when for her iniquity she is handed over to the spirits of wickedness, seeks a comforter outwardly in vain, she who has lost spiritual comfort inwardly. Rightly therefore the Lord hath commanded against Jacob, etc., that is, against the soul once supplanting vices, now glorying in the name alone. Whence spiritual enemies besiege her round about, that she cannot escape; and often, seeing herself hemmed in, she spreads forth her hands in the straits of her thoughts, and she has no voice of the mouth nor any excuse of speech, because she is defiled with menstrual blood, that is, stained with bloody works, from which she will never be freed without the comforter; since the prophet too bears witness that “all our justices are as the rag of a menstruous woman” before him.
35_marg2633: Sion hath spread forth her hands, etc. As often as the Church is hemmed in by the army of the heretics, the Lord commands against Jacob, namely the Church, which ought to supplant vices, armies of enemies; because she has lost the Holy Spirit, the comforter and teacher, without whom none is taught the faith, none relieved from the vices. Therefore she spreads forth her hands amid pains and pressures, and she has no voice of the mouth worthy to overcome the enemies’ doctrines and defend her own; whence she often becomes defiled with the foulness of fleshly works and the blood of fleshly longings among the enemies, by whom she is attacked within and without. Whence: “Woe to them that are with child, and that give suck in those days.”

35_marg2634: The Lord is just, etc. Sade, which is set first and is interpreted “of justice”, signifies that the Lord’s justices are right, as is well shown by these words. The Lord is just, because I have provoked his mouth to wrath; because I have justly borne the judgement of his mouth; whence I have not delayed to confess that the Lord is just. And it is to be noted that above she invited those passing by the way, as fewer, but now Jerusalem, or the prophet, invites all in common to consider her sorrow, that theirs may be one suffering whose condition of nature is one. For above she mourns the virgins in affliction and the children captive; now also the stronger young men and the virgins captive; and the more the evil is heaped up, the more the mourning is multiplied. Hear therefore, all ye people, and see my sorrow. For these things are discerned with a great gaze and keen consideration.
35_marg2635: The Lord is just, etc. The soul which is chastised by the judgement of his mouth rightly confesses that the Lord is just, because by wicked longings she provokes the mouth of the Lord to wrath, so that he speaks a hard sentence against her; because “the Lord is just in all his ways”. Whence, covered with her confusion, she does not dare lift her eye to the angry judge, but invites all to see and hear her sorrow. For such is the affection of human nature, that we seek sharers of our sorrow and joy, by whose sharing we may bear it more easily; whence: “Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep.” The soul therefore seeks many intercessors, because she fears even to lift her eyes to the judge whom she has offended. My virgins and my young men are gone, namely when she sees her pure thoughts and stronger affections, as it were the offspring and hope of her womb, perishing as the enemy lays waste, and loses the hope of a generation to come.
35_marg2636: Paschasius. The Lord is just, etc. The Church, which above bore the judgement of his mouth, who in the holy Scriptures provoked the Lord’s mouth to wrath, has learned to confess: The Lord is just, etc. For nothing is done on earth without a cause, and in God’s great commonwealth nothing is done without the providence of God. Because she provoked his mouth to wrath: not that God has human members, but as human affections are ascribed to him figuratively, so are members too. By the mouth is signified the Word begotten from the mouth of the Father; as if she said: by my crimes I have provoked just judgement, and compelled him who is merciful by nature to pass a hard sentence against me. Hear therefore, all ye people, etc. She weighs her calamity, twofold and unspeakable. Whence she invites all to grieve with her, that by the compassion of many her anguish may become lighter. The virgins, of whom it is said: “For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” The young men, whom mother Church begets again in the font of baptism. These, when they are either corrupted by heretical wickedness or defiled by vices, are carried captive, not in place but in mind, into Babylon, that is, into confusion. For “he who is joined to a harlot is made one body” with her. See: so great a mourning and so great a sorrow is heaped up that it is hardly believed it can be seen or understood by all.

35_marg2637: The eleventh topic of indignation: for it was done by those who ought to forbid it if others did it.
35_marg2638: Historically. I called for my friends. Coph is interpreted “calling”; whence he at once adds: I called for my friends, the Egyptians, on whose friendship and help the Jews relied. But they deceived me, because at the time of the first and the last captivity they gave no help; whence Isaias: “And the land of Juda shall be a terror to Egypt”, etc. And rightly were they deceived, because they hoped more in Egypt than in God. My priests, etc.: no one doubts that these things happened under the Romans.
35_marg2639: I called for my friends, the sweet affections of the flesh; but they too deceive the soul that is intent on them. And because in her the royal priesthood has perished and the aged counsel of ripeness, enticed by vain longings she labours to relieve the lust of the flesh. Egypt helps in vain, because “the world passeth away, and the concupiscence thereof”, which is a staff of reed that pierces the hands of him who leans on it.
35_marg2640: I called for my friends. The Church often calls as friends those whom she thinks companions in the faith; but they deceive her who corrupt the faith, either by lying hidden within or by breaking out into open heresy. Bad Catholics too, set in places of power, in whom the Church often trusts as friends, often deceive her; and what is worse, they rage more cruelly then, when the priests and ancients have pined away with famine of the word of God; who, following the gains of the fleshly life, seek the food of the animal life rather than the heavenly food from Solomon’s litter, or the gospel dinner, or the banquet of wisdom, to which the calling of all is marked in the letter Coph.
35_interl11417: of the head, that is, of the mind
35_marg2641: The fifteenth topic of complaint, or rather the fifth, because there she sets out the hardships one by one, that he may as it were see the things themselves and come down to mercy.
35_marg2642: Historically. Behold, O Lord, etc. Sometimes Jerusalem is confounded with shame, sometimes, trusting in mercy, she is lifted up; whence she says: Behold, O Lord, for I am in distress; that her torment may bend the kind judge to mercy, her shame to pardon. My bowels are troubled, as of one in labour. I am full: she signifies that she is not touched in part, but full of the bitterness of pain and sorrow. My heart is turned by the weight of tribulation. The sword of the persecutor kills me abroad, and at home there is death alike, for the bitterness of tribulation.
35_marg2643: The soul, vexed with various pains, groans that her bowels, that is, her mind, are troubled. Whence: “The spirit of a man is the lamp of the Lord, which searcheth all the hidden things of the bowels”, that is, of the mind. Well therefore is this groaning of the head, for the mind is signified by the head; whence elsewhere Jeremias says: “My bowels, my bowels are in pain”, and explaining it he adds: “the senses of my heart are troubled.” For the bowels signify the mind, because as food and offspring are conceived in the bowels, so thoughts in the mind. For the faithful soul, wearied by temptations, shows herself worn down by temptations within and without: without by persecutions, within by pains. For when we are worn down by scourges outwardly, within we are wearied by the suggestions of the flesh. Whence she adds: abroad the sword destroyeth, and at home there is death alike.
35_marg2644: Behold, O Lord, etc. Res is interpreted “of the head”. For the troubling of the bowels or the turning of the heart is the groaning of the mind, which is signified in the head. Rightly therefore is it called the troubling of the head when the Church is filled with bitterness at the falls of her own, she who daily lays out her pain and tribulation to the most merciful judge. The belly is the receptacle of all foods, in which they are digested; by it are understood those who do not fail to chew over and store up within the bread that came down from heaven, as clean animals receive this food by faith and digest it by charity and meditation on the law of God; whence Isaias: “From thy fear, O Lord, we have conceived, and brought forth the spirit of salvation.” These bowels the Church laments as troubled when she is dashed by various temptations and weighed down within and without. My heart is turned, she, namely, who did not put the seal of God upon her heart; whence: “Put me as a seal upon thy heart.” For if she had been sealed, the enemy would not have overturned her. She is struck, therefore, abroad by the sword of the persecutors, within by the teaching of the heretics or by wickedness of manners, which are more bitter than gall.

35_marg2645: The second topic of indignation: for it shows to whom the matter chiefly belongs, that is, to God himself, whom the enemies despise in his own; whence: Let all their evil be present, etc.
35_marg2646: Historically. They have heard, etc. No one doubts that the nations round about Jerusalem mocked at her captivities. For they rejoiced that she was forsaken by the help of God, she whom they envied as she held out amid so many storms. That thou hast done it: she lays it to the judgement of God, by whom she knows all things are ordered. Thou hast brought a day of consolation: these are the words of the prophet, who, because he foresaw the consolation to come most surely, announced it as past, for the consolation of the captive people. He speaks in the manner of the rhetoricians, who win the judge over to themselves and stir him up against their adversaries.
35_marg2647: They have heard. The soul laments that the enemies have heard the evils she endures, and there is none to comfort her. To the anxious soul it is an increase of pain that he in whom she hopes delays his help. Here too she grieves unspeakably that the invisible enemies, who before flattered her, mock her. And the conscience accuses her, insulting more heavily, and the vices which before seemed sweet are laid open as bitter; and those who before seemed friends, who ought to have suffered with her, if perhaps they know our crimes, mock as if enemies. Whence David: “They that watched my soul have consulted together.” But the soul has teeth, that is, virtues, thoughts, which know how to divide prosperity from adversity and to seek the comforting Spirit and to hope in God’s mercy; whence she adds: thou hast brought a day of consolation, etc. For the strong soul knows that after straits pardon is given to the penitent and punishments are repaid to those who insult.
35_marg2648: They have heard, etc. The Church laments her own evils and those of her own; whence the letter Sin is set first, which means “of the teeth”. This is the weeping of the teeth, of which we read in the Canticle: “Thy teeth are as flocks of sheep that are shorn”, etc. These are they who do not need the milk of infancy but eat solid bread; whence it was said to Peter: “Kill and eat”; as if: I have set before thee to eat not bread only, but creeping things. For such men, by the keenness of their teaching, know how to kill vice and bring creeping things over into the body of Christ. But the teeth have different offices: some divide, some grind, some form sounds; so too the mystical teeth. Some are as flocks of shorn sheep, who, stripped of the old, serve their young the milk of teaching and the clothing of the virtues. Others, whiter than milk, adorned with the beauty of their office, serve the word with the highest subtlety; whence the Apostle: “Strong meat is for the perfect, for them who have their senses exercised.” They have heard that I sigh. The enemies heard the bride weeping, who feels the bridegroom absent; who, though he is always present by his majesty, yet allows the bride to be shaken by temptations, that she may always be watchful and fearful lest she accept the suggestion of the corrupter. They have heard that I sigh, which they always wished, which they never suspected. There is none to comfort me, because “the holy spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful”, and daily my evil is multiplied. The demons are the Church’s enemies, and the heretics, and false Christians. That thou hast done it; whence: “I the Lord, making peace and creating evil”, that is, permitting it by just judgement. Thou hast brought a day of consolation: this fits the Church better, because after the last captivity no consolation remains for the Jews; in the day of judgement the Lord will give consolation to the good and punishments to the wicked.

35_marg2649: Historically. Let all their evil be present. Thau is interpreted “signs”, in the plural, because by this sign is shown that to which many things that signify are referred; whence in Ezechiel: “Mark Thau upon the foreheads of the men that sigh”, etc. In this the Lord’s cross is signed, as its very shape bears witness; and as among the Greeks Omega is the last, so among the Hebrews is Thau. Whence the Lord says: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end.” In like manner, therefore, Thau signifies the cross with which the foreheads are signed, that they may not be slain by the slayers. For Thau is the sign of the cross, nay, almost the cross itself; whence it was set on the foreheads of those who grieved; but then it was the sign of the cross to come, now it is the cross itself. Moreover, Thau is the end of the Hebrew letters, which are as many as the books of the Old Testament, of which they are the signs. For as Thau is the end of all the letters, so of those books the end is the cross of Christ, who “is the end of the law unto justice”; and all those signs of the books are sacraments of the Lord’s incarnation and our redemption. Therefore Thau is rightly interpreted “signs”, that through these same signs this one thing may be announced to which all signs are referred; and also the signs of the lamentations, in which the signs of the judgements of God meet. It is a worthy end that to those who sigh and grieve, on whose foreheads the cross of Christ is signed, the wages of their labours should be repaid by the Lord, and to those who troubled them and would not acknowledge the signs of so great a work a worthy vengeance should be rendered. Hence it is said: Let all their evil be present; and according to the letter it was so done: read the law and the prophets and you will find everything fulfilled.
35_marg2650: Let all their evil be present, etc. The soul, laid open in the sight of God, asks: Let all their evil be present, namely what they press upon her without and within. Let it come in before thee, that I may escape by thy help, who do not trust in myself. Make vintage of them, of all their deceits, lest they take my fruit from me. As thou hast made vintage of me, when in thy anger thou didst withdraw thy gifts, for all my iniquities; wherefore thou art just, O God, and thy judgement is right. And these are the signs for whose sake all the miracles of signs were done. Whence: “Thou hast given a warning to them that fear thee, that they may flee from before the bow, that thy beloved may be delivered.” But those who would not take heed will fall into what the Scriptures threaten. Whence: “Raise up thy fury, and pour out thy wrath; hasten the time, and remember the end”; as if: lest the saints be always afflicted, let each receive what he has done; and change the wonders, the things signified for those that signify. Therefore at the end of this lamentation he has set the letter Thau, that is, signs, and in tearful verses, prophesying, has fulfilled the things to come.
35_marg2651: Paschasius. Let all their evil be present: as if: why, O Lord, dost thou not avenge our blood? and “Revenge, O Lord, the blood of thy servants which hath been shed.” Make vintage of them, etc. This will be fulfilled in the judgement, when the wicked will receive what they deserve. But the wicked here take away temporal things; in the future they will lose eternal ones; and as they oppressed the saints by God’s permission, so by God’s oppressing they will bear eternal punishments; fearing which, the Church adds: for my sighs are many, etc.

35_marg2653: Historically. To the first several stanzas of three lines in Sapphic metre I have given the several letters with their interpretations; not that the prophet strove to play with worldly elegance or metre, but worldly wisdom of its own accord serves the divine. But because there are twenty-two Hebrew letters, with which everything that is said begins and ends, it pleased him to begin as many openings of verses with those same letters, so that both the discipline of poetry might serve and the divine mysteries might shine. But because it is long to insert and expound the several letters with their interpretations in the several stanzas, I have decided to note their connections at the beginning of the second alphabet, and to leave it to the reader’s judgement how to render the meaning of each letter to its verses. The first connection is of four letters, Aleph, Beth, Ghimel, Daleth, that is, “teaching, house, fullness, of the boards”; of which, if the two outer ones are joined, they will make “the teaching of the boards”, namely those on which the law of God was written by his finger; and “the fullness of the house”. For from the teaching of the books or of the boards the fullness of the house of God is made. And if you join Ghimel and Daleth, the sense will be that the fullness of the boards, that is, of the Scriptures, is the teaching of the house, namely of God. And since we read that the house of Solomon was boarded within, by the boards we can understand those by the breadth of whose charity the higher parts of the house, joined together, are adorned; whose teaching is the fullness of the whole house, which is born from the fountain of the fear of the Lord, that one may come to the summit of God’s wisdom. Whence Isaias: “From thy fear, O Lord, we have conceived, and brought forth the spirit of salvation.” The second connection is He, Vau, Zain, Heth, that is, “this, and, these, life”. If you join the two outer and the two middle ones, this meaning will come out: “And these things” which we have set out, namely, are necessary “in this life”: the knowledge, namely, of the Scriptures, by which Christ is known in this life and the everlasting one is prepared. This is the book in which are contained lamentations, and a canticle, and woe. For we must lament for sins and for the putting off of good, so that at last, glad in God, we may sing canticles and not incur everlasting woe; and for the present, this is the life of those who are weaned from infancy into the perfect man. The third connection is Teth, Jod, that is, “a good beginning”, in which, with teaching, we conceive from the fear of God the institutes of lamenting, until we come to the spirit of salvation. Whence: “Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted.” So one comes to the canticles of the heavenly life if a good beginning of life is set first; then “God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes”. There follows, in the middle of the seven, the connection Caph, Lamed, that is, “the hand of the heart”, or “of discipline”: the hand, that it may be stretched out to works of charity; of the heart, understand mourning, or the meditation of discipline, that all things may be clean to us. Which the fifth section of the letters shows, which is Mem, Nun, Samech, that is, “out of them everlasting help”; which is so plain that it needs no exposition. From the two middle ones the higher are embraced as much as the lower are reckoned up. Whence the sixth connection follows, Ain, Phe, Sade, that is, “the fountain” or “eye of the mouth of justice”; because from the groaning of the heart a fountain of piety flows forth and the eye is enlightened by which God is seen. Whence: “Blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God.” And by the hand and the speech of the mouth the riches of divine justice are laid up in heaven; whence he laid up riches in heaven with mouth and hand, which riches are understood as the justices of a perfect life; whence: “His justice remaineth for ever and ever.” There follows the last and seventh connection, Coph, Res, Sin, Thau, which is interpreted “the calling of the head, the signs of the teeth”. By the teeth the articulate voice is understood, because the letters which have been set out are the signs of all the words of the holy Scriptures; and the calling of the head, that is, of Christ, through whom one comes to the Father. Nor is there any doubt that the Holy Spirit mystically set these meanings in a seven; whence the middle one fitly refers to each set of three.
35_marg2654: Historically. How, etc. It is to be noted that the three alphabets in Sapphic metre have one beginning and one cry, full of grief, wonder and amazement; whence it is to be noted with how great feeling, how great charity the holy fathers make all men’s causes their own, and with how many tears they wash away others’ laughter. Whence Jeremias so often sets a tearful beginning: How doth she sit, How hath he covered, How is it darkened; as if: so unforeseen, so unhoped, he hath covered with obscurity her whom he had chosen out of all nations and glorified. There is a good obscurity, of which it is said: “Moses went to the dark cloud wherein God was”, and elsewhere: “Darkness was under his feet.” But Sion is covered with the obscurity of the whirlwind and of grief, and is cast down from heaven, from the height of glory, from the throne of the kingdom, from the protection of God. And because she would not keep the day of the Lord, which Abraham saw and was glad, she ran into the day of the Lord’s fury.
35_marg2655: How hath he covered, etc. The soul had the light of knowledge and the mirror of divine contemplation, and her name was written in heaven before she sinned; but cast down by sin she is prostituted on the earth and defiled with vices, and she has forsaken the feet of the Lord, that is, the footsteps of his precepts, though she was the temple in which God would dwell and walk. Therefore in the day of the Lord’s fury she is trodden down by enemies, and the Lord does not remember her. Because she would not stand in the day of the Lord and in the light, he handed her over in the day of his fury. Whence elsewhere: “Cursed be the day wherein I was born; let not the day in which my mother bore me be blessed”; in which, namely, the soul fell from heaven and, taking the members of Christ, made them the members of a harlot, that is, of Babylon. And therefore the Lord does not remember, but avenges his injury.
35_marg2656: How hath he covered, etc. The mystical Sion is covered with the obscurity of sin and error and ignorance, she who before was enriched with such great gifts by her bridegroom. We see the glorious land of Israel cast down from heaven when she clings to earthly deeds, whose true conversation is in heaven; but she is cast off by God’s just judgement, and the Lord hath not remembered his footstool. For although Sion was the most beautiful dwelling of God, with angels ministering, honoured by the protection of God, brought up with many miracles and divine comforts, so that she was rightly called the footstool of God because of the state of divine worship, yet the Church is proclaimed more glorious. Whence Moses saw the Lord of Israel, “and under his feet as it were a work of sapphire stone, and as the heaven when clear.” This is the heaven of which it is said: “The heavens shew forth the glory of God.”
