35_marg2657: Historically. Hath cast down headlong, etc. It is plain that all these things happened to the Jews. The Lord is said to have done all these things of old, not that he compelled Jerusalem to sin, but that by just judgement he punished her when she sinned, and allowed her to be punished. The beautiful things of Jacob: the famous temple, the worship of the ceremonies and the like. But the Lord in anger cast them all down headlong, that you might understand that the Lord kept these things not for their sake, but for men’s sake. But the Jews, boasting of these things, gloried, and wallowed in their crimes. It is only to be known that all these things were more fully fulfilled under the Romans; for all those things of the law were as it were a great prophecy, and when the truth came all were fulfilled. Therefore all were cast down headlong, destroyed, cast out and profaned, and they did not come, that they might seem to prophesy things to come.
35_marg2658: The Lord hath cast down headlong, etc. The Lord casts down the soul’s beautiful things and does not spare when she commits fornication with wicked longings, having left the love of the bridegroom, to whom it had been said: “Forget thy people and thy father’s house, and the king shall greatly desire thy beauty.” He hath destroyed the strong holds when faith grows weak and cannot bear the temptations that are brought upon it, because she has lost the comeliness and beauty in which the bridegroom delighted; so the walls of the virtues, which held off the violence of the enemies, are destroyed. She is cast down from heaven to the earth because she has violated the wedlock of chaste love and prostituted herself to the filth of the vices; to her, forsaken, it is said: “Earth thou art, and into earth thou shalt return.” He hath made the kingdom unclean and the princes thereof, namely her who had been the temple of God, with her senses, which rule her wickedly; he hath brought her down to the ground; she has lost the kingdom and the princedom to which she had been anointed through baptism.
35_marg2659: The Lord hath cast down headlong, etc. These things are rightly referred to the Church when the people sins; because “if God hath not spared the natural branches, neither will he spare us”, who have been cut from the wild olive; and if he despised their offices, how much more are ours made unclean when mind and conscience are defiled. And the Church is beautiful; whence: “The queen stood on thy right hand”; and elsewhere: “Thou art beautiful, O my love, and comely”, etc. But when many sin, the Lord has cast down her beautiful ones, who of old strove manfully, and they are handed over to the enemies. And for God to cast down is by just judgement to leave each one to the desires of his heart. And he destroys when he withdraws the help of his grace. The Church’s strong holds are destroyed when the worshippers of God are stripped of God’s help and depraved by pleasures. And because they themselves understand too little that they are destroyed and scattered, the choir of the saints laments that their beauty and strength have perished. For the Church of Christ is Jerusalem, “which is built as a city”, and “as the tower of David, with bulwarks: a thousand bucklers hang upon it, all the armour of valiant men.” But when the walls, that is, the pastors and teachers, are destroyed, the enemy enters the city and lays it waste. Whence it follows: he hath brought her down to the ground, namely when she is taken up with earthly deeds and vices. Nor is there any to hold her up, either by words of teaching or by examples of works. Therefore the divine vengeance follows: he hath made the kingdom unclean, and the princes thereof. And God makes unclean when he justly shows them unclean who ought to have shown and kept themselves and others chaste and spotless before God, who had been made a royal priesthood. Whence the fault of the priests is the ruin of the people.

35_marg2660: Historically. He hath broken. In his fierce anger he broke the horn of Israel when he destroyed the kingdom of the Jews. He drew back his right hand when he withdrew his defence as the enemies pressed on, and gave their land into the enemy’s hand, when the vices of the enemies consumed everything like a devouring flame.
35_marg2661: He hath broken. The soul is said to have her horns, of which it is said: “I will break all the horns of sinners, and the horns of the just shall be exalted.” For the horns of souls are the strong defences of the virtues, with which she strikes back every adversity and tosses it into the air and scatters it like hay or dust. For horns are not born with animals, yet the cause of their growing is in them; nor is the soul armed with virtues by the prompting of nature, but filled with them by the gift of God; though she herself had before, by nature, the grace of conceiving and the power of nourishing; but she lost both herself and the freedom of nature, and therefore the horns which are born from the origin of sin are broken. Other horns grow and are exalted by the dew of divine grace; but here they are opposed to one another. Whence the Lord broke all the horns of fleshly Israel, that they might no longer lift themselves up. And the prophet weeps, not because they are broken, but because with them the soul is crushed in the fury of God, of which it is said: “O Lord, rebuke me not in thy indignation.” And the Lord draws in and turns away his hand from before the enemy who pursues the soul, because she first exposed herself to the enemies and received the adulterer; because she went out with Dina to see the daughters of this world, she was deflowered by the devil and made one body with him; and therefore the Lord turns away his hand and withdraws his help, because she first exposed herself to the corrupter. For this cause too he sent the Jews into exile, because they were lepers, not with a passing leprosy but an abiding one; which Moses signified when he stretched out the hand that had been leprous, and it was clean when he drew it back into his bosom. Whence David: “Why dost thou turn away thy hand, and thy right hand?” The outstretched hand signified that the Jews had gone out from God and were stretched out to wicked works, and therefore covered with leprosy; but called back in mercy, they were made clean, like the hand drawn back into the bosom. Whence David, seeing their captivity beyond recall and the indignation of God, says: Why dost thou turn away thy hand and thy right hand? as if: while thou turnest away thy hand, unless thou put it back into thy bosom, they, stretched out among the nations, are unclean and lepers. In like manner the soul that goes out from the bosom of God to the longings of the world will be defiled. For the Lord warms and protects those whom he carries in his bosom, or otherwise overshadows them; but of those who have gone out, hear what follows: he hath kindled in Jacob as it were a flaming fire devouring round about. For the soul left to the unclean spirits is kindled, harried, devoured by the flames of the lusts, until she is called back into his bosom. This is the Babylonian furnace, which is heated seven times over, to burn whomsoever of the Chaldeans it finds.
35_marg2662: He hath broken, etc. Our Jerusalem, who is the bride of the most high God, when she has departed from God and served crimes, has her horn broken, which the Lord raised up in the house of David his servant, so that she cannot resist her enemies. The Lord drew back his hand from before the enemy, which he held stretched out for defence and vengeance; but she first turned backward. By the right hand of God the Son is understood, the power of God and the wisdom of God, whose help is withdrawn when the bride is prostituted to her lovers; hence the prophet laments that God has broken her horn. He hath kindled in Jacob as it were a flaming fire devouring round about. For when she is left desolate by the grace of God and weakened in her strength, she is kindled with the fire of lust, by whose flames she is devoured within and without.

35_marg2663: Historically. He hath bent his bow. It is clear that the Lord did all these things when he carried out his judgements by the Chaldeans or the Romans, fighting against him or against Jerusalem. For the bow itself in the hand of the Lord had been bent long before the vengeance; but because Sion would not return, when the measure of time was filled the measure of sin was filled, that at last he might strike. And because they would not be friends, the Lord became their enemy, according to that: “With the perverse thou wilt be perverted.” He hath fixed his hand as an adversary, because they too were adversaries of the divine law; that even so they might learn that “they got not the possession of the land by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them”; and because they did not understand this, he killed all that was fair to behold. And to the slayer, namely the enemy, he gave power; he did not let it drip but poured it out like fire. Which is more truly fulfilled under the Romans, when the whole indignation of God is poured out.
35_marg2664: He hath bent his bow, etc. The Lord bends his bow as an enemy against the sinning soul when he does not soften her in her sin to penance, but with outstretched hand lets her go after fleshly longings, and does not turn her away, but kills what was fair to behold, namely the comeliness of manners in her conscience. And the Lord is said to destroy when he suffers destruction, and he handed her over to shameful affections and the flame of lust, that, kindled by her longings, she might follow her lovers.
35_marg2665: He hath bent his bow. The Lord bends his bow against the Church as an enemy, because she is an enemy and will not hear him calling her to repent and return. By the bow is understood judgement, by which each one is now struck that he may be corrected or punished more gently, or it is bent long, that when sins have been completed it may be loosed to punish more heavily. In the bow there are divers arrows: some are sent to destroy the old man with his deeds; others to scourge, or for a crown, or for correction, or for punishment. And the Church groans and laments for those whom the Lord strikes as an enemy, either through the devil or through the heretics, of whom it is said: “The wicked have bent their bow, they have prepared their arrows”, etc. For arrows of this kind come from the bow of the Lord, that is, from the divine judgement; whence: “The arrows of the Lord are in me”, and elsewhere: “Thy arrows are fastened in me.” But some the Lord does not strike that they may be corrected, because the bow is bent in fury, that, hardened in heart, they may be struck more hardly; whence: “Thou hast given a warning to them that fear thee, that they may flee from before the bow.” The Lord fixes his hand as an adversary against the Church when he afflicts her unceasingly, that corrected she may return, or hardened may pay her punishments. He kills what is fair to behold when he suffers her precious members to perish. He pours out his indignation like fire. You see all things burned by the fires of discord and the flames of lust; this we read more surely in ourselves than we remember it in Scripture.

35_marg2666: Historically. The Lord is become. There is no doubt that all these things happened to the Jews in history. The tearful telling, therefore, warns us to suffer with them, inclines us to lamentations; as if: The Lord was the leader and keeper of the Jews, to whom he spoke as a friend to friends; he is become an enemy. Whence it is said above: The Lord hath cast down headlong and hath not spared all that was beautiful in Jacob; the Lord hath destroyed in his wrath the strong holds of the virgin of Juda. What he said there, in his wrath, he says here, as an enemy; there, the beautiful things, here, the walls; as if he were saying other things. But going over the same things again he would call back to tears more fully, that at new words you might pour out new tears, and never grow weary of repeating the same things very often; lest perhaps, when the Lord calls us through Isaias “to weeping and to mourning, to baldness and to girding with sackcloth”, you run off to joy and vain gladness. Whence: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting.”
35_marg2667: The Lord is become, etc. The soul has walls of the virtues, as a city has walls for adornment, and strong holds to defend itself; so there are gifts which fortify, others which adorn the soul. In like manner the Church too: as the gifts of prophecy, and kinds of tongues, interpretations of speeches and the like. These are the walls of the mind; and if anyone does not have them, he can stand only by faith and charity and the other virtues, without which he cannot be saved. When the Lord took away from Juda prophecy and the teaching of miracles, he cast down her walls; but when he allowed hope, faith and charity to be taken away, he destroyed her strong holds. In these, therefore, the right order is kept: when the sinful soul is forsaken, first the gifts of the virtues which were given for the manifestation of the Spirit are taken from her; then the foundations of faith, hope and charity are overthrown. All these the Lord took away from the faithless Jews and bestowed on the Gentiles; whence: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you”, etc. But when the soul is stripped of these, the Lord becomes her enemy as he did to the Jews; and he who said: “I will be an enemy to thy enemies, and will afflict them that afflict thee”, himself becomes her enemy and afflicts her. Whence there is multiplied in her the afflicted man and the afflicted woman, that is, unclean sense and thought, so that she may be driven by insults within and without, until, confounded, she returns to penance.
35_marg2668: The Lord is become, etc. When the beautiful bride of the Lord turns away from her bridegroom’s embraces by acting against his precepts, she incurs the enmity of God; but God tempers the sentence of severity, because he is not called an enemy absolutely, but as an enemy. For although she is afflicted and seems utterly forsaken, yet she is scourged that she may return. It is to be noted that first he casts Israel down headlong, when he takes away cleanness of heart; then her walls, which belong to the beauty and comeliness of religion. This city has strong holds, lest the enemy break in; it has comely and uncomely parts, but those that are uncomely we surround with more abundant honour. There are simple folk in the Church, there are those cast down by rustic lowliness, but certainly necessary. But often the Lord allows some to be cast down headlong who seemed to be the ornaments of the Church, either into heresy or into any vices. He destroys the strong holds too when he lets the defenders go astray and be scattered by wicked deeds. And he multiplies the afflicted, both men and women, when he allows very many everywhere to be brought low in earthly works by the deceit of the demons.

35_marg2669: Historically. And he hath destroyed … as. It is to be noted with what elegance of words, with what splendour of song the Hebrew truth shines, which, translated, is strong with such elegance. For after he said How hath he covered, so he bewailed step by step one thing after another, so that How can be fitted to them all: so How hath he cast down, How hath he cast down headlong, How hath he destroyed, How hath he brought her down and made her unclean, etc. So therefore he laments alike and grieves for all, that each one may be full of amazement, wonder and groaning; so that it may be said: How hath he destroyed his tent as a garden? And it is to be known that the Lord destroyed this for the sins of the Jews, that is, he gave the power to destroy. And tabernacles are where curtains are hung, with ropes stretched and boards set in, by which the tents are held up. The tent, too, is what Moses set up in the desert; the tabernacle is the temple of Solomon; which, for the crimes of the Jews, were handed over to the power of the enemies. First the Lord cast off the tabernacle of Silo; whence: “I will do to this house, in which my name is called upon, and in which you trust, as I did to Silo.”
35_marg2670: And he hath destroyed. The soul has a tent and a tabernacle in which she has converse with the Holy Spirit. But it is destroyed as a garden if she loosens herself into riot and the delight of the flesh. But it is not destroyed as the garden of God’s delights, but as that over which we read that Sargon the captain of the Assyrians was set, which is interpreted “prince of the gardens”, as one given over to pleasures and luxury. Achab too, king of Israel, wished to turn the vineyard of Naboth into a garden; and he, understanding it (read it tropologically), chose rather to die than consent that his father’s inheritance and so great a possession of virtue should serve the delights of a wicked king. But because the unhappy soul has let her tent, that is, the flesh, which is put together with bones and sinews, be destroyed by delightful riot, and her tabernacle, that is, herself, be thrown down in her pleasures, she consents that the vineyard and inheritance of the most high Father be changed into a garden of lusts for the most wicked king. Therefore the Lord forgets her feasts and sabbaths, because the temple in which vows are worthily offered and solemnities kept has been thrown down by alluring delights, and the tent of the flesh has been destroyed by divers pleasures. King and priest are given up to reproach, because, these offices being lost, the unhappy soul has made herself subject to wicked kings: to one who lays waste the people of Azotus, those who serve generation and lust, for Azotus is interpreted “the fire of generation”; to another who longs for the flourishing vineyards of Christ to be changed into gardens of lusts. Whence it follows: The Lord hath cast off his altar.
35_marg2671: And he hath destroyed. In the Church we see many destroyed as a garden. The garden here is the Church, of which it is said in the Canticle: “My sister is a garden enclosed.” There is the well of living waters, there the south wind blows and the north wind is driven away, the spices flow, the bridegroom eats the honeycomb with honey. But there is another garden of delights, as it were the paradise of God, of which it is said that “Lot, lifting up his eyes, saw all the country about the Jordan, which was watered as the paradise of the Lord, and like Egypt”, so that it was as a garden of delights and pleasure. For these delights the Jews sighed, longing for the fleshpots, the onions and melons and cucumbers of the Egyptians; all which are in the mind of those who savour earthly things. After the likeness of this garden the Lord destroys in the Church those who run wanton and sigh after the longings of Sodom and Gomorrha and of the Egyptians, as in the Synagogue those who went astray. He throws down the tabernacle when he lets some living in the Church be destroyed by crimes and burned up by vices. For none dwells in God’s tabernacle but “he that walketh without blemish, and worketh justice”. These things being neglected, the Lord has given our feasts and sabbaths over to forgetting; not that the feasts of our religion do not please him, but because in us the tabernacle, that is, the temple of God, is violated; for there is nothing in us by which what is offered may please him; whence he is said to forget what, the temple of God being violated, is not reckoned to us for justice. Hence king and priest are given up to reproach, who, according to Isaias, are set over the Church as nursing fathers; whence: “Kings shall be thy nursing fathers.” But because they violate the temple of the Holy Spirit, they are rather the Church’s reproach than her glory; of whom David says: “And now, O ye kings, understand”, etc. By which words he implies that we are a royal race and a holy priesthood; if we wish to offer saving victims to God, let us be a saving temple of the Holy Spirit, in which victims are worthily offered to God. Let us carefully take heed that this is not thrown down by vices.

35_marg2672: Historically. The Lord hath cast off, etc., the altar, namely, on which victims were offered; he hath cursed his sanctuary, that is, the sacrifices, the people, and handed over the towers to the enemies. Whence the enemies, having entered there, exulted with a loud voice where once on solemn days the priests of the Lord gave praise; whence Isaias: “The house of our holiness, where our fathers praised thee, is made desolate.”
35_marg2673: The Lord hath cast off, etc. This is done when the altar of our heart is profaned, and the mind and conscience, prostituted to vices, is defiled, where the sacrifice accepted from us is rightly offered to God, according to that: “A sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit.” The sanctuary is cursed when the soul is laid low by a curse, because she would not sanctify the name of God in herself with a worthy sacrifice. The towers of the soul are faith, hope, charity and the other virtues, by which she is raised up to heaven. The walls by which she is fortified are the works of the other virtues; these are handed over into the hands of the enemies, because the soul is scattered in her deeds without or within. The enemies make a noise in the house of the Lord as in a solemn day when the unclean spirits clamour in monstrous vices in the soul, the temple of the Holy Spirit being defiled, where the instruments of the Holy Spirit and the harmony of the virtues used to sound.
35_marg2674: The Lord hath cast off, etc. There is one altar in the Church of God, Christ, who is called victim and sacrifice, high priest and priest; on him we offer all sacrifices. But the saints are called altars from this altar, as lights from the light, and mountains from the mountain, shepherds from the shepherd. That altar the Father cast off in the passion, as he prayed for the Jews: “Father, remove this chalice from me.” Cast off by them, by the Father’s judgement he is passed over to the Gentiles; whence David: “But thou hast rejected and despised.” For as those sacrifices bore the figure of Christ, so the altar of unhewn stones which iron had not touched foreshadowed the Lord’s body, defiled by no human work. Because, therefore, Christ is passed over to the Church, on him, as on an altar, the vows of the faithful are offered; and for them the Church laments, suffering with the apostles, as it were; not that she grieves that he has been passed over to her, but with the apostles she was saddened at his death, that afterwards with them she may rejoice at the resurrection. Whence the custom has grown up in the Church, handed down from the apostles, that on the day on which Christ suffered the victim of the body and blood of Christ is not offered, for three reasons: either because he is offered in truth whose mystical sacraments these are on the other days; or because Christ the high priest himself rightly offers them, since on that day he went down to hell in his own person; or because, the temple being destroyed and the altar cast off, there is nothing on which the victim of the Lord’s body and blood may be offered. There follows: he hath cursed his sanctuary, namely Christ, who, though he had no sin, was made sin and a curse for us; whence Moses: “Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.” He is our sanctification, who was crucified for us. And so it was fulfilled: The Lord hath delivered the walls of the towers thereof into the hand of the enemy, the apostles, namely, who are the walls of the rest of the faithful; he handed them over to the temptation of the enemy, who desired to sift them as wheat. They have made a noise in the house of the Lord, etc. How great was the confusion then in the house of the Lord, how great in the courts, how great in the streets, how great in the whole city, since it was a feast day, the gospel declares; whence Isaias: “I looked that he should do judgement, and behold a cry.”

35_marg2675: Historically. The Lord hath purposed, etc. He disposes with deep counsel; and lest he should seem to have purposed and gone beyond human justice, he adds: he hath stretched out his line, that is, his measure of punishment according to the size of the fault. And “to purpose” is carried over to God by metaphor. From men he hath not withdrawn his hand from striking, namely until the measure of the punishment is filled, according to that: “His hand is stretched out still.” This indeed is what is lamented: that he hath not withdrawn his hand from their destruction, nor brings them back into the bosom of his protection, but among the nations, as with the outstretched hand of Moses, they remain lepers and unclean to this day. The bulwark is said figuratively to have mourned, because, seeing them stripped of the guard of the corners, he made the bulwark as it were mourn.
35_marg2676: The Lord hath purposed, etc. When the Lord sees the soul tending from the citadel of contemplation to the depths, he purposes to destroy her walls; but first he stretches out his line, to see in what measure she is to be punished. First indeed he deliberates, that he may leave her the power of returning, that she herself may think over how she has sinned. Before he destroys the wall he stretches the line over her, as if weighing how great and of what kind her sins are, so that she likewise may weigh them and afterwards amend; otherwise let her know that he does not withdraw his hand. But because she would not think over how she had sinned, but “blood touched blood”, therefore the wall is destroyed and she herself made subject to enemies. Let those hear this who do not fear to judge rashly, nor weigh causes with just examination: the Lord does nothing without deliberation and measure; he weighs all things with just examination, who created all things perfectly. The bulwark is faith, which is said to mourn when the wall is destroyed; not that which “worketh by charity”, but that by which the demons are said to “believe and tremble”; through which, before the wall was destroyed, namely the building of the other virtues, Christ was her wall and bulwark, set in the soul by the same faith. But because she would not have Christ as keeper and defender through faith, the working of the virtues is destroyed and the bulwark mourns, namely the faith by which she believes in the judgement and trembles. So she cannot resist the enemies; not that the place of penance is taken away, but because she scorns to return.
35_marg2677: The Lord hath purposed, etc. The Lord stretches over the Church the line of our sins and the rule of strict judgement, to afflict her according to the deserts of her sins. The wall is destroyed, namely the rulers and defenders, when they are either taken away by untimely death or overcome by the enemies. But because it is done by God’s just judgement, he hath not withdrawn his hand from afflicting those who are lost. For Sion, the city of our strength, is laid waste no less by invisible enemies within than by visible ones without. The wall mourns, that is, the Saviour, while he makes us mourn; Christ in this city is both bulwark and wall, to whom the mourning of his members is ascribed. This wall is destroyed when the Church is left desolate of his defence.

35_marg2678: Historically. Are sunk, etc. The gates are sunk into the ground, the bars destroyed and broken, when the teachers or defenders of the Synagogue apply their minds to earthly things. Her king and her princes are among the Gentiles: he seems to repeat the same, so that by the gates are understood the kings, by the bars the princes. These, broken and destroyed among the Gentiles, are sunk into the ground, that they may not return to him whom, promised in the law, they would not receive. The law is no more, because it was burned by the Chaldeans; or, Christ being lost, they have no law; whence among the Jews now there is no keeping of the law. The prophets have found no vision from the Lord, because they saw their lawgiver and the Lord of the prophets present and despised him.
35_marg2679: Are sunk. The soul of manners is lamented, whose senses are sunk into the ground, that is, into the mire of sin, and she has no substance of virtues to escape; who, because she would not enter by the narrow gate, has sunk her gates, that is, her senses, in earthly delights; she has lost the bars and bolts of the virtues, so as not to bar the way in to the unclean spirits; so the princedom of the commandments of God is taken captive. She has no law nor vision from the Lord, that she may hear within what God speaks, but, unbridled, she is snatched after vain longings.
35_marg2680: Are sunk, etc. The gates of the Church are the teachers, who bear the key of knowledge, who are sunk into the ground when they are taken up with earthly things. Above he said the gates were broken down; here something more, as it were: sunk into the ground. What is sunk in can hardly be moved; whence: “Draw me out of the mire, that I may not stick fast.” The bars are destroyed and broken, those namely who before opened the doors of the divine law to believers, or who ought to have been put into the golden rings to carry the ark. These are broken by the strength of the heretics, who are depraved by their own lost manners. So kings and princes are taken captive by the vices of the fleshly life, as it were among the Gentiles. The law is no more, as regards those, namely, who daily heap up evils for themselves and think they can sin without the law’s vengeance. Such teachers of the churches, like the prophets of the Jews, do not deserve the vision of divine inspiration, to teach rightly of things to come, because they entangle themselves in wicked and vain longings.

35_marg2681: Historically. They sit upon the ground. The history is plain: that after their custom the Jews, oppressed by such tribulations, lamented in wretched garb; yet not without cause those especially weep and lament in whom both the authority of religion and the comeliness of purity are proclaimed.
35_marg2682: They sit. When the soul loses the Spirit of counsel, she clings to earthly things as if to the old age of gravity and the dignity of ripeness, and becomes foolish; who, seasoned with no salt, follows earthly allurements. So the ancients sit upon the ground, namely the thought of counsel and the acts of prudence, in pleasures; and when the soul is taken up with them, all her strivings fall silent before God, according to that: “Because I was silent my bones grew old.” While they grow old from the things that are within, as they follow the gain of the old man, like curious old men fallen from the watchtower of the heavenly life to the earth, they fall silent from good things. But for the business of this life they do not cease to cry out all day long; so they sprinkle their head, that is, their mind, with dust; that is, the soul, girded with the bristles of the vices and the hair of goats, loses the glory she had in heavenly things, and is rolled on the earth until she returns to dust.
35_marg2683: They sit. The ancients in the Church of God rightly hold their peace, because they sit upon the ground; nor are they justly called ancients unless the choir of God’s elders suffers with those who mourn and is humbled for the lowly; but if such were among us they would not be mourned, but would mourn for them. But the prophet mourns those whom the Greeks call presbyters, adorned by no work of their age, who sit foolish upon the ground while they cling to earthly things; to whom it is said: “O thou seed of Chanaan, and not of Juda”, and “O thou that art grown old in evil days”, etc. The virgins of Juda and of Jerusalem signify the same, because the souls of those born again are the daughters of the heavenly Jerusalem. These are the daughters of Juda, that is, of confession, and the daughters of Sion, that is, of divine contemplation; to whom it is said: “I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved”, etc. But these do not sprinkle their heads with dust, nor clothe themselves in haircloth, who, composed and adorned, hasten to the bridegroom’s embrace. But there are daughters of Sion in name and sacrament only, who have fallen into heresy from the throne of the kingdom, or slipped into the dust of earthly action; whose mouth is stopped, and who dare not lift their eyes to God; whose heads, that is, minds, are sprinkled with works of dust, and are clothed in sackcloth of haircloth, woven of the bristles of beasts and the hair of goats. And because they have once hung their heads down to the ground, they will not raise themselves, will not shake themselves from the dust. Of these perhaps is she who elsewhere adjures, lest by herself she lay claim to the bridegroom of the Church, but now repenting, now mourning her sins. These are called daughters of Jerusalem and of Juda, that hearing their name they may remember the Catholic confession.

35_marg2684: Historically. Have failed, etc. As if: with what heart shall I be able to bear it? Neither sex nor age is spared; therefore my eyes fail with weeping, gladness is turned into anguish of heart; the ancient nation is slain, the daughter of the patriarchs, taught by the laws, but now forgetful of her God and for her crimes handed over to the enemies. Praiseworthy is this failing, not from weakness of the flesh; whence David: “My eyes have failed for thy word”, etc. The eyes of the saints, when they long inwardly and more ardently for invisible things, fail from looking at visible ones.
35_marg2685: Have failed. The eyes of the soul fail with weeping when, faint with love, she sees her bowels troubled within, and is not able to direct the intention of the mind to the things on which she sets her eyes; her bowels are the conceptions of the thoughts; these being troubled, she cannot freely behold what she longs for, for the bitterness of grief. The liver is poured out upon the earth, the riot, namely, of pleasures and lusts, by whose filth the divine fire is put out. The fire of the human body (so they say) dwells chiefly in the liver; from there it flies up to the brain, then to the eyes and the other senses, and so is spread through the members. When, therefore, the mind’s lust is prone to evil, and the fire, poured out from the liver upon the earth, is carried to the eyes, a failing of right intention will follow; whence she says: my eyes have failed with weeping. For from the grief from which tears are born a failing of divine contemplation is begotten. And it is to be noted that such a pouring out of the liver comes from the destruction of the soul, who ought to have been the daughter of the saints, but, trodden down by enemies, gave way. Whence the outward sense, a child in the strength of grace, and the mind within, a suckling, having lost the virtues, slips away through the streets of this world, and has nowhere to turn but to tears, by which, though the eyes are weighed down, yet by weeping she is strengthened.
35_marg2686: Have failed with weeping. The Church with Jeremias runs back to tears as to remedies for grief, and pours herself out in tears for her members, saying: My eyes have failed with weeping, my bowels are troubled; of which it is said: “My belly is troubled.” For these are the bowels which the belly is; by it, as has been said, is understood the multitude of the faithful, which is filled daily with divine foods within the womb of the Church, but is troubled like the sea by the temptation of pressures or by wickedness of manners; for whom the greater ones are anxious, as women in labour. Whence the Church says: my bowels are troubled. By the liver are understood the rich, who in the Church serve cares and pleasure. For the physicians say that pleasure and lust are held in the liver. When these pour themselves out through vain longings and slacken the reins of the lusts, the Church’s liver is poured out upon the earth. And it is to be noted that the liver is not found without gall, nor are earthly riches possessed without bitterness. It is said that the liver draws to itself the juice of foods by heat and turns it into blood, and divides parts to each member; so let those who have be as though they had not, and turn their riches into the blood of their redemption, and give food and nourishment to each member of the Church as from an abundance of blood. For the destruction of the daughter of my people: the Church is rightly called the daughter of the saints, who is then destroyed and afflicted with temptations when the liver, that is, the powerful and rich, is poured out into earthly longings. Then the child and the suckling faint away in the streets of the town, when such men are seen to abound in every happiness; who, were they not children and sucklings in the teaching of Christ and in faith, would not faint in the streets because of such men. Whence David: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps had well nigh slipped.” And the feet are moved when the children in faith, imperfect in teaching, envying earthly happiness and leaving the narrow way that leads to life, go out into the streets to pour out their longings.

35_marg2687: To their mothers, etc. The tenth topic of complaint, in which weakness and want are lamented.
35_marg2688: Historically. They said to their mothers. The histories declare that these things and worse than these happened to the Jews.
35_marg2689: To their mothers, etc. The moral and the allegorical sense are almost the same. The soul, when, having forsaken the right road, she has begun to spread herself out through outward things and as it were to walk through the streets of pleasure, seizes the wide and broad way that leads to death. So our childlike thoughts and the mind’s suckling knowledge, if they have gone out to the outward things of the flesh and the streets of delight, have nothing to ask of their mothers, that is, of the allurements that flatter wickedly, with whom there is not the bread that strengthens man’s heart, that is, spiritual teaching, nor the wine that makes glad, that is, the grace that makes minds drunk; therefore they breathe out their souls in their mother’s bosom. While the flesh, which they believed to be their mother, returns to the earth, they breathe out their souls into the bosom of hell, which bore them unto death. Whence: “He that is hardened in mind shall fall into evil”, and “Blessed is the man that is always fearful.” And because Jerusalem would not hear this, the prophet, turning his complaints to her, says: To what shall I compare thee?
35_marg2690: They said to their mothers. Because the child and the suckling, of whatever sex, wander riotously through the streets of this world, like the prodigal son they are stripped of their goods and are in peril of hunger; whence they say to their mothers: Where is corn and wine? But wretched are the mothers who have led their children so far from their fathers to such want. And it is to be noted of how great a nature, of how great nobility they are who, though in want, do not seek husks or barley and such things as the hungry gulp down most gladly, but corn and wine; and they know, though degenerate by their own fault, what their father begot and nourished them to be. Whence the prodigal son, who had not even husks: “How many hired servants”, he says, “in my father’s house abound with bread”, etc. Whence elsewhere: “With corn and wine I have established him.” With these two the free are fed: with bread the heart of man is strengthened, with wine it is made glad. This is the bread which is made of the wheat that fell into the ground and died, and came down from heaven. This wine is taken from the vineyard of Soreth, that is, from the vine which is Christ. This the child and the suckling seek, but it is not found in the streets, nor is it worthily received by the wounded; therefore they breathe out their souls in the bosoms of their mothers, who had nourished them ill and enticed them into the bosom of the worst delight. Wiser is the prodigal of the gospel, who says: “I will arise and go to my father”, etc., than these who seek from the pleasures of the flesh, as from mothers, the things that are their father’s. If they were with their father or returned to their father, they would not breathe out their souls with hunger; but they were deceived by the pleasure of the flesh; not because they seek these things, but because they seek them from the flesh. “And they who are in the flesh cannot please God”; but these are sons of the Father, “who are born not of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.”

35_marg2692: Historically. To what shall I compare thee. No one doubts that the more glorious the Jewish nation stood above the rest, the more, as its sins demanded, none is now lower.
35_marg2693: In the moral and allegorical sense, mixed with the historical. As Judea was more glorious than the other kingdoms, so the Church, the mother of us all and the daughter of the heavenly country, the bride of the highest king, is glorious above all; so too is the faithful soul, whose inheritance is in heaven. Their justification is from God alone; and of all of them one Church and one body of Christ is joined to its head by faith and charity. And as of all there is one glorious city, of which it is said: “Glorious things are said of thee, O city of God”, so one is she who in Babylon, committing fornication away from Christ, degenerates. Whence, to spare the weariness of readers, against the order of the exposition one mourning is applied over the ruins of these three and the like, so that of all and of each it may be said: To what shall I compare thee, etc. For as she who has come to good, or to the prize of the heavenly calling, is more glorious than all, so the shame of her who falls back is to be compared to none. For the threefold repeating of the words under one meaning seems to gather into one the blindness of these three, who from so great a height of dignity, nay, from the loftiness of godhead, have cast themselves down to so great a depth of misery, nay, below the baseness of beasts. Whence: “I have said: You are gods, and all of you the sons of the most High. But you like men shall die.” But now, because that nation, or the mystical Jerusalem, has slipped from so great a glory, the prophet, or the choir of God’s elect, says mourning: To what shall I compare thee? as if: no fit comparison or likeness or equal is found for thee, where neither comeliness nor form is found. Thou art wholly misshapen, wholly horrible; destruction possesses thee wholly; thou tendest to not being. I do not know whether thou canst be called back. As if: to what shall I compare the leprous soul, or the Church forsaken by her bridegroom, or that nation cast down from the throne of glory? There is none by whose fall or ruin any of them can be comforted. For great as the sea is thy destruction. For the destruction of that nation, or of the corrupted Church, or of the falling soul, once she has been made subject to the enemies, like the sea never rests, but dashes against itself unceasingly with the waves of the billows; for, handed over into the hands of the enemies, they are crushed by persecutions and temptations. Whence it follows: who shall heal thee? as if he said: none will heal thee, unless thou return to him from whom thou hadst departed. Who: either none, namely, or few. “There is none that doth good, no not one.”

35_marg2694: Thy prophets. The allegory is mixed with the history. Jerusalem had false prophets; the Church has heretics and schismatics, wicked teachers, who daub without the tempering of charity, and by deceitful arguments or false opinions turn the hearts of the simple from the truth of right faith and the state of good work; whence Peter says: “There were also false prophets among the people, even as there shall be among you lying teachers”, etc. Nor is there any doubt that the fault of the masters and priests is the ruin of the peoples. For they teach false and foolish things as if they had seen a vision, and the peoples stroke iniquity. Many things too which they teach by words they destroy by bad examples, like the harlot who suckled her son while awake and smothered him while asleep. These do everything for the sake of gain, or of error, or of boasting and sloth; of whom it is said: But they have seen for thee false revelations and banishments. For where in Isaias Jerome translated “the burden of Babylon”, or of Tyre, or of Damascus, the Seventy said “vision” or “word”; Symmachus and Theodotion interpreted it as “assumption”. For when the false prophets see the burden of the people, that is, their affliction and the punishments of sins hanging over them, they soothe them with false comforts and strive to cast the burdens of sins hanging over them off their backs. But both are false, namely the assumption and the casting off; because often for lighter faults they foretell heavier burdens or assumptions to the people, and for heavier ones they announce lighter ones to sinners as if by divine authority. But “woe to them that call evil good and good evil”; or, according to Aquila, who say to the evil man, Thou art good, and to the good, Thou art evil. With these two letters, therefore, the prophet laments wicked teachers and hearers, as their interpretation shows: Mem, Nun, that is, “out of these everlasting”, understand punishment, for those, namely, who either teach those under them badly or are badly heard by those under them.
35_marg2695: Thy prophets, etc. The soul too has false prophets: outwardly, namely, of the flesh, who announce present things and care nothing for things to come; inwardly she has false thoughts, which the prudence of the flesh begets, which show us false and foolish things. For these judge it to be loss if the mind lets slip anything of pleasures in the present; they do not think it iniquity so long as something is gained or retaliation paid back to enemies; they judge the flesh must be indulged; they promise us longer times; the judgements of God to come they either deny altogether or make light of, or prophesy things to come in some other way. This they lighten, that they make heavier; they think their own crimes lighter and make others’ heavier. Whence “the prudence of the flesh is death.” These thoughts see false assumptions or casting off, and always either make heavier or add or cast off or lessen; out of these they gain for themselves everlasting punishment.

These, when they learn that anyone has been cast down, clap their hands, not with the feeling of one laughing but of one grieving, because the Synagogue or the Church or the soul, slipping from so great a height, has come so suddenly to so great a ruin. For the movement of the head or of the hands, like a hiss, is wont to signify divers feelings; whence it follows: Is this the city, etc. Not the enemies of the soul or of the Church think her to be of perfect beauty or the joy of all the earth, but only the saints and friends, who, the more glorious and beautiful they saw her, the more they wonder and mourn when they see her cast down into the hands of the enemies. They have hissed like serpents, they have gnashed with the teeth like lions roaring to devour. 35_marg2701: Historically. The Lord hath done that which he purposed, etc. Very often the Synagogue, provoking God by her evils, deserved just punishment; but the divine goodness bore with her for repentance; but because by her crimes she overcame God’s patience, at length she bore fitting punishment according to her deserts. Whence to Moses, praying for the people, the answer was given: “I have forgiven according to thy word; but in the day of revenge I will visit this sin also”; not that the Lord was bound to punish the same sin in the day of revenge, because he does not judge twice for the same thing, but because they did not wholly abandon the sin of idolatry nor repent. Whence he says: The Lord hath done that which he purposed, etc., namely he fulfilled the plagues which he had foretold in the law and the prophets.
35_marg2702: The Lord hath done that which he purposed, etc. The soul too is handed over into the power of the enemies, because in the day of good things she was unmindful of evils. Therefore the day comes which the enemies looked for, when the Lord did and fulfilled his word foretold in the Scriptures. Whence the Lord, seeing in the figure of Jerusalem about to perish the soul surrounded by evils of this kind, wept, saying: “If thou also hadst known”, etc. So the perverse soul has her day here, which enjoys passing goods, and to whom are present also the things that are for her peace, while she rejoices in temporal things, while she is lifted up by honours, while she is melted by the pleasure of the flesh and is not frightened by fear of the punishment to come. She has peace in her day, but eternal damnation remains in another’s day, in which she will be tormented in eternal punishments for her iniquities. Then the things that are now for peace will be in bitterness; then she will begin to quarrel with herself, saying: Why did I not foresee damnation? why did I shut the eyes of the mind? why did I not dread these punishments? Whence: “But now they are hidden from thy eyes.” So he does suddenly what, waiting long, he deliberated; the Lord fulfils his words which he commanded, when he bids come what he foretold. He hath destroyed and hath not spared, that she may not always have the power of sinning; and her who neglected to spare herself he handed over to be plundered by the enemies, whose horn is set up while the power of ruling is granted them; and she who would not tear herself from the yoke of the enemies is put under it. Whence he adds: Their heart cried.
35_marg2703: The Lord hath done that which he purposed, etc. As the bodily enemies did these things against Jerusalem, so the spirits of wickedness and the ministers of the old enemy do them against the Church, when, God justly taking vengeance on the wicked of her, they afflict with punishments and pains those handed over to them. This is said only of those who seemed to be in the Church, not of her of whom it is said to Peter: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it”, but of those of whom it is said: “They went out from us, but they were not of us.” The horn of the adversaries is set up when the Church is weakened, namely the kingdom and power of the devil.

35_marg2704: Historically, in the moral sense. Their heart cried. It cried with intent more than with voice. Enemies visible or invisible cry upon the walls of the daughter of Sion, namely of the soul, or of the Church, or of the earthly city, when they ascribe the power by which they rule them not to the divine judgement but to their own might; and they cry against the Lord, whose power protects and defends as a wall. But when he withdraws his help, the enemies are said to cry upon the walls of those whom they oppress against the Lord, when, namely, they draw to themselves whatever they can do against those whom God’s help formerly fortified, as if he could not set them free. For such oppression comes from the equity of judgement, not from the weakness of the protector; this too the prophet laments among the rest. And it is to be noted that these things look back to the sense above; for as often as those who write in metre cannot complete the sense in one or two lines, they make the break at the beginning or the middle of another. Whence the speech is at once turned to Jerusalem herself: Let tears run down like a torrent. A torrent does not always run or flow down with one and the same rush, but as a flood pours together from the sky, so too tears, namely those which are begotten by divine inspiration and compunction of heart. No one indeed can bring down tears like a torrent; but by these words it is hinted that the mind and the eyes ought always to be ready to pour out tears according to the grace of divine inspiration, and never to rest in prosperity or in adversity; that no one spare himself while he lives, and no one grow sluggish as if he had received security, until he comes to that rest in which God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes. Whence: “Going they went and wept”, etc. These are the souls of true justice, which are signified by Sade. And let not the apple of thy eye cease. The apple of thy eye both prays and obtains, pricked by divine inspiration. It must not be silent until God puts an end to these evils and wipes away every tear.
35_marg2705: And let not … cease, etc. There is an inner eye which drops tears to God, from which the outer one weeps with it; and then “the stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful”, etc.; otherwise the tear is barren, because the apple of the eye is silent.

35_marg2706: Arise, give praise, etc. He arises in the night who, lifted up by hope from the tribulation or straits of the present life, shakes off the sluggishness of negligence and, unwearied, girds himself against all adversities and praises God in all things; whence he adds: arise and give praise in the night, in the beginning of the watches; because the cunning enemy, while he brings scourges upon us, aims that God may be blasphemed; whence Job says: “As it hath pleased the Lord, so is it done: blessed be the name of the Lord.” In the beginning of the watches we ought to give praise, that we may refer all that we do or suffer to his glory and praise, lest, growing sluggish at the beginning of the work, we be overcome by the sleep of deceit; whence: “Do all to the glory of God.” Many indeed are the watches in which the Lord is to be praised, and most of all we must beware that the work be not condemned from the beginning of the intention. But when the work is well begun, there still remain watches in which it may be completed to the glory of God until the end. Pour out thy heart like water. He pours out his heart like water before the face of the Lord who brings forth tears of compunction from the inmost feeling of his heart; because “a sacrifice to God is an afflicted spirit.” Yet if so great a shower of tears is not there, he must not despair; whence: “My soul is as earth without water unto thee.” The penitent spreads out before the Lord his soul, dry as earth without water, that he who brought water out of the rock for the thirsty people may water it with his showers. The heart too is poured out like water when, melted by the love of God and of the neighbour, it is loosened as ice by heat; whence it follows: lift up thy hands to him. He lifts up his hands to God for the little ones who exalts the works of mercy for the lowly members of Christ, who perish with hunger and thirst because they have clung to earthly things. And this is perfect charity: that the heart be poured out like water to God and the hands be lifted up for the neighbour. As Moses is said to have lifted up his hands lest the people of God be overcome, so to hold up the thoughts of the soul that the little ones of the Church may be kept; whence: “My soul melted when he spoke.” For the heart or the soul is not loosened from the cold of unbelief except by the heat of divine inspiration. And therefore we must always pray that the north wind arise and the south wind come and the spices flow. For then the spices of prayers flow, when the mind is breathed upon by the divine Spirit. But lest love alone seem to suffice, the hands are to be lifted up for the little ones who perish for hunger of the word at the top of all the streets. For if they were not in the ways and at the top of the streets, they would not have suffered hunger or thirst for the word. But they are to be called back from the crossroads, from the streets and from the top of all the streets, that they may come to the Lord’s dinner and not perish of hunger for ever. The hands are to be lifted up that Amalec may be overcome, lest the little ones be crushed; whence Paul: “lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway.” After he has stirred wretched Jerusalem, or the Church, or any soul, to tears, he turns the word of supplication to God himself, if perhaps he can call him back from vengeance, saying: Behold, O Lord, etc. And the diligence of the devoted prophet is to be noted, who is carried by manifold ardour to divers things: now he goes over the evils of his nation, now he mourns its sins, now he recalls the goods lost, now he grieves that God has been offended; yet he does not cease to pour out prayers; whence he adds: Behold, O Lord, etc.

35_marg2707: Behold, O Lord, etc. The fourth topic of complaint. For she bewails base and unworthy things; whence it follows: shall women then eat, etc.; The child and the old man lie without on the ground.
35_marg2708: Behold, O Lord, etc. Nothing is hidden from God; yet she asks him to behold, that by words and feelings she may bend him to mercy. For she knows God to be merciful by nature, and therefore asks him to look upon the evils of her nation. Whom thou hast thus dealt with: as if: to no nation hast thou given such great benefits, on none have such great punishments been laid so justly; because instead of grapes she brought forth wild grapes, and instead of fruit thorns. There is none whom the Lord has so made a vintage of, except one who imitates her example, from whom he took away the adornments of the law and of all the ceremonies. For when they killed him who had given everything, they lost all the goods of the heavenly and the earthly life alike, they who out of so great a love earned offence, out of so great a glory shame. To see these things she calls on God, that he may spare those so afflicted, though undeserving. Shall women then eat, etc. As if: how shall they do these things? For we read in the book of Kings that women did this, and Josephus bears witness to the same. Their children of a span long: in other copies it is read more expressly, “to the measure of a palm”; nor is it unbelievable. For so great was the famine that they spared neither comeliness nor nature. Shall the priest be slain in the sanctuary of God, etc. As if: by God’s just judgement those are punished who polluted the sanctuary of the Lord with the blood of the prophets. This too the Church of Christ and the faithful soul must fear. For if, bound to divine offices, we commit the like, we shall be punished alike and our religion will be profaned. Women too, that is, the souls of sinners, eat the children of their womb to the measure of a palm, because whatever vices they beget from themselves they receive back to the measure of their works and are filled with their own fruits. Whence we must mourn rather than explain, lest, exalted up to heaven, we be sunk down to the abyss.
35_marg2709: Lie without on the ground. He shows that the warrior people was slain by the sword with the kings and princes, and the rest of every age taken captive.
35_marg2710: Lie without on the ground. The prophet laments the evils of all as his own, who, eyed all round with charity, and all in all, searches out and laments his own evils in the several members of each body. So whoever is filled with the love of God and of his neighbour ought to pour himself out to all, and weep for the evils of all as his own, that he may see whether any members of the Church lie without on the ground, that is, are taken up with earthly business; of whom it is said: “No man, being a soldier to God, entangleth himself with secular businesses.” They lie without who go out from us and do not remain in the works of faith; but many are within in body and live among us, but are lost before God. The child who lies on the ground is not strengthened by the virtue of the old; and the old man, because “the child of a hundred years shall be accursed.” The virgins and the young men, the flowering and pleasant age, are struck in the mind by the sword of the adversaries; and what is worse, they are slain in the day of his fury. In one way the old man is struck, that he may fall and the new one rise again; in another way they are struck and slain who seemed to stand, who are slain without mercy in the day of fury. Thence is born the weeping beyond remedy, with which they are lamented who do not know that they have already been slain by the sword of God’s fury, consigned to eternal damnation.

35_marg2711: Thou hast called as to a festival, etc. The last captivity is described, lamented with the mourning of all the elect. The letter Thau is set first, that it may be found signed on the foreheads of those who sigh and grieve; but those on whom it is not found will be exposed to their enemies, gathered from every side as to a festival, who said above: This is the day which we looked for; we have found it, we have seen it. It is called a festival, not because it pleases God, but because then the long-awaited wantonness of the wicked is fulfilled; at the day of whose solemnity, that is, of the last examination, Satan will be loosed; whence he adds: those that should terrify me round about. For the elect too will see the demons gathered from every side, horrible to see, unbridled to devour souls, and, terrified, they will be cleansed; nor will there be any who escapes or is left unexamined. Whence the Church, conscious of the saints, groaning and in harmony with their mourning, bewailing the members taken from her, says: those that I brought up, namely by the discipline of a recruit, and nourished with the teaching of milk, because they did not come to the perfect man so as to fight against the army of the enemies, my enemy hath consumed them, namely with the delights of the vices. Therefore there is none of them who escapes, except him who bears on his forehead the signs which Thau signifies; whence: “If any man will come after me, let him deny himself”, etc. The rest will not escape the sword of the Lord’s fury, though born, brought up and nourished in the Church, because the enemy has consumed them.

35_marg2715: Historically. Jeremias laments the ruin of the people no less than his own distress, who is troubled with them in poverty. He suffers the indignation of God. He is brought into darkness and not into light; the hand of the Lord is turned and turned again upon him, to try whether he will follow it. By these things the skin and flesh of Jeremias are afflicted with famine, as with old age; and the vigour of the people is broken, as by the hammer of persecution, and its strength for war fails. He laments the siege too, saying: He hath built round about me, etc.; whence: “If thou also hadst known”, and a little after: “Thy enemies shall cast a trench about thee.” He laments his people too, compassed with the bitterness of miseries and the labour of straits; which happened in the first siege, in which Jeremias was harried by the people with exceeding bitterness of heart and afflicted for the people with the labour of tribulation; and this is what he says: He hath compassed me with gall, and set me in dark places as those that are dead for ever. This plainly fits Jeremias, who was shut up in the darkness of the prison so as to be almost dead, as if he had deserved to die for his own guilt.
35_marg2716: I am the man that see my poverty. “Only the spirit of a man knoweth the things of a man”; and as often as it is touched by the divine Spirit, understanding its poverty, it is moved to weeping, saying: I am the man that see my poverty; because when it is scourged by the indignation of God, when it is moved to weeping, it knows itself to be nothing, to have no comparison of virtue, so that it cannot presume on itself. For no one rightly glories that he has a chaste heart. Now humble, therefore tearful, he confesses: I am the man that see my poverty. For corrected by the rod of indignation he does not presume on himself; whence he adds: he hath led me; because every soul, when it remembers the wrath of God and examines the terror of the judgement and sets its deeds before its eyes as at the point of death, sees itself, slain by its errors, dwelling in darkness, while it acknowledges the poverty of its deserts by the rod of his indignation, that is, of God’s. Whence he rightly says: he hath led me and brought me into darkness. Even when it feels nothing of itself but what is weak, it laments that it has been brought as it were into darkness. Such a soul, while it looks on the rod of God’s examining and his threats and searches out its evils on every side, is rightly believed to be brought into darkness and not into light, lest it presume on itself, lose humility, and fall into pride; because “blessed are the poor in spirit”. Well does the spirit of man tremble, seeing its poverty, while it does not doubt that it dwells under the rod of indignation and understands that it has been led and brought to this. This is the teaching which is signified by Aleph: that the soul should always look into herself and go over all her deeds and mourn, until “the Orient from on high” enlightens her, who came “to enlighten them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death”. Only against me hath he turned his hand: with a mother’s heart God exposes the soul to temptations and casts her off, sometimes weeping, sometimes grieving; he takes her into his bosom, gives her the milk of teaching, caresses her; this is what he says: Only against me he hath turned, and turned again his hand all the day.
35_marg2717: I am the man that see my poverty. This can be the voice of all the saints, inasmuch as they are united in the body of Christ, inasmuch as they have imitated the same poverty, inasmuch as they are gathered by faith and work into the perfect man; whence it follows: by the rod of his indignation. One rod is of fury, another of indignation, another of correction, another of the kingdom. For there is a rod of iron with which the earthen vessels are broken in the wrath of fury; another by which the saints are ruled in equity, that they may be directed to the prize of the heavenly calling. There is a rod of indignation, of which it is said to Jerusalem: “In my wrath have I struck thee, and in my reconciliation have I had mercy upon thee.” For with this rod he strikes that he may have mercy; with this rod Christ was struck, not that he was worthy of indignation, but for the wickedness of the people he was struck. This is what he says: by the rod of his indignation.
35_marg2718: I am the man that see my poverty, etc. Though this may seem to fit all, it is understood more excellently of Christ, in whom, as all things excel, so does this seeing. For what wonder if each one sees his own poverty, under which almost everyone labours, pressed down? But as the poverty of Christ is more glorious and more wonderful than all the riches of the world, “who thought it not robbery to be equal with God”, etc., so this seeing of poverty is deeper. Therefore it is to be considered with the whole intent of mind and body; whence: “Blessed is he that understandeth concerning the needy and the poor.” For if the poverty of Christ were common, it could be discerned by the senses and would not feed the understanding alone; but now he is proclaimed blessed who understands. And well is the poverty of Christ to be wondered at and searched out, since, according to the Apostle, the poverty of the saints is “very deep”, which is understood by few; so much the more is that to be wondered at which even the angels wonder at, and from the understanding of which blessedness is born. Blessed indeed are the poor in spirit, but in that spirit by which this poverty is understood, which is unlocked by the Holy Spirit. Therefore among the Hebrews the beginnings of three verses are marked with Aleph, which is interpreted “teaching”. For this sense needs much teaching, of which our author glories, and, as if he alone saw and understood, says: I am the man that see my poverty, etc.; as if: I, with whom are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, see my poverty, which I took on of my own will for others; which the wretched will not understand, who will not even notice their utter misery.
35_marg2719: By the rod of his indignation. For the indignation of our crimes he bore poverty and suffering, that by his bruises we might be healed. The mystery of this poverty either none of the saints or few see fully: how great the goodness of God, how great the love towards the children of wrath, how great the mercy towards the children of reconciliation; therefore, as if he alone saw it, he says: I am the man that see my poverty. He sees his own, wonderful and unspeakable; he sees the poverty of his members, by which they are joined to him, knowing that “the patience of the poor shall not perish for ever”. Rightly therefore is it one voice of the head and the body: I am the man that see my poverty, because “God scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.” Prolepsis is noted in this place, that is, the anticipation of things yet to be said. For he puts “his” first, when he has not said to whom it refers, because he does not doubt it is known that the Father struck the Son with the rod of the passion. No wonder, then, if his members are struck with the rod of indignation for correction, that there may be one voice, one groaning, one weeping in the valley of tears; whence: He hath led me, etc.

35_marg2720: He hath led me and brought, etc. When, namely, the Father willed to bruise the Son in infirmity, and he was reckoned as a leper and as one struck by God and humbled, he was led as it were into darkness and not into light; but the darkness did not overcome him. The Church too he subjects to threats and terrors and brings into the darkness of affliction and not into the light of present prosperity; whence it follows: Only against me, etc.

35_marg2721: Only against me he hath turned, etc. This too is referred equally to the head and the members; for “all that will live godly in Christ shall suffer persecution”, whose voice is: Only against me. For others he does not correct, but lets them wander freely; but the Church, from the Jews as well as the Gentiles, he afflicts with many anguishes of discipline; he puts out his hand to scourge, because “he scourgeth every son whom he receiveth”, and mercifully turns it again that he may have mercy. For we turn the hand again when we draw it back from striking; he turns his hand again, therefore, by sparing and helping those whom he amends by punishing. But of others it is said: “They are not in the labour of men, neither shall they be scourged like other men”, etc. Which is well signified when, in the building of Solomon’s temple, neither hammer nor sound was heard, because all things were so prepared and hewn without that they might be fitted within into their own places of joining. Whence he says: he hath turned his hand, namely filing, hewing, smoothing all things that they may fit in the building. He hath turned it again, namely by ceasing, when he assigns the justified to their own mansions and orders. Of those, therefore, whose structure is one, whose joining of members is one, the voice is one, the weeping one; and the voice of Christ and of the Church is so united that it is found whole in Christ.
35_interl11665: as if he said: who would not pity one so wretched?
35_marg2722: He hath made old my skin. The soul laments the oldness of her sin; she groans not for skins, but for the skin infected with oldness, with which the first men were clothed when they were driven from paradise. This one skin of many, darkened with oldness, through the first man’s prevarication and mortality and the horror of sin has clothed all; whence: “I have grown old amongst all my enemies.” Hence the soul groans, while outwardly the conscience grows old like skin, and inwardly, once adorned, it is consumed like flesh corrupted by the wasting of sin; whence: “to eat my flesh”, that is, the fleshly affections, to which, as to neighbours, the devil draws near, to bring those in whom they are into his own body like flesh; when this flesh is ended the spirit will go out, so that the enemy finds nothing to eat. He hath broken my bones, namely the virtues of the soul. For the bones are the firmness of the body, and the virtues of the mind; and when these are broken by the delights or torments or wiles of the old enemy, rightly the soul laments her bones broken.
35_marg2723: He hath made old my skin. Christ is not touched by the oldness of sin, but his members, grown old in vices, are corrupted; which head and body lament in common; whence David: “I have grown old amongst all my enemies.” This man who sees his poverty has skin and flesh grown old; he has rams’ skins dyed red for covering the tabernacle, and violet ones for its beauty: poor in those things which are touched by oldness, rich in those which for the glory of his name are dyed red in their own blood, or are likened to the colours of the sky. The rams’ skins are dyed red, because the bodies of the saints are crowned with martyrdom; whence: “Bring to the Lord, O ye children of God.” The violet ones are those whom virginity raises to heaven, where “they shall neither marry nor be married, but shall be as the angels of God”. Hence in the tabernacle they are nearer to heaven, like the skins of Solomon, that is, of Christ, whose skins are all the saints, who, mortifying themselves with Christ, have crucified their flesh with its vices and lusts, by which the vital members of the body are covered, that they may imitate the passion of Christ. Whoever is his skin will hold in the recesses of the soul, as in the holy of holies, the divine mysteries of the highest king. But because the work of the skin is varied, in some beauty is praised, in some the depth of mysteries is covered, in some the Church is defended; whence: “Skin for skin, and all that a man hath he will give for his life.” For it is certain that the saints were handed over to sufferings that their own souls and others’ might be saved, to be formed by teaching and examples; as if Satan said: Why delayest thou to give this man to me, thou who handest over all the saints to sufferings to save souls? Because, therefore, the glory of the skins is so great, Christ, or the Church, groans because some are touched by the stain of sin, like skin grown old. Sin belongs to oldness, virtue to newness; whence: “stripping yourselves of the old man with his deeds, and putting on the new.” With this oldness the Church is worn, which in the present cannot be without spot and wrinkle. By the flesh the whole people in the body of Christ is signified, because it is soft and tender; whence: “whilst the wicked draw near against me, to eat my flesh.” For unless the flesh were in the oldness of sin, it would not be food for the enemies. He hath broken my bones, that is, the stronger; because in the passion of Christ even the apostles were broken and scattered by fear. He says God did this because he permitted it by just judgement.

35_interl11671: “They gave me gall for my food”
35_marg2724: He hath built and compassed me round about. So any soul grieves, shut in by the gall of malice, wearied with labour, most of all when she perceives herself pressed on every side and driven back by her own iniquities. For this the unclean spirits try: whether at any time, in any way, they may entangle the wretched soul in wicked delights and fill her with the worst longings, the last of which become more bitter than any gall.
35_marg2725: He hath built round about. The voice of the Church groaning, nay, of Christ in his members, who, taken in the passion, says: “I was delivered up, and came not forth”; because the Father, namely, had built a siege round about, when they surrounded him with weapons and torches and led him bound before the governor. Fenced round by this rampart, the manhood of Christ was afflicted as with the gall of bitterness and the labour of tribulation; so too, hemmed in, he was led to the passion, and there he was fed with gall and labour; whence: “They gave me gall for my food”, etc. In the gall is signified the bitterness of the passion in the mind; in the labour, tribulation in the flesh; that the whole passion of Christ may be understood. The same sufferings Christ suffers daily in the Church, which is of his flesh and of his bones, that she may “fill up those things that are wanting of the sufferings of Christ”. Hence he says: He hath built round about me. For the Church, besieged by all evils, walks among scorpions, where the seat of Satan is; she is hemmed in by the army of the heretics, she is given gall and labour to drink by false brethren, she is oppressed on every side by persecutors; torments of the mind; here the delights of the world and the longings of the flesh flatter her; the old enemy lays snares on every side; whence rightly she cries: He hath built round about me; whence elsewhere: “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly and be at rest?” By these things and the like she is made bitter in the mind as with gall; in the flesh she is wearied with labour.
