35_marg2726: With these three verses the letter Beth is filled up, which is interpreted “confusion”. For he who has fallen into oldness, his strength broken, is hemmed in by the siege of the old enemy, filled with the gall of bitterness, and set in darkness, that is, in confusion. Which is lamented as the true confusion of the human race. Rightly under this letter he laments the ruin of the whole house and the stains of oldness. For Beth is interpreted “house”, which for its confusion says: My skin he hath made old, etc. The oldness of the skin can indeed be referred to Christ, according to the mortality of the flesh which he put on; but the rest under this letter are more fittingly applied to himself.
35_marg2727: He hath set me in dark places. The soul, set in confusion, mourns step by step. First, because she lies withered by the oldness of sins; then, because, hemmed in by the enemy’s deceit, she cannot go out to freedom, compassed with the gall of the lusts and the stain of sins. At last, having lost the light, set in darkness, she cannot even see herself, how wretched she is, how unhappy, how oppressed with evils or stripped of goods. For this the enemy tries most of all: that the soul should lose the light, and not receive it again once lost. Hence the Philistines put out Samson’s eyes and then send him to the mill, that walking round and round he may never find the way of life. Hence Nabuchodonosor dug out Sedecias’ eyes and then led him bound into the dungeon of Babylon, that, shut up in confusion, he might see the light no more. But when such a soul, still bound in the flesh, weeps, she is not truly but as it were dead, while room for penance is given her, before “the pit shut her mouth upon her”. Which often, by God’s mercy, returns from the depth of iniquity to life. The letter Ghimel follows, which is interpreted “retribution” or “fullness”.
35_marg2728: He hath set me in dark places. In the prophets Christ is signified; whence: “By the ministry of the prophets I was represented”, and “at sundry times and in divers manners”, etc. The passion of Jeremias, therefore, signifies the passion of Christ; whence: He hath set me in dark places; which seems to belong rather to the head. For Christ died for us, not as the dead of the world, who receive death as the wages of iniquity and from the stock of sin; whence: as those that are dead for ever. For though he truly died, God does not cast him off for ever; he was set in darkness, either of hell, or of the tomb, or of the passion, but not dead for ever, because he was free among the dead, because without sin; whence he rose again quickly.

35_interl11678: Jeremias was fettered in prison; Christ bound by the Jews; the soul by the vices
35_marg2729: He hath built against me round about, etc. He seems to lament for himself and for the people: because he was weighed down with fetters in prison, and he grieves at the siege built against his people and the city, because he foresees that, sins standing in the way, they cannot escape. He hath shut out my prayer; whence: “Do not take up praise and prayer for them.” The ways and paths are shut up with square stones and turned upside down; which is meant by “made heavy”, so that they cannot flee; for the enemy has shut off all the outlets of the wretched city.
35_marg2730: He hath built against me round about, etc. The soul, over whom retribution (which Ghimel signifies) now hangs for her crimes, cries out: He hath built against me round about, etc.; as if: “The sorrows of death surrounded me.” Weighed down with these fetters, she fears that she cannot escape; hers it was to fall, but it is God’s mercy to rescue. To her this is pitiable: that, shut up in the prison of the worst captivity, she cannot enter into the freedom of good action. She is weighed down with the fetters of sins and fleshly pleasures, weighed down by the wiles of the enemy, so that, bound by these snares, she cannot freely hasten to the things that are not seen. We are weighed down with fetters as often as we add iniquity to iniquity, which is rightly described as sitting upon lead. He hath shut out my prayer. Tears and prayers win the mercy of the judge; whence she may well be saddened when she feels the judge so offended that her prayer cannot pass through to the fountain of mercy. Which happens as often as God so lets us sin that our crimes stop the ears of the kind judge; whence: “He that turneth away his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be an abomination.” He hath shut up my ways. Sins have their four-squareness; whence Virgil says: “Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice.” By these the roads of our sins are squared, that at length the unhappy soul may come back to herself, infected with oldness, hedged about by enemies, hemmed in by the gall of iniquity and misery, wearied by vain labours, against whom the enemies rage within and without. Weighed down by these fetters, let her ask the kind judge and press unceasingly, that at least for her importunity she may receive what she asks; because “the Lord is nigh unto all them that call upon him”, etc.; otherwise she cannot pass over to the country. The concupiscence of the eyes, the pleasure of the flesh and the pride of life have blocked her way. And if she turns to the holy Scriptures as to the pastures of life, in which she finds the right way, at once the square stones of the heretics meet her, by which the way of faith is blocked and the paths turned upside down. Whence let the soul say with the prophet: “Who will give me wings like a dove?” and with the Apostle: “Unhappy man that I am”, etc. For from all these grace alone sets free.
35_marg2731: He hath built against me round about. As if Christ said: The Father stirred up the hearts of the Jews against me, he built round about with cohorts, that I might not get out of their hands until the prophecies of the prophets were fulfilled; he shut out this prayer, namely: “Father, if it be possible, let this chalice pass from me.” The Church too is shut in by the doctrines of the heretics, hemmed in by the punishments of sinners or of persecutors; lamenting which, she ascribes it all to God, by whose judgement it is done. He hath made my fetters heavy, that is, the savagery of torments or of deceits; which no one doubts has often happened. She groans too that her prayer is shut out, while for her proving the divine help is put off, but not taken away; but she has an anchor, that is, her hope, fixed in heaven, lest she be drowned in the waves of this world.

35_marg2732: A bear lying in wait, etc. What more terrible than that the author of our salvation should become a bear and a lion to us? The bear is a treacherous beast, very strong in the arms and loins. And in Nabuchodonosor and in Titus and Vespasian, who elsewhere are called the boar and the wild beast, the Lord is called bear and lion, in whom the power of God takes vengeance on his enemies. He laments therefore that the kind and merciful Lord, as sins demanded, is a lion or a bear, that by his power the most wicked enemies may besiege and afflict her. Jerusalem is set as a mark for the arrow, because she is besieged with enemies poured round her on every side, that, often wounded as with arrows, she may return to the physician, even if compelled. These nations, as with a bow bent (yet with tempered judgement), he often sent against Jerusalem, that even so she might often learn to fear God, lest, wounded by the arrows of her enemies, she should fail. Her paths are turned aside by the enemies, and she herself is broken.
35_marg2733: A bear. Under the letter Daleth, which means “fear”, the soul, struck with fear, laments: He is become as a bear lying in wait; because, having experienced both the force of arrows in the open and that of ambushes in secret, she laments as one made desolate. He hath bent his bow, that is, his judgement, and yet he delays, because he would rather find those whom he may reward than those whom he may condemn; whence: “Thou hast given a warning to them that fear thee, that they may flee from before the bow.” By the bow the holy Scripture can be understood, in which the string of the New Testament bends the hardness of the Old. From it arrows are sent by which the hardness of the heart is pierced; and from the bow of judgement arrows are sent to destroy vices, and others which wound with charity. And the soul is as a mark, that from one side she may receive the wounds of charity, from the other drive back the darts of the enemy.
35_marg2734: A bear lying in wait, etc. It is the common voice of the head and the body, that he became a bear lying in wait to them who is eternal and unchangeable; not that he is changed from his nature of kindness and goodness, but because of the effects. For he allowed him to rise up against his Son who came as a bear lying in wait, and tried to destroy and deceive him by fraud and strength, as he did his body too from the beginning to the end: a lion in secret places. By these two beasts all the savagery of the devil is shown: by the lion the devil himself, by the bear his members, namely the heretics and false brethren. For the bear, though very strong in the arms and loins, is weak in the head; as all the wicked have a weak head, that is, the devil, who, either openly as a lion or in secret as a bear, goes about seeking whom he may devour. It is plain that he trusts in his own strength, who goes about roaring and gnashing; of whose ambushes the psalmist says: “He lieth in wait in secret, like a lion in his den.” With these weapons he fights against the members and the head; whence the prophet, nay, Christ and the Church, groans: He is become as a bear lying in wait, etc. These are the beasts that come against David, the shepherd of the sheep, and long to devour the flock. But David took the sheep out of the lion’s mouth and broke the jaws and arms of the bear; this is Christ, who leads his sheep to the pastures of life and takes them out of the lion’s mouth and breaks the arms of the bears; “and we are his people and the sheep of his pasture”. They take a ram out of the midst of his flock, as David himself, who, had the Lord not rescued him, would not have escaped. These beasts rise up against David, that is, Christ. David killed the lion and the bear; which was done in the death of Christ, when he set free the sheep. My paths, etc.: these he repeats mourning. He hath made me desolate: Jerusalem, namely, whom the prophet lamented above. Now perhaps come back to herself, nay, the bride of Christ dowered with his blood, she groans that she is desolate and forsaken by the bridegroom as an adulteress. As a mark for his arrows, etc. For Christ and the Church are set up as a target against all the powers of the air; whence: “We are made a spectacle to angels and to men”; Christ, in himself and in all his members, is set against the darts of the enemy.

35_marg2735: He hath shot into my reins, etc. The Lord by just judgement, as with a bow long bent, at length shoots into the reins arrows, the daughters of his quiver, to punish their lust, of whom it is said: “Every one neighed after his neighbour’s wife.” By the quiver is signified the hidden judgement of God, by which Nabuchodonosor and others are aimed like arrows against Jerusalem, that, set up as a mark, she may be wounded; she who, when the prophet rebuked her already besieged, mocked him as a trifler; whence he adds: I am made a derision to all my people, etc. He hath filled me with bitterness: he grieves that what the Lord had foretold was fulfilled in himself and in his people, namely the threat: “I will feed this people with wormwood, and give them water of gall to drink”; whence: he hath inebriated me with bitterness. For Jerusalem was filled both in the first captivity and in the second, and given wormwood to drink, namely straits and necessities. By the water of gall is signified the greatness of the evils, and the everlasting yoke of captivity, and the ignorance of the law, by which, filled with the bitterness of gall, they will receive Antichrist instead of Christ.
35_marg2736: He hath shot into my reins, etc. The soul too is made drunk daily with these and the like bitternesses, so that nothing seems sweet to her in the present, while she is unceasingly afflicted with such great evils.
35_marg2737: He hath shot into my reins, etc. The letter He is interpreted “I live” or “he is”. For from the beginning of this alphabet the emptying of Christ is shown, according to that: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant”, etc.; for which he bore reproaches, sufferings and death. But yet he always and unchangeably is and lives; as if he answered: I am mocked and afflicted, I am tormented, I die; but yet I truly am and truly live, and I do not will the death of the sinner, because life does not will death. For this is the common voice of the bridegroom and the bride, that she may confess that he is and lives, and he may answer, I am and I live; according to that: “I arose, and am still with thee.” This is I, “who is” and who lives, and laments for us and for them: He hath shot into my reins, etc. The quiver of God the Father is Scripture, from which the body of Christ received the judgement of God (as arrows from a bow), which he himself bore first. These arrows he sometimes makes burning, to wound cold hearts with the heat of charity. The heretics too sometimes bring out of this quiver the arrows of unbelief, poisoned, and strike the hearts of the innocent. From this quiver come the arrows by which the outer man is pierced with fear and the inner moved with love; whence: “Pierce thou my flesh with thy fear.” For when he says: He hath shot into my reins the daughters of his quiver, that is, the affections of divine fear or love. In the reins is fleshly begetting, and in faith the spiritual generation of the virtues. From these reins Christ begets in the womb of a chaste mother, that is, the Church; he shoots into the reins the daughters of his quiver, that is, arrows by which they are wounded to love or to fear, that vices may be destroyed and virtues begotten; whence David: “Burn my reins and my heart”, and elsewhere: “Thy arrows are fastened in me.” The holy preachers of God too are aimed from this quiver like arrows; whence: “In his quiver he hath hidden me”; as if Christ said: He hath hidden me as a chosen arrow in his quiver, that, hidden by the darkness of the Scriptures and at length shot from the bow, I may try the reins and hearts of all. I am made, etc. Like to which is: “I am a worm, and no man”, etc.; which was made plain in the passion. He hath filled me with the bitternesses of the passion, he hath inebriated me with wormwood, that is, with wine mingled with myrrh; whence: “They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” When he says he is inebriated with wormwood, he shows that he was touched by the bitterness of the passion within as well as without. With these and the like pains the whole body of Christ is tormented until the end.

35_marg2738: And he hath broken my teeth one by one, etc. No one doubts that Jeremias was afflicted by the people, and the people by the enemies; for the one was here almost destroyed by hunger, the other was devoured by every kind of punishment. Whence he laments that he was fed with ashes, so that the soul might be believed driven out of the body; whence he has forgotten good things, the remembrance of which quickly slips away amid punishments. The prophet mourns, therefore, the end of his people, and that the hope of their turning has perished. For “the wicked man, when he is come into the depth of sins, contemneth.”
35_marg2739: And he hath broken my teeth one by one, etc. The soul, seized with disgust for holy Scripture, laments the breaking of the teeth with which she ought to have ground and chewed over the word of God. For the animal which does not chew the cud is rejected in the law; to grind and chew over the word of God with the senses as with teeth is health and food. Whence it is said in praise that the teeth of Moses were not worn down, because he always chewed over the word of God in heart and mouth and ate the bread of angels unceasingly. But he whose teeth are broken is rightly fed with ashes, in which sadness of heart and penance are signified; whence Job, when he had seen and heard the Lord, said: “I do penance in dust and ashes”; because, namely, having seen the beauty and loftiness of God, he knew himself to be ashes and dust; and elsewhere: “They would have done penance long ago in sackcloth and ashes.” She says therefore: he hath fed me with ashes; as if: because I put off chewing over the word of God, I groan, fed with the ashes of mortality. My soul is removed, etc. She grieves that she is driven back by God and exposed to temptations, so that she cannot freely return to the good things she feels; who, oppressed by the sharpness of grief, cannot remember good things; whence she adds: my end is perished, etc. For this the letter Vau signifies, which means “it is not that one”; for he has perished and is not with the Lord, who is the true end and fulfilment. Therefore she mourns that her hope from the Lord has perished, because she cannot raise herself to the Lord. Whence well follows Zain, which is interpreted “lead thyself” or “hither”, as if it were said in the voice of a guide: Do not be long entangled in these evils, but lead thyself; and as if she asked where she ought to go, he answers pointing: hither, namely into the way of praying; and what and how she ought to pray he adds: Remember my poverty, etc.
35_marg2740: And he hath broken my teeth one by one, etc. The teeth of Christ, that is, the apostles and the other disciples, were broken and scattered in the passion; by whom, as by teeth, Christ passed believers into his body. He hath fed me with ashes, according to that: “I did eat ashes like bread”, etc. By which evils my soul is driven back: those whom he most loved and for whose sake he came persecuted him with every hatred; whence Jesus began to be weary and to fear. Under the letter Vau, therefore, these things are heightened, and by what has been said the harder things are tempered; it means “not so that one”, or “not that one”. For though he said: My end and my hope is perished from the Lord, that one did not think so, and that one did not forget the good things which he always had with the Father, or received according to the manhood; of which: “I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.” He did not, therefore, think so, though his soul was driven back by the hardness of the Jews; but he hints at the excessive pain and sorrow of his mind, as if, drunk with the bitterness of the passion, he could not remember good things, and, embittered, said: My end is perished. Among men he seemed to have perished, who said: “Himself he cannot save.” So the Church, driven back by the evils of heretics and persecutors, forgets past good things and, oppressed by new pains, says: My end is perished; whence: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps had well nigh slipped.”

35_marg2741: Remember my poverty, etc. From the beginning of this alphabet he describes the miseries of the wretched city, and of the passion of Christ, and of the Church in her labours, so that he even said, as if despairing: My end is perished. But as soon as it was heard from God, “Lead thyself”, at once, raised by new hope, turned to the Lord, he sends forth prayers, and promises that he will hope for better things from now on, forgetting his past sins. Whence it is to be noticed that these letters have been marked out with great mystery, by which, with sacraments of great understanding, the Spirit in the prophet mourned as in metre; and because the hidden word of God is overshadowed on this side and that with mysteries, which when unlocked lie open to human senses, the Spirit excellently put in these things and the like, to take away the readers’ weariness and, amid tears, to refresh the souls of those who understand.
35_marg2742: Remember my poverty, etc. The soul too is brought to life and led back by this word, to which it is said: “Lead thyself hither”; as if: “Take up thy bed and walk.” Whence she says in supplication: Remember my poverty, etc. For this soul in Adam, that is, in her first flower, transgressed and was stripped bare in poverty; but when in this letter she was bidden to lead herself away, she remembers with remembrance, and like the daughter of Abraham she is raised “against hope in hope”, and comes to the letter Heth, which is interpreted “life” and “fear”; that, after the tears of complaint, she may conceive the fear of the Lord, of which it is said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom”; and taste no less the word of God, and say the word of confession: The mercies of the Lord, that we are not consumed.
35_marg2743: Remember my poverty, etc. These are the words of Christ; they are of the Church, who shares with him, to whom it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Yet Christ did not transgress; nor does anyone offer his transgression to judgement, but modestly he says: “Turn away thy face from my sins.” But Christ was made transgression of the law for us, as he was made a curse and sin; whence: “Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree”, and “Him that knew no sin, for us he hath made sin”, that he might blot out both the sin and the curse, our transgression. Great therefore is what is said: Remember my poverty, etc.; because for us he was made poor, that he might make us rich and join the body to the head, that by the prayer of the head it may be cleansed. But the body, because in the present life it does not live without transgression, is filled with many miseries and with the bitterness of wormwood and gall; whence the Church is wearied with labours and pains, that, refined by sufferings, she may become more acceptable to her bridegroom; whence she says: Remember my poverty; as if she said: Remember what I suffer for my transgressions, that is, the wormwood and the gall. I will be mindful and remember, namely the eternal life; and therefore my soul will soon pine away, sighing for it, according to that: “My soul hath fainted after thy salvation.” Whence she adds: These things I shall think over in my heart, therefore will I hope in God. For when the Church directs herself to contemplating him, she groans as one fainting, and says as plainly as she can: I will be mindful and remember, from that remembrance namely of eternal life, which, breathed in within, gives life; that the members of Christ may learn to remember, think or love nothing else than to be formed again into newness. And the sudden progress of the Church is to be noted, who before came even to despair; but from the moment she heard the saving word, “Lead thyself”, at once she pined away with remembrance, and, thinking over what she had borne, she was led far away by that word. Yet in God, in whom I will hope; as if: “At thy word I will let down the net.” So against hope she grows strong in hope, refreshed by the remembrance of eternal life.

35_marg2744: The mercies of the Lord, etc. Laying aside the complaints of the lamentations, he begins to explain in the moral sense the way of returning to God, that no one may dare to presume on himself, because “it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy”; whence he adds: the mercy of the Lord, that we are not consumed, because, namely, “the remnant of Israel shall be saved”. So any soul ascribes it to the Lord’s mercy that she is not consumed by her crimes, in the weakness of the flesh, the delight of the world, the snares of the enemies, because his commiserations have not failed; whence David says: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy”; as if: great is the mercy, and great the sins, and many the iniquities, but many too the commiserations. Whence no one must lose trust lest the commiserations fail; the fountain of mercy is not dried up unless you have first been dried up. This is the beginning of our conversion and the beginning of life, the fear of the Lord; whence: “Blessed is the man that feareth the Lord”; for those who fear are blessed and wise; whence: “Blessed is the man whom thou shalt instruct, O Lord, and shalt teach him out of thy law.” For fear belongs to the saints too; whence “a dread fell upon Abraham” when he sacrificed, and David says: “I said in my fear: Every man is a liar.” Those who have this fear have life too; and how acceptable it is is laid open when it is said: “I knew it in the morning; great is thy faithfulness”; as if: after the tears of the complaints, after so great a punishment, after the confession of crimes, after prayer and confession, I will not put off mercy. I have known thy tribulation and thy patience. I have known the constancy of the faith of one who says: The Lord’s commiserations have not failed. I have known it in the morning, because great is thy faithfulness; as if he said: I have approved what thou hast numbered, humbly groaning, and I have made thee know that great is thy faithfulness, in the morning, when the ray of faith arose, namely when Christ rose again; in which morning she is commended by the Lord, who before seemed by weakness to have perished, according to that: My end is perished. After their manner the prophets often change speakers and tenses; whence in the Canticle of Canticles now the bridegroom speaks to the bride, now she to the bridegroom, now to the companions and friends; many times the bridegroom is absent, many times present, that the bride’s longing may be kindled. Here too the bridegroom is at once present to the bride lamenting her straits, to comfort her, saying: “I knew it in the morning; great is thy faithfulness.” Whence she answers: The Lord is my portion, said my soul: therefore will I wait for him. Happy he who can say this, a stranger to the vices, set apart from every stain of sin; which David too set in the eighth place under the same letter: “I have said, O Lord, my portion is to keep thy law.” For this is the voice only of him who passes from the seventh to the eighth, that is, from the present and old life to the life to come and new, which does not covet earthly things, waits only for God, whom it loves, and lives not to itself but to God. Whence it comes to the letter Teth, which is interpreted “shutting out” or “good”. For such a one clings to the highest God, shut out from all worldly business; he neither fears threats nor embraces delights, because “perfect charity casteth out fear”. Whence it follows: The Lord is good to them that hope in him.

35_marg2745: The Lord is good, etc. Or according to others: It is good to wait and hope for the salvation of God. For who truly waits for the Lord but he who by the zeal of charity is shut out from every stain of iniquity? Who hopes, unless he truly loves and longs? For what we hope for we wait for with patience; so he who hopes waits with patience and shuts out the fleshly affections. And so under this letter both interpretations, which seem to disagree, fit together, that the Lord is good to them that hope in him. For those who hope do not sin; whence David says under the same letter: “Thou hast done good to thy servant, O Lord”, and elsewhere: “How good is God to Israel, to them that are of a right heart.” But with the perverse he is perverted, though he is good by nature. And lest hope be idle, he at once adds: to the soul that seeketh him; because he who hopes does not yet have, but enjoys in hope what he will have in reality. Whence: “In my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loveth”; where four things necessary to everyone who seeks are noted: that he should consider what he seeks, and where, and when, and how long, namely until he finds. For no one doubts that he who seeks God in the bed of rest and in the night of blindness cannot find him; but let him leave the bed, come to the day, seek until he finds. And where he is to be sought Moses hints: “The word is nigh, in thy mouth and in thy heart”; of which it is said: “His place is in peace”, of him, namely, who “will speak peace unto his people, and unto them that are converted to the heart”. Because, therefore, he is immeasurable, he is always to be answered and waited for; whence it follows: It is good to wait with silence for the salvation of God.
35_marg2746: It is good to wait, etc. Note how far he has advanced after he has regained his strength in the moral sense: shutting out all the things of the world, he passes beyond the angelic dignity to find him whom he loves; which he confesses as the highest good to be waited for and hoped for; and that he may always cling to him he says: It is good for a man if he has borne the yoke of the Lord from his youth, namely to sit solitary and hold his peace. All these good things are a shutting out, that he may sit alone with God who feels himself bearing a heavy yoke from his youth. But because this instruction is said only in the moral sense, let us see of what yoke it is said. For there is a heavy yoke upon the children of Adam; there is a yoke of unbelief; there is the light yoke of the Lord, lightened by the hope of eternal reward, of which it is said: “Take up my yoke upon you.” And if anyone, burdened with the load of sins, has borne this yoke, he will sit singly with God, namely, and with him who hopes singly in him. This yoke, for the harshness of correction, is heavy, but for the hope of reward sweet. He who has borne this yoke will sit solitary with God, not mixed with crowds of business or longings; he will be silent from all the din of the world, or no excuse for sin will be needful to him. And it is a great thing for the young to keep themselves from vices and to flee the error of a slippery and tangled way; whence David adds: “The sins of my youth and my ignorances do not remember, O Lord.” For this age is frail and slippery, and its justice rash. He takes this heavy yoke up upon himself who from his youth renounces the world and is silent, as if deaf, to the tumults of troubles. He is rightly said to have taken this up upon himself, because whatever newness is commanded is beyond the strength of corrupted nature.
35_marg2747: There follows Jod, which means “beginning” or “desolation”, under which he laments who puts his mouth in the dust; or, according to others, who will give his mouth in burial, in the digging, if so be there is hope of patience. But in the moral sense, after the punishments of miseries, faith being restored, the beginning of our profession is to put the mouth in the dust and every moment to think that we are dust. Whence hope is doubled and charity enlarged. All these things said above are understood of the head, with whom if we suffer we shall also reign; whence it follows: He shall give his cheek to him that striketh him, etc.; like to which: “If one strike thee on thy right cheek, turn to him also the other.” These things can be understood of the earthly Jerusalem humbled in captivity, but it is better to ascribe them to Christ and the Church. And this is the gospel precept, a good beginning namely, when we have begun to keep and fulfil it; as if we said: This will we render to the Lord for all the things that he hath rendered to us; we will take the chalice of salvation. 35_marg2750: To crush under his feet. In a wonderful manner, after the way of poets, since three verses begin with one letter, they end with one word, one clause; so that the sense is: The Lord hath not approved to crush under his feet all the prisoners of the land, and the Lord hath not approved to turn aside the judgement of a man, to destroy a man wrongfully in his judgement. This too he has not approved, because he would rather save than condemn; and this is great discipline, or confession of the heart. For Lamed signifies both, or “I keep”; by which senses a great obscurity is cleared, that we may understand that the things he says are to be kept under the discipline of Christ and with purity of heart. For he who has the discipline of Christ professes that he keeps the precepts of salvation with purity of heart, because he did not so cast off the prisoners of the land as to crush them, etc., that is, he does not know how to crush those bound by the crimes of the earth; because he did not so cast off as to drive away; he of whom it is said: “Thou hast subjected all things under his feet”, because he has been made the judge of all. Confidently he adds: the Lord hath not approved to turn aside the judgement of a man, because he knows how to judge justly; and he has not approved to destroy a man wrongfully in his judgement; which can be taken either of the present or of the future. For the evils that are brought on by the Lord are either punishments of deserts or the cause of good things to come; for “all his ways are mercy and truth”. So according to the discipline of Christ he professes innocence of heart, and the man who sees God says: I keep the divine precept. Well said against the heretics, who affirm that God cruelly afflicts souls handed over to bodily prisons, and in the Old Testament punished much with indiscriminate prejudgements. This man, taught by scourges according to that, “With the rod shalt thou be chastised, O daughter of Sion”, confesses with purity of heart that all things are done by the just judgement of God, that he may give salvation to all who call upon him in truth; and according to the interpretation of the letter he cries: I keep the discipline of chastisement, I keep the purity of my profession, I keep among the heretics an inviolate faith. Great is the progress of the soul, that amid so many perils it is not separated from the charity of Christ, but says: “Our eyes are unto the Lord our God.” After the constancy of this faith he comes to the letter Mem, girded to defend justice against the Epicureans and against those who say that God does not care for mortal things; against whom that psalm is directed in which it is said: “How doth God know? and is there knowledge in the most High?” whom too this great man rebukes with these words: Who is he that hath commanded?

The Scriptures too are pastures, by which we are fed and instructed; but the only-begotten is the spiritual pasture, to whom we ought to lift up our hearts with our hands to heaven, where the true pastures are. And it is to be noted that hearts are not lifted up without hands, nor hands without hearts, that soundness of faith and working may commend us to God. For that is true faith “which worketh by charity”. And so, going over our poverty, let us say to God: We have done wickedly, and, what is worse, we have provoked thee to wrath; therefore thou art inexorable. All the teaching of the Scriptures is rendered in the understanding of these three verses: that we should search our ways, that is, our actions, and seek what we have been and what we are, and return to the Lord by repenting, from whom we departed by sinning. It is a great thing for each one to know himself; whence Moses: “Take heed to thyself, lest perhaps a wicked thought steal in upon thee”; take heed to thyself, not to riches, not to possessions, not to strength, but to thy spirit and mind, whence come deeds and counsels and thoughts; take heed to thyself there, where the better things are. (The heathen fable ascribes this to Apollo, as if he were the author of the saying “Know thyself”, though it was carried over to the philosophers from Moses, who was earlier.) Hence too Solomon: “If thou know not thyself, O fairest among women, go forth, and follow after the steps of thy flocks.”

35_marg2755: Samech is interpreted “hear”, or “firmament”, or “help”; which sense is made plain by the words that follow: Thou hast set a cloud before thee, etc. For those who do not mourn past sins and provoke God with new ones make God inexorable daily by sinning; which is lamented above under the same letter: The Lord hath taken away all my mighty men out of the midst of me, etc. For he did not take away all the mighty men then, when the people was led into Babylon, but when Christ came and Judea did not know the time of her visitation and would not raise her captive neck and receive the light of faith. Though he seems to weep for the captivity of the Chaldeans, yet by the prophetic spirit he laments the spiritual captivity, into which the true Chaldean takes captive with the chains of error. These streams of water wash away sins, pour into the beds of delights, that all the spices of the virtues may flow. These streams of water the Church brings down with force from Libanus, washing away sins. For this grace of the Holy Spirit is to some a fountain, to others a well, to others a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed, to others a stream of gardens; which are numbered as it were as streams. And he brings down streams of water who pours them out washing away each crime, or soothes the wounds of love; whence: “I am wounded with charity.” She brought down that stream of water who watered the Lord’s feet with tears; David brought down streams according to the multitude of his sins; and Peter wept bitterly. Christ wept in the passion, when, being in an agony, he prayed the longer. He wept over Jerusalem and over Lazarus; and the saints weep, “going and casting their seeds”, and bring down streams of water, that they may receive fruit more richly.

35_marg2761: It is interpreted “fountain” or “eye”; whence: My eye is afflicted, etc. My eye hath wasted my soul, whose office, namely, is to announce what it sees. Christ too is set for the ruin of some, for the resurrection of others. In this letter the office of the eyes is declared, that so, namely, they should weep for sins or for longings for heavenly grace; these delight in sweet things and are offended by harsh ones. Whence Ennon is called “the eye of punishments”, or “of temptation”, or “of the kid”, or “of the heifer”, or “of generation”, or “the fountain of generation”, where namely John baptized, that, through their affliction, born again by the fountain of generation, they might pass into the adoption of the sons of God. And this is: My eye is afflicted with pains, that is, I am afflicted, and I have not been quiet; for tears rise from the cheek to heaven. It is called the eye of temptation because through it we are tempted; whence: “Whosoever shall look on a woman to lust after her”, etc. He does not simply say, whoever shall look on a woman, but adds: to lust after her, etc.; where he has acquitted the eye and bound the mind; nor did he say he committed adultery in the eye, but in the heart. And it is the eye of the kid, which is namely on the left; for the sinner cannot see the things on the right; whence: “I set the Lord always in my sight.” It is the eye of the heifer, when sinners draw their iniquities as with the heifer’s constant strap. And it is the eye of generation, or the fountain of generation, because from the sight of the eyes either good or evil things are begotten; and it is the eye of punishments, because the one born again shudders with fearful heart at the punishments of his sins. And therefore Ain is called “eye” or “fountain”.

35_marg2762: Sade: comfort, or of justice. In these words is shown us the comfort from the Lord’s passion, and the justices by which we are made just; though the wickedness of the faithless (as if hunting a bird) seized Christ with swords and clubs without cause. Jeremias too was taken without cause, was put in the pit, and the persecutors flowed over his head like waves of water; but these things are said more plainly of Christ, who is lamented as caught like a bird. Whence Job: “The bird hath not known the path.” This bird is perhaps the eagle that “enticeth her young to fly”, that is, the Jews, “spreading her wings over them”; who, when he wished to gather them under his wings like a hen, was made weak and taken; whence: My life is fallen into the pit. This pit the Lord alone trod, when by dying he destroyed death and by rising restored life. They have laid a stone over me: what plainer? For the stone was laid, and sealed too, and after the resurrection rolled back by the angel. Christ was counted “with them that go down to the pit, as a man without help”, but was found “free among the dead”. Waters have flowed, that is, the multitude of the people, over Christ, who is our head.
35_marg2763: They have chased, etc. The voice of the Church, that is, of the body, over whose head the waters, that is, the peoples, flowed to destroy him without cause; whence in the voice of the Church, as if frustrated in her hope, it is added: I am cut off; because the disciples too, leaving him, fled, denied, doubted. Whence rightly Sade is set first, which is interpreted “comfort”; because, unless the comfort of the kind shepherd were present, no sheep would be safe. Whence it is plain that the temptation of the passion was not without the comfort of the Holy Spirit, who would strengthen the despairing and restore or uphold faith; whence: “I have prayed for thee, Peter, that thy faith fail not.” As far as in him lay he denied, but in God his faith remained. So, therefore, in the voice of the Church it is fittingly said: I am cut off; but by the foreknowledge and promise of the kind master faith was unconquered. And comfort comes in many ways: for Scripture comforts, and the mercy of the judge, and the penalty of the sin paid. Whence: “Be comforted, my people”, and a little after: “Her iniquity is forgiven: she hath received of the hand of the Lord double for all her sins”; and if faith were lacking, the penalty would make satisfaction. Comfort comes in divers temptations, because “tribulation worketh patience, and patience trial, and trial hope”. Tears too comfort, by which crimes are washed away; whence: “The Lord hath heard the voice of my weeping.” So when the punishments we bear for sins have run their course, we are sure of pardon. For in these the comfort of the Holy Spirit is not lacking, if hardness of heart is not present. These are “the justices of the Lord, rejoicing hearts”. For Sade is interpreted “comfort” or “justices”; for from the Lord’s passion we have received manifold comfort, and, made like to him in scourge and sufferings, we are justified; whence: “Son, remember that thou didst receive good things in thy lifetime, and likewise Lazarus evil things; but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented.” Now after the passion, after the comfort, after the temptation, let us see what follows, that is: calling, or shutting in, or behold; whence alluding to it it is said: I have called upon thy name, O Lord; and above under the same letter: I called for my friends.

35_marg2764: I have called upon thy name, O Lord. The voice of Christ according to the manhood; as if: although my life is fallen into the pit, yet I have called from the lowest pit, as Jonas from the belly of the whale; like to which Job said: “If I go down into the depth of hell, thence wilt thou deliver me”; whence the head too says confidently: In the day when I shall call upon thee, O Lord, thou hast said: Fear not. Whence here too: Thou hast heard my voice, etc. Thou drewest near: he cannot perish to whom the Father is near; he whose voice he had heard could not doubt. But because Coph is also interpreted “shutting in”, rightly he who has perished prays groaning: Turn not away thy face, etc. For, made flesh, he had gone down to the lowest parts of the mountains, shut in by the bars of the earth, and he knew with confidence that the Father would set his life free from corruption; pressed by which, grieving with us for us, he said: I have called upon thy name, O Lord; which Jonas in the belly of the whale had foreshown. Therefore Coph is rightly called “shutting in”, because the Lord “hath concluded all under sin”, that the door of life may be opened to us through him who in the corruption of the flesh came even to the lowest parts of the pit, but, calling, was heard for his reverence. We too, shut in by corruption and sin, believe that the same will be present to us; therefore he says: Thou drewest near, etc., that we may confidently say and hope the same. And we who are so shut in ought to behold and look about us; whence Coph is interpreted “behold”; as if: behold how mortality and corruption have brought me to the lowest parts of the pit; behold with what snare I am shut in, and do not pretend not to see the weakness and the danger; each one is shut in by countless snares. Coph is also called “calling”, that, shut in, we may call continually on him who, coming from heaven, bore our infirmities, who says: “They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill.” You have wounds: do not put off the medicine. Behold with spiritual eyes how you are shut in; whence David: “I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me; my help is from the Lord”; and elsewhere: “Our eyes are unto the Lord our God.” Hence too above, under the same letter: Pour out thy heart like water before the face of the Lord. Therefore under this letter the form of our Redeemer is set before us, who calls from the lowest pit and prays confidently and groans and cries, not with the voice but with the mind; everywhere he feels the Lord present, and drawing near in the day of calling, and God saying: Fear not; who says: “Have confidence, I have overcome the world.” Whence: “The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear?” etc. Such a voice of the heart, such faith, is a great cry. For the voice of the heart is a cry, and the voice of blood, which reaches the Lord; this voice is lifted up by the loftiness and harmony of the virtues, not by the straining of sounds. Great is the cry of faith, by which “we cry Abba, Father.” The Spirit too cries for us “with unspeakable groanings”. Great is the voice of justice and charity, by which the dead not only speak but cry, like Abel. Great is the voice of the apostles, because “their sound hath gone forth into all the earth”. With this voice our head cries, and the members; Rachel cried, weeping for her children, saying: Turn not away thy ear from my sighs, etc. Moses cries, to whom it is said: “Why criest thou to me?” But it is to be known that some cry in the heart, others speak in the heart: Anna spoke, because she prayed for private things, that is, for children; Moses cried with the ardour of charity. Under this letter, therefore, the shutting in of our drowning is expressed, and calling is shown, that we may cry the more. To each it is said: Behold how thou art shut in; cry to God, who is near. Turn not away thy ear, etc., because the Lord hath concluded all under sin, that he may have mercy on all. Whence: Be afflicted, weep, behold your shutting in, call from the lowest pit.

35_marg2766: Res: head, or of the head, or primacy. The head is ours, or the form of the head, that we may consider the author of life, who is our head, cherishing all, ruling all, filling all with the senses; for “the eyes of a wise man are in his head”; the head being taken away, the body is not known, nor does any cause of living remain. Let us hear, then, what the head thinks of itself: Thou hast judged, O Lord, the cause of my soul, etc. This voice is of the head as much as of the body; neither is the head without the body nor the body without the head. The cause of the soul is the justice which is fitted to the head; the redemption is of the body; for what is sold is redeemed. Under sin the body does not trust its own strength, unless the justice of the head supports it. The justice of Christ, therefore, is the judgement of the Father, the redemption of man. In the manner of rhetoric, then, he seeks favour from the person of the judge: he praises the just judge; then he shows the cause of the soul; at last why he came, that is, the redemption. For he is the Redeemer of our life, which he declares to be his own because of charity, that we may live in him and he in us. At length, by indignation against the adversaries, he recalls their iniquity and fury, to make the judge merciful towards himself and indignant towards the adversaries; as if he said: though thou hast approved the cause of my soul, yet thou hast seen their fury against me. Judge, therefore, my judgement. In which it is plain that he punishes iniquity by condemning it, loves equity, and discerns the thoughts of each; who (as the head rules and quickens the members) dispenses all things justly. And this is the voice of the elect, that is, of the body of Christ, who have obtained the primacy of the blessing. For Res means “primacy”: one is the people which in Esau sold the birthright, another which bought it. Each member of the body, therefore, shares the grace of the head and lays claim to the primacy of grace, that the vigour of the head may reach each member. In the head is the vigour of life and the primacy of our inheritance; for this we ought to guard with the whole body exposed, as the serpent guards its head and exposes its body, as if it knew that life is in it. Without this head we do not live. So in these three verses the elect are commended to the Father through the head, which is Christ, and are offered, justified and redeemed by his judgement; and the iniquity and fury and thoughts of the adversaries are condemned; and the wonderful unity of head and body is declared. Redeemer of my life; others, defender: the redemption is of the members, the defence of the head and body; redemption and defence, therefore, of our whole salvation is offered to the Father through Christ, that by his single death the redemption of our double death may be shown. It remains, then, that we keep the primacy in the head, which cannot be taken away unless Christ is taken away. Let the guarding of the head, therefore, be the sum of our zeal and work, the sum of our hope and virtue, that we may be joined to our head in the unity of the body of Christ. Whence Isaias: “The Lord shall destroy out of Israel the head and the tail”, that is, the beginning and the end. Judea lost the head when she did not receive Christ, who is the beginning of the Church, and the primacy, and the firstborn from the dead. He is “the end of the law unto justice to every one that believeth”, through whom iniquity is condemned, equity crowned, the fury and thoughts of the adversaries rejected. Now let us see what the letter Sin brings against them.

35_marg2767: Sin: of the teeth, or upon the wound of the teeth. The reproaches against Christ are lamented, of which it is said: “whose teeth are weapons and arrows”, etc.; whose lips rise up against the truth, as “deceitful lips; with a double heart have they spoken”. Under this same letter David says: “Princes have persecuted me without cause”, etc.; who elsewhere, as if expounding the interpretation of this letter, says: “They have added to the grief of my wounds”; as if they took death from the medicine; whence: “Add thou iniquity upon their iniquity”, etc. For this letter is interpreted, as we have said, “upon the wound”; whence the prophet laments that, while the wounds were being cured with this medicine, they added to them, because they rendered evil for good and reaped faithlessness from the faith of the prophets, and adding murders to faithlessness; these evils, completed, the just arbiter offers to the just judgement of the Father to be punished; whose unbelief was a wound upon a wound, the killing of the Lord. Upon a wound a remedy is rightly laid, by which the wound’s harshness may be soothed; upon a wound oil is poured, that it may be softened. But these, rejecting the remedy, added faithlessness and death upon the wound of unbelief; as all the reprobate, from the patience of God which leads us to penance, according to the hardness of their heart treasure up wrath for themselves. All their thoughts, etc.: he hints that God is everywhere present, to whom all thoughts and hearts are at hand. Thou hast heard their reproach, etc.: for him to hear is to see, and to see is to know, from whom nothing is hidden, to whom all things lie open. But the reprobate, as if upon the wound of sin, treasure up wrath for themselves; whence he adds: Their sitting down and their rising up, etc. For by insulting and sneering they rage no less against the head than against the body, as judges and teachers “sitting in the chair of pestilence”; of whom none is cherished by the remedy, because “the whole head is sick and the whole heart is sad; from the sole of the foot unto the top of the head there is no soundness therein”; and where the whole is imperilled, the whole body is consumed. It is no longer for laying on a plaster. But there is also a wound of the mind, which is cherished with the oil of the Holy Spirit and with peaceful words, by which the poison of wickedness is driven out. For there are the poultices of words and the medicines; there are the bonds of the law, by which the bound are loosed, the broken made firm. So under these verses is lamented the madness beyond recall of the wicked, who drive back every medicine which Christ brought as upon a wound; who poured wine and oil into the wounds of the man left half dead, and bound them up, and committed him to the innkeeper to take care of him, who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho. Let us beware, then, lest we go down from Jerusalem by sinning, but let us go up by doing good. Yet if we have sinned, let us not despair, because we have a physician who has laid the binding, namely of heavenly words, upon the wound, saying: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” He cures wounds, he makes the broken firm. Therefore those are lamented as despairing who rave unceasingly against Christ and the Church, mocking and sneering, who will be judged according to their works; whence it follows: Thou shalt render them a recompense, O Lord, etc.

And here we must seek some things of the Church and some of the passion of Christ in a higher sense, which we cannot do without tears. Let us ask, then, as sitting upon the ass, that is, upon the wanton flesh, that God may deign to water the dry soul, and if not the upper watering, at least grant the lower.
35_marg2713: … in the funeral lamentation of the whole body, deep mysteries of Christ and his body are opened, and the mournful speech runs now to the Synagogue, now to the Church, then to the passion of Christ. Now it treats of Christ and his body, as the first verse of this alphabet hints; now the moral sense is mixed in; if perhaps the hardness of our heart may be melted into tears, either for those who slip from the body of Christ, or for the things which happened to the Jews in captivity, or for the things which are done in the head, or for those which the members suffer, or because we are deprived of good things. And that we may better discern what belongs to the head and what to the body, let the first rule of Tyconius be looked to, which is of Christ and his body: when there is a passing from the head to the body, or from the body to the head, without change of person, or when the same sentence seems to fit the head no less than the body, and yet there is no departing from the same person; as in this verse: I am the man that see my poverty, etc., and: My skin he hath made old, etc. For the one of these, though it fits the whole body, is yet more fittingly applied to the head; the other to the members, so that by the flesh and skin and bones those are understood who in the Church are touched by the oldness of contagion and broken by the pressures of tribulations. For what he says, I am the man that see my poverty, though it fits the lamenting prophet, yet sounds more plainly the voice of Christ, who “by the ministry of the prophets was represented”, and gathers all into himself by regeneration, that we may meet “unto a perfect man”, and the fullness of the body of Christ.
35_marg2714: To the careful reader it is plain that almost all the lamentations of Jeremias are marked by the fifth topic of complaint. For the several hardships are bewailed, so laid out before the eyes of the judge that he may seem to see them and, from the thing itself, come down to mercy.

35_marg2768: Thau: signs, or he erred, or he fulfilled. For the things said here are signs of things to come; whence the psalmist: “Thou hast shewn thy people hard things”; “Thou hast given a warning to them that fear thee, that they may flee from before the bow.” But because they would not turn away, thou shalt render them a recompense, O Lord, according to their works. This he first rendered to the Jews, who, hardened in heart and blinded by faithlessness, were driven further from faith and truth, so that they could not enter into the justice of God and the way of salvation; for those who killed life deserved death. For they erred, according as Thau is interpreted “he erred”. And every reprobate errs who is hardened with an impenitent heart. Therefore the Lord too fulfilled his justice, which is signified by the letter Thau, namely fulfilment, which means justice. Whence it follows: Thou shalt give them a buckler of heart, etc.; who, while they mocked the labour of the passion, covered their heart with the same, and did not let it be pierced by the darts of preaching. So too the reprobate, whom the patience of God invites to penance, set the same against themselves as a buckler of heart, that they may not see what he labours in bearing; and so they treasure up wrath for themselves. The bow of judgement is bent while the patience of God bears with them; but these throw up hardness of heart and excuses, that they may not receive the words of life. Hence the prophet says: “I have laboured in bearing”, when the faithless saw the Son of God labouring in the passion. Because, therefore, they despised the warning to flee from before the bow, rightly it follows: Thou shalt persecute them in anger, etc.; that, because, hardened, sitting in the chair of pestilence and rising up against the Lord, they may be destroyed like dust from the face of the earth under the heavens, because they would neither be heaven nor cling to heavenly disciplines. For those who persecuted Christ and his members were rightly destroyed in the persecution of fury, that they may hear: “Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire”, etc. For these are the signs which ran before, that they might flee from before the bow, and they would not. Whence earlier, under this letter, it was set out in the voice of the Church: Let all their evil be present before thee, and make vintage of them for all my iniquities, etc. And in another alphabet: There was none in the day of the wrath of the Lord that escaped and was left, etc. Rightly, therefore, Thau means fulfilment, because under it justice, which is Christ, received its end and fulfilment; and wickedness the fulfilment of damnation and its end, that it may no longer be lifted up. In both, the signs that went before bear witness to the truth of their meaning. For the Lord showed his people hard things in the sign of the cross, “that thy beloved may be delivered”. But those who would not be signed with the sign of the cross the truth of the signs will overtake, and the destruction of eternal punishment, who threw up the buckler of faithlessness against teachings and against miracles. But the elect have the shield of good will, with which they are crowned, because those whom God helps by protecting he crowns by rewarding. Of the shield of the reprobate it is said: “His body is like molten shields.” For the reprobate are the body of the devil, like molten shields, fragile and weak. Molten shields are strong against arrows but fragile in a fall; so the reprobate are hard through obstinacy, fragile through their life; they are pierced by no dart of preaching, because they are protected by the shield of wicked defence. Of such, therefore, it is rightly lamented: Thou shalt give them a buckler of heart, etc. For, abusing the patience of God, they think that God does not care for such things, or does not see such things, or that the maker is at fault; like Adam, who said: “The woman, whom thou gavest me, persuaded me, and I did eat.” The woman too, turning the blame back on the serpent, aims it slantwise at the author. Protected by this shield, Cain said proudly and insultingly, with deceitful humility and false denial: “I know not, Lord; am I my brother’s keeper?” etc.: a stubborn upbraiding against God. So each one, while he abuses the patience of God and scorns to fear the signs of judgement and is not fortified by the sign of this letter, is punished with the just vengeance of damnation, who not only erred but also fulfilled and filled up the measure of his sins; whence: “The iniquities of the Amorrhites are not as yet at the full”; and when these were full, at once the promise and the vengeance came; which is shown here too by the letter which is interpreted “he fulfilled”. “Sin, when it is completed, begetteth death”; the hard and impenitent heart is the fulfilment. With groaning and tears, therefore, let us pray that the Lord may soften our heart, that we may fear his signs and, given to drink of the wine of compunction, flee from before the bow.

35_marg2769: No one is unaware that the Lamentations are composed in the grand style. For the words of each thing are set down adorned, whether proper or figurative; weighty sentences with amplification and pity, and adorned sentences with weight of words; as here: How is the gold become dim, etc.
35_marg2770: How, etc. The voice of one grieving and rebuking, like that other: How doth the city sit solitary that was full of people, etc. The hardness of the Jews is lamented, whose fathers shone like gold and precious stones in the sanctuary of God, glorious in faith and works; their descendants, when Christ came, were turned to faithlessness.
35_marg2771: Gold, etc. Because faith remains in us and the sacrament of baptism, we are called gold and the stones of the sanctuary; but we are dimmed by the soot of sins and scattered through divers kinds of business.
35_marg2772: The stones of the sanctuary: the virtues of the faithful soul. It is to be noted how great the force of this lament is, how the prophet’s charity stretches itself to all things: he laments the blindness of the Jews, the scattering of the churches, the nakedness of souls.
35_marg2773: How is the gold become dim, etc., namely the splendour of faith and innocence which once shone in that people; and they are scattered, not only through the business of vanity, but into foreign nations, who before had been scattered in the top of every street, walking, namely, the wide and broad way. For justly those who drove themselves out of the sanctuary of God into the business of the world are driven out from faith into faithlessness, and then taken captive.
35_marg2774: How is … become dim. The soul laments herself: in baptism made white as snow, coloured more beautifully than gold by the pouring in of the Holy Spirit, but afterwards either infected with heresies or darkened with vices; whose wisdom shone brighter than gold, marked out with the colours of eloquence; but while she takes delight in lusts, the gold is dimmed and the colour is blackened by vices. The soul has the divine word, more shining than gold, which is coloured by inner charity. But when it is applied to earthly things, the gold is dimmed and the colour is changed, namely into love of worldly things from love of heavenly ones; the stones of the sanctuary, that is, the virtues of the soul, are scattered in the top of every street, because, charity being lost, the rest are dissolved and bend to the lust of the worldly life, as it were in the top of every street. And the stones which she ought to have borne on her breast, fastened upon the rational of judgement, for the glory and praise of God and of her own beauty, the colour of the love of God being changed for the worse, lie scattered in the top of the streets. Yet because the substance of the word of God remains uncorrupted in us, though dimmed by sins, it is lamented not as the substance of nature destroyed but as dimmed; and though the heretics seem to corrupt the soundness of the faith, the force and nature of the word is not dissolved: it is dimmed indeed, but not corrupted. So the gold is dimmed, namely “the word of God is fire-tried”, and “the commandment of the Lord is lightsome, enlightening the eyes”; as if he said: how is that dimmed to me which gives light to others and converts deserters.
35_marg2775: How is … become dim, etc. The voice of the Church. The gold was the innocence of God and the privilege of the patriarchs; but they have been dimmed by the filth of sins. Or the gold dimmed is the reprobate life of the ministers of God, darkened by filth, once glorious with virtues, now dimmed by the business of the world. The finest colour, the garb of holiness, is changed by earthly and base things. The stones of the sanctuary are scattered, etc., those namely which were kept within for the uses of the high priest when he entered the holy of holies. The stones of the sanctuary too are the priests of Christ and ministers of the altar, the choirs of monks and virgins, who ought always to stand in the sight of God, who ought not to go outside nor be taken up with worldly things; but when they are scattered outside by restlessness of mind, rightly they are lamented as wandering in the top of the streets. There is no action of worldly life which priests and ministers of the altar do not administer; monks are entangled in worldly business; the chastity of virgins is exposed to many allurements. Platea in Greek is named from breadth; for “wide and broad is the way that leadeth to destruction”. So the stones are scattered not only in the streets but in the top of every street, when through longing they do the works of this world, and from the religious habit then seek the height of honour and praise. The order of these stones the Lord promises, saying: “I will lay thy stones in order, and will lay thy foundations with sapphires, and I will make thy bulwarks of jasper”, etc. Christ laid in the Church the souls of the elect, marked out by the variety of their deserts; he founded her on sapphires, which are of the colour of the sky, that is, on souls that seek heavenly things; he set jasper, which is of green colour, for bulwarks, namely those who in the greenness of faith defend the Church against the dry and withering.

35_marg2776: The sons of Sion, etc. The privilege of the Jews is shown, who were not only sons of the earthly Sion but of the heavenly, noble by birth and teaching, adopted by the privilege of grace before all as sons of God and called friends; whose fathers were patriarchs and prophets, of whom is Christ. Clothed with the best gold, that is, the wisdom of God; whence: “There is a treasure to be desired in the mouth of the wise.” Clothed with this gold they shone as lights in the world: with the best gold, that is, heavenly wisdom, not the second, that is, worldly; according to that: “Her first and purest fruits.” For since the root of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, its fruit is to see him.
35_marg2777: With this gold the Church too glories that she is clothed; but both the Jews, changed, are esteemed as earthen vessels, and members of the Church. For the members and sons of the Church, clothed with the wisdom of the love of God and of the neighbour, slip to frail and earthly works, and become earthen vessels, who ought to have been incorruptible and heavenly vessels. Clothed with this gold is the Church, “fair as the moon, bright as the sun”, and her noble sons, clothed with the best gold, in whose newness there is nothing filthy, by which they are restored to the rank of their first dignity, which is the first robe, that is, immortality; whence: the noble sons of Sion, clothed with the best gold. The best gold is the Arabian, the purest, which is offered to the Lord from Saba. The most precious is what is brought from Ophir. For Ophir is interpreted “laughter” or “grassy”, of that laughter, namely, in which are all joys, where the souls of the saints rest among green grasses; this is rightly called the best. For this wisdom and immortality is more precious than all works. They are esteemed as earthen vessels; whence Job: “I am compared to dirt”, etc.; whence elsewhere: “I will destroy them as the dirt of the streets.” For earthen vessels are of clay, but some unto honour, some unto dishonour, of which it is said: “The furnace trieth the potter’s vessels.” Therefore it follows: the work of the potter’s hands; because as the potter has power to make of the same lump one vessel unto honour and another unto dishonour, so Christ can make of clay golden vessels, refined by tribulation, and leave others in their confusion.
35_marg2778: The thirteenth topic of complaint. For she complains with indignation that she is ill treated by those who ought to have helped her.

35_marg2779: Even the sea monsters, etc. The hardness of the scribes and Pharisees is reproached, who, harder than lamias, denied the milk of teaching to the little ones. And the lamia is said to be more cruel to her young than the other beasts; whence lamia is named as if lania, because she is said to tear her young; so the Pharisees denied teaching to the people and tore them besides, like ostriches, which, as they lay their eggs, abandon them and do not warm them into young. The lamia is named Lilith in Hebrew; for some of the Hebrews suppose her one of the furies of hell, which are called Parcae because they spare none; like whom are the scribes and Pharisees, who laid hands even on the Son of God. The Synagogue is lamented, therefore, who, like the ostrich, has left no hope for herself or her descendants in the future.
35_marg2780: Even the sea monsters, etc. By the lamia the prudence of the flesh is signified, which, like a most savage beast, nourishes her young, that is, the deeds she has begotten, with the milk of death. But often, changed for the better, it is made the prudence of the spirit, and lays bare cruel crimes, and with the milk of teaching and the breast of piety suckles and nourishes her young, namely her manners and deeds, that they may pass from savagery to gentleness. But the prudence of the flesh, that is, the daughter of my people, which has long been hardened, is cruel like the ostrich, which leaves her eggs without the warmth of love and the cherishing of piety and without hope of offspring; so the prudence of the flesh does all its works for present things, without care for the future.
35_marg2781: Even the sea monsters, etc. By the lamias the cunning perversity of hypocrites and heretics is signified, who bear a human face but the hearts of beasts. They draw out the breast when they preach their error freely; they suckle their young when they delight their followers with perverse teaching and confirm them in wickedness by nourishing them ill. The daughter of my people, etc., namely the church of the sinning people, which is called the daughter of the saints, through whom she is born again in Christ; but, like a beast entangled in the habit of sinning, she is like the ostrich, thinking only of the present, hoping nothing for the future; she abandons her offspring without the warmth of charity, she takes no care of the life to come.

35_marg2782: The tongue … hath stuck, etc. The mothers being dead, the sucklings were tormented with thirst; and the little ones, namely the older ones, asking their mothers for bread, there were no loaves. So the sucklings perished without milk, the little ones without food.
35_marg2783: The tongue … hath stuck, etc. Without the milk of gentle persuasion and the dew of the Holy Spirit, the thirsty tongue of speech, sticking to the roof of the flesh, makes the infancy of the mind dumb, and smothers the conceptions of our heart with the sword of unbelief, lest they be brought to light; whence: “With the heart we believe unto justice, but with the mouth confession”, etc. For what avails it to conceive good in the mind unless it is nourished with the milk of teaching and the richness of grace? The little ones have asked for bread, namely the little thoughts; when they are conceived of Christ and eternal life, at once they ask for the bread that came down from heaven. But the mind, weighed down by the sluggishness of its idleness and the cares of the present life, does not know how to break bread for them by understanding, nor to break it small by chewing over, nor to fill them by dispensing; whence it is added in lamentation: there was none to break it unto them; because, even if for a time it is quickened within by divine inspiration, without, emptied and wasted by lusts, it is drained of strength.

35_marg2784: They that were fed, etc. The faithlessness of the Jews is laid open more clearly than light: their gold is become dim, the finest colour is changed, which they had in the patriarchs and prophets, and they are scattered (as we see today) in the top of every street; and though noble and clothed with the best gold according to the privilege of the fathers, yet they are esteemed as earthen vessels, more savage than lamias and ostriches; by whose faithlessness the sucklings failed with thirst and the little ones perished with hunger; so that those who fed delicately in the ways of God perished with hunger, because they stubbornly cast out all the mysteries of the Scriptures, on which the prophets and patriarchs fed delicately, and denied that Christ is the Son of God, who is the beginning of all ways; and therefore they perished in the ways of the world. Whence it follows: They that were brought up in scarlet have embraced the dung. The saffron colour is fiery, by which is signified the fire of the Holy Spirit, by which hearts are kindled. In such saffron the holy fathers were brought up, in the sacraments of graces; but the sons, denying the Lord, embraced the dung, of which the Apostle: “I have suffered the loss of all things, and count them but as dung”, namely the literal sense of the law, which the Catholics cast away “that they may gain Christ”, wishing to have “the justice which is of the faith of Jesus Christ”; to which the Jews are not subject, who wish to establish their own justice and defend the letter of the law. In the siege too they embraced dung for food, so that pigeons’ dung was bought for a price; and yet they did not return to the Lord.
35_marg2785: They that were fed, etc. The virtues of the soul are seen to be fed delicately and brought up in scarlet when they are filled and enlightened with the love of God and of the neighbour. For the saffron colour signifies the brightness of love; but when charity is lost, the remaining virtues embrace dung, passing from the good odour of the love of God and of the neighbour to the stench of wickedness; whence Paul: “If I have not charity, I am become as sounding brass”, etc.
35_marg2786: They that were fed, etc. The Church laments the sinners, who, forsaking charity and the other virtues, in which they were brought up as in scarlet, embrace the dung of sins; whence: “The beasts have rotted in their dung.” Like beasts they rot in dung who in the stench of their lust serve crimes according to the desires of their heart. And because there are very many who do not return to penance, the Church laments them, because they do not know how to lament, and from love of sinning do not cease to embrace dung.
