35_marg2787: And … is made greater, etc. By heightening, the crimes and miseries of the Synagogue are lamented, according to that: “From the sole of the foot unto the top of the head there is no soundness therein.” The sin of Sodom, according to Ezechiel, was “pride, fulness of bread and abundance, and idleness; and they did not put forth their hand to the needy and to the poor”. Whence here too: and hands took nothing in her (understand: anything good), in comparison, namely, with the evil she did; to whom it is said: “Sodom thy sister is justified by thee”; by thee, namely, who received the commandments of God and began to do what God bade, but afterwards despised them, so as to outdo by thy sins Sodom, which was overthrown in a moment. How much heavier, then, the punishment of the Synagogue, who is more wicked.
35_marg2788: And … is made greater, etc. The crimes of the soul that slips into hypocrisy are lamented, whose iniquity is greater than the sin of Sodom, who covers evil things by gilding them and does good things deceitfully. Whence the iniquity of my people is greater than the people of Sodom; as a people rises up against itself, so the manners and deeds of hypocrites fight against themselves, and the good things they do are worse than the vices of Sodom; because when the unclean spirit has gone out of a man, if he returns with spirits more wicked, “the last state of that man becomes worse than the first”. The spirit goes out of a man when he is born again in Christ. It returns when it finds the soul empty of good work, swept of filth by hypocrisy and adorned with pretences. Then the soul is filled with a people of unclean spirits and a crowd of vices, and its iniquity is greater than the sin of Sodom. It becomes the iniquity of a people, namely of vices and works, and they do not put their hands to the fruit of good work, adorned outwardly with false goods, within full of vices. Whence it follows: Her Nazarites were whiter than snow, etc.
35_marg2789: Is made greater, etc. The Church laments the sins of the people as greater than the sins of Sodom. For we see that faith and justice have left the earth, there is no humanity or kindness, discord and lust set the world on fire, and the devouring flame of anger and envy; the Church is laid waste by robberies and frauds, the poor are stripped to the bone; now the world lies untilled among the briars, the rights of the laws are held as fables. Things divine and human, right and wrong are confounded; daily countless evils are heaped up. Our iniquity too is greater than theirs who did not know the way of truth and therefore deserved lesser punishments, which was overthrown in a moment. All that we live is a moment, and by sinning daily we are overthrown as in a moment to punishment, who deserve worse things, who treasure up wrath for ourselves in the day of judgement.
35_interl11932: the first topic of complaint: the judge’s indignation is stirred up against the adversaries, whose Nazarites are afflicted
35_interl11936: in the strength and spiritual fervour of the ancient fathers
35_marg2790: Her Nazarites were whiter, etc. According to the letter the beauty of the Nazarites is described, white with abstinence, sleek in flesh, pleasant with the redness of the face; who are praised by heightening, that their foulness may be shown the greater, whose face, wasted by famine, is lamented as blackened beyond coals, which, disfigured, is not recognised.
35_marg2791: Her Nazarites were whiter, etc. The Church has her Nazarites, whiter than snow and purer than milk, by whom the life of those who abstain is signified; for snow comes from above, milk from the flesh, as from below. By snow, therefore, the whiteness of the heavenly life is shown; by milk the dispensing of temporal things. So the Church has Nazarites who lead a heavenly life by contemplation, and by the dispensing of the active life shine whiter than milk to the praise of the creator; so that often they surpass by works of virtue those who had held the heavenly life or had dispensed earthly things well. And because by fervour of spirit they seem to surpass the life of the ancient and stronger fathers, rightly it is added: more ruddy than the old ivory. For while the beauty of redness is praised, the flame of their longing is expressed; and ivory, as everyone knows, is the bone of the elephant. Fairer than the sapphire: the sapphire is of the colour of the sky; where the whole life of the Nazarites is briefly expressed, because, tending to higher things by action and excelling by contemplation, they seem to surpass the fathers. But because “plenty has often made a man poor”, and a man is happier than is good for him, the mind, often presuming on itself and yielding to vain favour, is darkened, and what seemed to grow white is blackened and grows filthy; whence it follows: Their face is now made blacker than coals, etc.
35_interl11937: having lost their whiteness, because they presume on themselves; whence: “Be not over just”; because before they were in the narrow way that leads to life, now they are in the broad one that leads to death
35_interl11939: to the strength of the virtues
35_marg2792: Their face is now made blacker, etc. Those become black after whiteness who, having lost the justice of God, seek their own praise, because they presume on themselves; whence, not knowing it, they rush into sin, and after the fire of the mind they go down to the cold of sluggishness, after the whiteness of life to the blackness of vain flattery. Whence they become like quenched coals; because of which it is said: “Be not over just.” And they are not known in the streets, in the breadth, namely, of worldly life. For nothing is narrower to the human mind than to deny its own wills, to break the desires of the flesh and the like, and to enter within by the narrow gate. But nothing is wider than to serve one’s own pleasures, to be under no laws, and the like. And they are in the streets who seek their own; for “wide is the way that leadeth to destruction”. But in the streets they are not known who are not what they seemed, who were one thing and showed another; whence it follows: their skin hath stuck to their bones, etc. By the bones strength is figured, by the skin weakness. The skin, then, sticks to the bones when the weakness of the vices is thought the strength of the virtues; the skin sticks to the bones while flattery for things well done without is joined to the virtues within; and when these are joined, the reward is lost. And because, deceived by flatteries, they think great things of themselves, they scorn to be amended; whence: it is withered, and is become like wood. For a fault is rendered the more insensible the more it is praised as if it were true virtue; whence it withers too, because no grace grows green within; because many, when they are corrected, are as insensible as wood and are strangers to the dew of grace and dry. This happens to them because they seek things above themselves and long to seem holy, but secretly serve vices. These are known in the streets. For spiritual men know that they are one thing and feign another. Outwardly they are whiter than snow, purer than milk, more ruddy than ivory; but within they are insensible as dry wood; whence often they are amended neither by caresses nor by threats.
35_interl11943: the want of the Church: while preaching ceases, the Church does not bear fruit
35_marg2793: It was better, etc. This the Jews suffered in the last captivity, when it was lighter for those slain suddenly than for those afflicted with slow and lasting torments, who were consumed little by little by hunger and thirst and the other miseries.
35_marg2794: It was better, etc. It is better for the senses to be slain outwardly by the sword of the word of God, living inwardly, than, the virtues heaped up without the food of charity, to perish as by hunger and thirst. For the barrenness of the virtues is the absence of charity; when it is absent, the virtues of the soul pine as for want of the true bread. Therefore the seven sons of Job call their three sisters to the feasts; for the other virtues are not filled without faith, hope and charity. Whence: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness.”
35_marg2795: It was better, etc., with them that were slain by the sword of the word of God than with those that died with hunger for the same word. For these are slain that they may live, those are killed that they may perish; whence: “Take the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” There is a sword by which death is destroyed, that his life may follow. Another, which cuts life off, kills the soul, of which: “My sword shall devour flesh.” There is the flaming and turning sword “to keep the way of the tree of life”. There is the sword filed and sharp, to which it is said: “Put up thy sword into its scabbard.” The sword of sorrow too pierced the soul of Mary, namely at the passion of Christ. But the Church rejoices over those who are slain by the sword of the word; she grieves over those who are killed by hunger for the same. She mourns those whom she knows consumed by hunger or thirst for want of the fruits of the earth; whence: “I will send forth a famine, not a famine of bread nor a thirst of water, but of hearing the word of the Lord.” He who has been destroyed by this famine will lie under eternal death, because “not by bread alone doth man live”. For as man is made of two substances, so he keeps his life by two: the flesh is sustained by bodily food, and the soul by the divine word; whence: “Give us this day our daily bread”; for we ask for both, who need both daily. The barrenness of the earth is the want of the Church, when (the masters failing) she is not watered by the showers of the divine word; for the wasting of the people follows the fault of the priests and their ignorance or negligence in teaching.

35_marg2798: The hands of the … women, etc. In the Church those boil their children, as if out of mercy, who, raised to the height of rule, inflame the souls of those under them with the fire of zeal or envy, while they long to seem over just and oppress with tyrannical power; who perhaps have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge. So they burn them with the harshness of condemnation, as if for justice, and gnaw their weak and fleshly life with threats and rebukes as with teeth. All these things are done in the destruction of the Church, which is the daughter of the people of God, namely of the apostles and their successors, by those who with worldly or churchly power burn souls tyrannically, while, inflamed by lust, they harry with the burning of affliction the children whom they ought to have nourished with the milk of teaching.

35_marg2800: The Lord hath accomplished, etc. The foundations of hypocrites and heretics are devoured by the fire of the Lord’s wrath, in whose mind the fire of his indignation condemns, and upon them the Lord’s wrath is accomplished. Whence Job: “I have seen a fool with a strong root, and I cursed his beauty immediately.” For though they seem made firm and rooted in works, they at once become cursed before God, whose hearts are inflamed by vain praises and favours; whence it follows: The kings of the earth would not have believed, etc.
35_marg2801: The Lord hath accomplished, … he hath poured out, etc. Upon the Church the Lord’s wrath is accomplished, because she has filled up the measure of her sins; whence: “Contempt was poured forth upon their princes, and he caused them to wander”, etc.; and elsewhere: “He that is filthy, let him be filthy still.” He hath poured out his fierce anger, because by sinning we are poured out. He hath kindled a fire in Sion: not that which came down from heaven upon the apostles, but that which consumed the children of Job. For God has various fires which he sends out from his treasures, “whose fire is in Sion, and his furnace in Jerusalem”; some he inflames to teach them, others to burn them; and when they are kindled he destroys every foundation, namely he lets the whole and true faith be utterly overthrown. Whence we ought to lament our own miseries rather than the Jews’, in whom the fire of lust is kindled, and the devouring flame of the other vices possesses all, and “the boiling caldron from the face of the north” boils, and the furnace of the Chaldeans burns whomsoever of the Chaldeans it finds.

35_marg2806: They have wandered as blind men, etc. The scribes and Pharisees, defiled by the blood they shed, kept themselves from entering the temple, wandering in the streets, not mourning their sins but tearing their garments in the streets. 35_marg2807: They have wandered, etc. Vain appetites walk like blind men in the streets, lacking the light which is Christ; and while they cannot keep hold of him who is the way, because they pour out outside themselves the grace of vain favour, holding the skirts of their oldness, they cannot fulfil the ways of life, because they are clothed with the oldness of the vices; of whom it is well added: Depart, you that are defiled, etc.
35_marg2808: They have wandered, etc. In the Church priests and teachers shed the blood of the just, who could have been just had they not perished by their negligence; whence: “If thou declare not to the wicked man his iniquity, I will require his blood at thy hand”; because, namely, his blood, that is, sin, is shed unto death by the fault of the priests; and often those who seemed just are perverted by the examples of the prelates and by wicked teaching, and die defiled with the blood of sin. Hence the priests and prophets wander blind in the streets, while they seize the wide and broad way that leads to death, and do not enter the narrow one that leads to life, nor let others enter; and this is: they have shed the blood of the just in the midst of her, that is, of the Church, which is the true Jerusalem and our mother. These, defiled with their blood, when they cannot enter the temple of God, hold up their skirts, that is, the torn life of their oldness. And they hold one another’s skirts, so that when the blind leads the blind, both fall into the pit. This the prophet laments, nay, the whole assembly of the elect: that, walking in the broad way and leading the old life, they did not seize the ways of life, and entangle themselves in their windings; blind, they follow one another, who scorn to follow Christ the true light.
35_marg2809: They have wandered, etc. He laments the blindness of the heretics, who, leaving the straight path of the Scriptures and spurning the rule of the Catholic faith, have chosen the breadth of error, defiled with the blood of those whose souls they deceived; and when they scorn to enter the Catholic Church, they cling to one another’s skirts, namely the rendings of the Scriptures, whose rags they have stolen deceitfully.

35_marg2810: Depart, you that are defiled, etc. The prophet weeps for the crimes of the Jews, at whom even the enemies, having entered the city, mock, crying: Depart from the sanctuary of God, you that are defiled with crimes; go away into captivity. 35_marg2812: Depart, etc. Often in the Church the blind and defiled cannot enter the temple of the living God and share in the holy mysteries; whom others (though they too are defiled) despise as if with zeal for God, who wish to seem just because they are not yet found out. Thence quarrels are often born, because they do not correct according to God, but long to seem holier by oppressing others; whence he adds: for they quarrelled and were moved; for first, being moved, they quarrel, then they are moved more sharply, because they do not stand in him who is the selfsame, and have left him who is the true peace. Therefore it is added: among the Gentiles: He will no more, etc.; because where there is no peace and concord, God cannot be, because “his place is in peace”, etc. For among the Gentiles the name of the Lord is blasphemed through such men.

35_marg2815: The face of the Lord, etc. Some in the Church, casting off the fear of God, have not respected the persons of the priests; who are divided by the face of the Lord and the wrath of his countenance from those, namely, who are called to life. Neither had they pity on the ancient, namely the prelates, who, suffering with them in all things, stoop to them. Note how terrible it is to despise priests and not to respect their persons, that is, not to cease from crimes when they warn and see. For of these the Lord says: “He that heareth you heareth me; he that despiseth you despiseth me.” Whence it is added: he will no more regard them, that they may be converted and saved, because the face of the Lord hath divided them from the saints. This face looked on Peter, and, turned, he wept bitterly, and, received back into the body, he deserved to hear: “Peter, lovest thou me? Feed my sheep.” But this division will be made fully in the judgement, when the Lord says: “Depart, ye cursed, into everlasting fire”; then the face of God, namely wrath or vengeance, will divide them into everlasting fire, because they despised the persons of the priests and had no pity on the ancients. And it is to be noted that above he lamented the priests as murderers, and here those are separated from the face of the Lord who did not defer to them. For though they are wicked, they are not to be despised; but he is to be worshipped and honoured in them by whom they were sent.

Whence, in the person of those who groan, it follows: Our steps have slipped, etc.

35_marg2818: Our steps have slipped, etc. This lamentation fits the Jews, who at the point of death go over their crimes. But the prophet takes all into himself and laments the crimes of all as his own, because so bitter and unhoped-for a captivity raged in his nation.
35_marg2819: Our steps have slipped, etc. It is the voice of the heretics lamenting too late, because their steps have slipped in the holy Scriptures, and because they seized the wide way, while they would not keep the rules of the Catholic fathers nor the way which is Christ; but each turned aside from the straight path, following the breadth of his own perversity, trying even the rules of the philosophers with the spark of his own wit and shamelessly finding fault; therefore, slipping, they fall into death, and when their crimes are completed the end of damnation comes.
35_marg2820: Our steps have slipped, etc. This too we rightly lament in the Church, when we look on those who live splendidly and delicately; we lament the wantonness of those who follow the slippery way, because they are not founded on the firm rock; whence, lamenting, we say: Our steps have slipped, etc. For if the feet had not gone out into the streets from the straight path, they would not have slipped; whence: “Go out quickly into the streets.” For those who keep to the wide and broad way are outside before the eyes of the highest judge, who are in the Church in body; slippery and downhill are the roads of the streets. David rejoiced that he had escaped these, saying: “He set my feet upon a rock, and directed my steps”, and elsewhere: “Who hath made my feet like the feet of harts”, etc. Wet is the way of the streets and muddy, in which one does not walk without falling; therefore it is fitly added: our end draweth near, etc. For fulfilment is not always taken in a good sense, according to that: “The iniquities of the Amorrhites are not as yet at the full”; whose fulfilment was their end and destruction, as it is said here: our days are fulfilled, for our end is come. The days are fulfilled while crimes and the measure of the fathers are heaped up; and the end comes, which before drew near; when they are fulfilled it drew near, while they were being fulfilled and the axe was laid to the root of the tree.

35_marg2822: Our persecutors were swifter, etc. The heretics in disputing are often swifter than the eagles of the air, that is, than the teachers of the people, whom they pursue upon the mountains, namely upon Scripture and the teaching of the apostles and holy fathers; they lie in wait for the hermits with deceits and honeyed words.
35_marg2823: Note by how many evils we are pressed. 35_marg2824: Our persecutors were swifter. Because the prophet takes into himself the lamentations and persons and properties of all (made all things to all), he laments the persecutions of the Church, whose persecutors are swifter than eagles. For the unclean spirits are swifter, by the fraud of wickedness and the nimbleness of their nature, to tear and devour, than the eagles of the air, that is, the preachers, to rescue; of whom: “Wheresoever the body shall be, there shall the eagles also be gathered together”; because where the memory of Christ’s passion is celebrated, and the bread and wine by the mystery of holy prayer are changed into the body and blood of Christ, the eagles of the air fly to it as to food, that from his death they may receive life. But the powers of the air are swifter, because “there is no power upon earth that can be compared with them”; these roar and seek whom they may devour. They pursued us upon the mountains, etc.; because when we are raised to the rule of the Church we stir them up more sharply to persecute; nor are those set in the watchtower of the apostolic see safe, because those whom they see raised upon the mountains, to guard the rest by watching over them more carefully and to call them to the heights of virtue, they attack the more boldly and hotly. They lay in wait for us in the wilderness: by the wilderness is signified the monastic or hermit life, which is led in deserts and solitudes; against whom, as stronger athletes, the invisible enemies rage; but because, freed from worldly cares, they are watchful and wary only against the enemies, therefore they lie in wait the more secretly for those whom they see hidden in secret places; but those who stand out raised upon the mountains they sustain, raised up, with open strength and frequent assaults. The enemies are often swifter to deceive these eagles of the air than they are to beware; who are fitly called eagles of the air, because, despising earthly things, they range in heavenly ones. And it is to be noted that they are not said to be swifter than sheep or oxen or horses or vultures or any birds, but than the eagles of the air; whence elsewhere: “My people hath been a lost flock, their shepherds have caused them to go astray, and have made them wander in the mountains”; who, namely, “have gone from mountain to hill, they have forgotten their resting place.”

35_marg2825: The breath of our mouth, etc. As we draw breath from this air and give it back to it, and live by it, so the inner man by faith draws in the Spirit of God and lives by it; and in turn gives back to it that he lives, that he does good, that he prays, that he thinks, ascribing all his good things to it.
35_marg2826: The breath of our mouth, etc. The Jews think these things were said of Josias, because the just king was slain not for his own sins but for the people’s, in whom they had placed their hope, whose wings they set against the nations everywhere. But most truly Christ is understood here, who was taken and slain by the Jews for the sins of the human race, not for his own; whose godhead is noted when it is said: the breath of our mouth (“Renew a right spirit within my bowels”); the manhood is hinted when it is added: Christ the Lord, etc. For because God and man are one person, where Christ is taken God is said to be taken. Christ is well called the breath of our mouth, because him whom we believe in the heart we confess with the mouth, according to that: “With the heart we believe unto justice, but with the mouth”, etc. It belongs to the mouth to breathe in; and what we receive by breathing in through the infusion of grace we confess by breathing out. But this voice belongs properly to those who have the word of truth, which is Christ, in the mouth as in the heart, because “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh”. He was taken in our sins, namely to blot out our sins, not for his own, because “I paid that which I took not away”; to whom we said: Under thy shadow we shall live among the Gentiles; because he is “the expectation of the nations” and the seed of Abraham, “in whom shall all the nations of the earth be blessed”. In him the prophet believed with the heart and confessed with the mouth: Under thy shadow we shall live among the Gentiles. For he was to come to save the Jews with the Gentiles; whence he said in the future: we shall live, we who were dead in sins. Under thy shadow, of which it is said: “Protect me under the shadow of thy wings.” Christ was taken and crucified; under the shadow of the passion he protected us, as with wings stretched out on the cross; his flesh was a shadow to us, which cooled the heat of our mind and tempered the various sufferings of the heats. For even the shadow of the apostles healed the sick. His flesh was as a shadow, because “we have seen him, and there was no sightliness nor beauty”; of which it is said: “The Lord will ascend upon a swift cloud, and will enter into Egypt.” This was the bright cloud over the apostles, that the heat of iniquity might not burn them; which the prophet foretold: now under thy shadow we shall live among the Gentiles. For the prophet too saw him in shadow, who, enlightened as in the mirror of the mind by the divine Spirit, foresaw things to come; but now he enlightens the whole world, though we still see through the shadow of his body, that is, the Church, since not face to face. Refreshed in this shadow, we live in hope. It is to be noted that the whole intent of the lamentation tends to this end, in which every trouble is ended; but afterwards a twofold thing is shown, because the chosen part holds the right hand, the reprobate, defiled by sins, embraces the left. Whence to the one eternal damnation, to the other eternal life, when “God shall wipe away all tears from the eyes” of the saints; which the cross of the Lord foreshowed as the judge’s tribunal, where of those who hung on either side one was taken up through faith, the other condemned through blasphemy, because he despised the life hanging before his eyes. It is to be noted too with careful discernment that the mourning of the saints is ended and joy begins after sadness. In the two following verses an end is begun with joy, which is ended by no remedy of grief; whence it is added: Rejoice, and be glad, O daughter of Edom.

35_marg2827: Rejoice, and be glad, etc. The histories and the prophets tell that the Idumeans and the other nations round about were always enemies of the Jews; and because they rejoiced at their evils, they will be made drunk with the Lord’s fitting vengeance; whence it is added: to thee also shall the cup come, etc. All these things were fulfilled when the Babylonians carried the Jews captive, who were themselves taken captive as the Persians and Medes laid them waste; but these things are better taken of the last judgement.
35_marg2828: Rejoice, and be glad, etc. Edom and Babylon signify the same. For two cities are marked out from the beginning of the world: the one Jerusalem, the other Edom, which is also Babylon; the one laments and travails with the prophet, the other does not know why she should be lamented; the one Christ builds, the other the devil, who is signified by Nabuchodonosor. Babylon is the city of the lost, which makes all the earth drunk with the wine of iniquity; whence: “Babylon hath been a golden cup in the hand of the Lord”; of the wine of his fury all nations have drunk; with which Edom too is lamented as made drunk. Therefore it is said to her ironically: Rejoice, and be glad, O daughter of Edom. Edom is interpreted “bloody” or “red”; this is the people that follows the vices of the flesh, that sells its birthright for the pleasures of the present life. Whence it follows: that dwellest in the land of Hus. For had she not set her mind on earthly things, she could not be made drunk or stripped of the virtues. But Jerusalem is above, whose conversation is in heaven; for “woe to them that dwell on the earth”. Edom, then, who dwells on the earth, though she seems to rejoice and be glad, is yet made drunk by the golden cup and stripped bare in the Lord’s fury; because she resolved to live not simply on the earth, but, according to other copies, in the land of Hus, that is, of the counsellor, namely the devil, who suggests perverse counsels against the angel of great counsel. For Edom too is interpreted “earthly”; in whom are signified those who follow earthly things, deceived by the devil’s counsel; whence the golden cup comes to them and they are stripped of the grace of God.

35_marg2829: Note that in the closing of the last verse he gives to each part what fits it: that Sion, namely, being afflicted, may not despair, and the daughter of Edom, who is to be afflicted, may not insult.
35_marg2830: Thy iniquity is accomplished, etc. The sins being forgiven, the people of Israel is promised a return to its own land and secure rest. But on those who persecuted it, that is, the sons of Edom, vengeance to come is declared. It is plain that these things happened to both according to the letter; but it is to be taken in general of all, to whom in the last examination sentence is to be given according to their works, that Sion may pass from sorrow to gladness, Edom from gladness to everlasting sadness.
35_marg2831: It is to be noted, nay, most of all to be wondered at, to what a height Jeremias has climbed, whence, as from a watchtower, with enlarged heart he considers the struggles of this world: now he laments all together, now each one, now the falls of the Jews; now he mourns the losses of the Church, grieves at the disorder of manners; now he looks on the restoring and glory of Jerusalem, and glories that the Church is to be exalted; he rejoices with the victors, mourns with the vanquished; in short, every sex, every age, prelates and subjects, as if he were one in all, if it goes ill he laments, and invites them to lament; to each person he gives its own laments, and always pours out new tears. Whence, while he brings in new persons by turns, at last he bears witness that our Lord Jesus Christ was taken for our sins; yet near the end he groans that he has not redeemed all from death, and rejoices that the malice of those who have been converted is ended, so that the Lord will no more carry them away, because they are planted in the house of God and will be as the angels in heaven, that is, will reign with Christ; but he affirms that those who persecuted the saints are to be punished for their iniquities, when their sins are uncovered. Hence it is to be understood that in the holy Scriptures there is nothing else but lamentations, which are to be often used in this world, and the canticle which we shall sing to the angels in heaven, and the woe which the sons of Edom will howl in hell. Let us mourn, then, with Jeremias in this world, lest we howl with the sons of Edom in hell; let us flee the joys of the present life and empty songs, that we may sing with the angels an everlasting alleluia.
35_marg2832: Thy iniquity is accomplished, etc. These are, as we have said, the two cities which are built from the beginning: Sion, which is also Jerusalem, is said by Isaias to have her evil accomplished and her iniquity forgiven, according to that: “Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven”, etc.; like to which is this: Thy iniquity is accomplished, O daughter of Sion: it is accomplished because it is forgiven and ended, “because she hath received of the hand of the Lord double for all her sins”; whence a glad promise is added: He will no more carry thee away into captivity. For when, the judgement having been made, iniquity has ceased and full rest has come, there will be no more change. He will visit thy iniquity, not to forgive it but to punish it, saying: “Depart, ye cursed, into everlasting fire”, etc. He will uncover the sins that were covered, and the iniquities, because then the hidden things of our heart will be laid open, when the Lord “will bring to light the hidden things of darkness”; what we cover here by concealing God will uncover there, and will cover what we uncover by confession and what we wash away with tears and blot out by the bruisings of heart and body. These indeed are the signs of the examination to come, which is signified by the letter Thau, which, as we have often said, is interpreted “signs”; whence the lamentations too end under the same letter; whence: “Thou hast given a warning to them that fear thee, that they may flee from before the bow.”
35_marg2833: Like a divine orator he sums up, gathering all things under one view, in the manner of rhetoric mingling complaint and indignation by turns: by complaint, drawing the judge’s mercy to himself and his own; by indignation, driving his wrath against the adversaries. By complaining, then, he sets out in what good things they were and in what evils they are, saying: Remember, O Lord, what is come upon us; or, according to others: Be mindful, O Lord, of what has happened to us, etc. So it is lamented before the most merciful judge what base and lowly things they have suffered. You will find, then, if you weigh it well, that the arts of speaking too passed from ours to the philosophers, not that they came up from them to ours; which you will fully grasp if you consider one by one the prophet’s intent and feeling and words. For he is “a lover of his brethren, who prayeth much for the people”, lamenting for all and inviting all to lament.
35_marg2834: This lamentation is called by some a canticle. For laments are rightly called canticles, and conversely. For as in the present there are no joys without miseries, so without laments there are few canticles or none. Yet the monks chant it as a psalm. But the true canticles are in the heavenly Sion; lamentations befit exile. Rightly, then, before one comes to the country to which one hastens, as if in the middle, songs are mingled with weeping and weeping with songs, while present evils are lamented and future joys hoped for.
35_interl12040: in the person of the judge, whose mercy he humbly implores
35_interl12041: who seemest to have forgotten, while thou dost not avenge
35_interl12044: in his own person, whose misery is set out
35_interl12045: whence: “We are become a reproach to our neighbours”
35_marg2835: Remember, etc. He sets the captivity and misery of his nation before the eyes of the Creator. Yet it is to be noted that he does not provoke the judge against the adversaries, but, lamenting, begs pardon for his nation. He does not say: Remember, O Lord, our enemies; as if he said: Take away, O Lord, the evils that we suffer, but forgive the doers what has befallen ours. For some evils in us are natural, but others accidental, which we add by sinning wilfully and in act. Consider and behold is the same thing, but the repetition is a sign of feeling; for it is to be read with the feeling of one in grief. For it was a reproach that a holy nation, endowed with miracles and made illustrious by the presence of God, should have sinned so much that by the just judgement of God it was punished with so monstrous a captivity.
35_marg2836: Remember is the voice of the martyrs, who cry out, afflicted with torments: Be mindful, O Lord, of what has befallen us. For when he does not avenge in the present, he seems to have forgotten. Whence: “How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget me unto the end?” And elsewhere: “Thou forgettest our want and our trouble.” For there is no one who doubts that reproaches and insults were heaped on the martyrs.
35_interl12048: the understandings of the Scriptures, or minds
35_marg2837: Inheritance, etc. He counts up the evils one by one. For when the Jews were carried into captivity, aliens possessed their inheritance. He touches also on the fathers’ privilege and the divine bounty, by whose gift the inheritance of the enemies passed to the fathers; which, as long as they possessed it under God’s protection, [is now turned] to aliens, that is, to those alien from God; not to superiors over the fathers, but to inferiors, which is most unworthy.
35_marg2838: Inheritance, etc. The heretics have handed over the inheritance of the Church either to the demons or to depraved teachings. Whence another rendering: Our inheritance is converted to aliens, and our houses to strangers. For what is converted was indeed something, but is changed into something else. For Scripture is the inheritance of the faithful; but those who are alien from God convert it. To aliens, namely, Scripture is converted to death, which to the Catholics is converted to salvation, because it is kept unchanged. Our houses to strangers: for whatever the people had within or without was possessed or carried off by the enemies (according to the letter). But tropologically the houses signify the divine Scriptures, in which the intentions of the mind dwell, as if the senses were opened doors; but the heretics turn them to the purpose of their own depravity. The strangers are also understood as the demons, who put a strange sense into the Scriptures; our houses too, that is, human minds, pass by sinning to strangers, that is, to unclean spirits.
35_interl12049: God being offended for our sins
35_interl12051: to whom thou oughtest to be a helper; whence: “Thou wilt be a helper to the orphan”
35_interl12052: the churches, or faith, hope, charity
35_marg2839: The fifteenth topic of complaint, by which we lament the fortunes of those who should be dear to us more than our own.
35_marg2840: We are become orphans, etc. Another rendering has: We are become orphans, as not having a father. For God adopted the Jews as sons to himself; whence: “Israel is my son, my firstborn”; but they became as not having a father, whom, though they had him, they provoked in their iniquities. Our mothers are as widows: namely the seven synagogues set on the mount of Olives, which, like mothers, should have suckled their sons and brought up those under them, and which were laid desolate and burnt in the Chaldean captivity.
35_marg2841: We are become orphans, etc. The Church groans with the same voice when, oppressed by straits, she feels less the help of fatherly kindness and comfort. One interpreter said “not having”, another “as not having”. For sometimes, offended by graver offences, the father is lost altogether; but sometimes he delays his help but does not take it away. Our mothers are as widows: the churches, namely, which nourish us with their milk, widowed when the shepherds flee or are negligent, cannot bear sons to God, because they have none who can make them fruitful; yet they are not called widows absolutely, but as widows, because they seem to have husbands. But the barrenness of the heretics is rightly lamented, whose churches are rightly called as widows, because even if they are joined to the true bridegroom in certain sacraments, yet they conceive no fruit for God. These are signified by the concubines of David, who went in to them first but did not join them to himself in full wedlock; whom afterwards Absalom, like Satan, defiled, and David shut them up in darkness, in eternal damnation.
35_marg2842: Our mothers, etc. The mothers of all the virtues are faith, hope and charity, by which we are born again to God and the other virtues are begotten; but when they are corrupted by the vanities of the world, and charity, by which true wedlock is kept, is turned aside to other things, they are lamented as widows (yet not widows absolutely), because even if in certain outward things they seem to embrace Christ, yet inwardly they have lost the power of begetting holy offspring; for “all that is not of faith is sin”, and what is done without charity cannot profit.
35_interl12056: against that: “You that have no money, come, buy”
35_interl12057: of the Scriptures, of spiritual gifts
35_marg2843: Historically. Our water, etc. He signifies the cruelty of the enemies and the affliction and want of his own, so that they even bought water at a price, when the use of water ought to be common.
35_marg2844: In the moral sense. Our water, etc. They drink water for money who, groaning, are made drunk with the streams of tears; with the money, namely, of the Scriptures, while in them they weigh the rewards of eternal life and the punishments, by meditating on which they nourish charity and fear; and in both ways the mind is made more ready to grieve; whence: “Thou wilt feed us with the bread of tears”, etc. We buy wood too to feed the Lord’s fire, when, putting earthly things after, we acquire spiritual ones. To drink this water is also to give the wisdom and knowledge of worldly things for spiritual ones, or else, putting the virtues of the mind after, to admit vices.
35_marg2845: Allegorically. Our water, etc. He says this against the priests who make the house of God a house of traffic, who sell for money the teaching of God or the sacraments and the gifts of the Holy Ghost, when Isaias says: “All you that thirst, come to the waters”, etc., and “drink wine and milk without any price”. Rightly, then, it is lamented here in the voice of the people, for whom the wood of the Scriptures and the gifts of the Holy Ghost, by which the fire is fed daily on the altar, are bought at a price.
35_interl12061: because they are driven to flee from place to place
35_marg2846: By the necks, etc. He puts before the merciful judge, who puts down the mighty and exalts the humble, the contempt and harrying of the captives. For with their necks struck they were dragged and driven, so that, weary, they ran and bore the toil of the work without rest.
35_marg2847: By the necks, etc. The Church laments that the martyrs are buffeted by the persecutors, dragged with bound necks, driven to flee from place to place without rest; which is signified when it is said: we were weary and no rest was given us. All affliction and contempt is shown in the striking of necks; yet because it has been said: “If one strike thee on one cheek, turn to him also the other”, we better take the neck for the pride by which we are struck and put to flight when we fear from the consciousness of guilt; because “God regardeth the humble, and the high he knoweth afar off”. Considering this, there is no rest, because the life of the flesh is toilsome, the spiritual life quiet.
35_interl12062: to the more powerful, who are darkened by the cares of riches
35_interl12064: to those who direct themselves to the gains of the world
35_marg2848: To Egypt, etc. It is lamented that the nobility, the privilege of the prophets and patriarchs, gave their hand for bread, driven by famine, to Egypt, which they had served before; whence those who before were full hired themselves out for bread. They served the Assyrians too under the pressure of famine, they on whom God had once rained manna and whom he had raised up with many miracles. But that another translation has: Egypt gave the hand to the Assyrians, unto their satiety, signifies that the Egyptians and Assyrians came together to tear apart the spoils of the Jews and to sate their own greed.
35_marg2849: To Egypt, etc. Egypt with the Assyrians fights against the Church, of which it is said: “I will not fear thousands of the people surrounding me.” By Egypt are understood the powers of the air, which are joined to the Assyrians, that is, the powerful, to persecute the elect of God through them. And they do this to sate their wickedness with the cruelty of punishments. Egypt also gives the hand to the Assyrians unto their satiety when heretics ally themselves with heretics, to sate themselves with the gain of a deceived people. But according to the Hebrew truth the Church laments that the ministers of the altar give their hands for earthly things to the more powerful, who are darkened by the shadows of riches or of offences. For Egypt is interpreted “darkness”; or to the Assyrians, that is, “those who direct”, namely those who direct themselves to all worldly things, to abound in riches and excel in honours; whom the ministers of Christ serve for perishing and passing things; and so the lights of the world become darkness, who should lift up their hands to holy things and stretch them to heaven with Moses, lest they grow heavy; whence: “In the nights lift up your hands to the holy places, and bless ye the Lord.”
35_interl12066: the churchmen, or Adam and Eve
35_interl12067: “The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the children are set on edge”
35_interl12069: original sin, or the punishment of the fault of the priests
35_interl12070: the words seem to turn aslant towards the judge, that he may not afflict further those who do not deserve it
35_marg2850: Historically. Our fathers, etc. The Jews, like their wicked fathers, drew the curses of the law upon themselves as an unbearable yoke, unwilling to receive Christ, who had come to take away the yoke of the law; to whom it is said: “that upon you may come all the just blood that hath been shed upon the earth”, etc.; and elsewhere: “Fill ye up then the measure of your fathers.” By which words it is shown that the imitators of the fathers who went before draw their offences upon themselves, who are not sufficient to bear their own. Because, then, the rivals of their fathers offended God by an inherited wickedness, both sins and vengeance came down as from the root into the branches; as if: being like our fathers, we bear both their iniquity and its punishment.
35_marg2851: Our fathers, etc. It is the voice of the Christian people, which is scourged for the sins of the priests and princes, saying: Our fathers have sinned, etc.; as if: they are not what they should have been, and we bear the vengeance of their iniquity. Yet let not the people presume on itself, because the choice of the shepherd is according to the desert of the people; nor is the fault lessened for the imitators, but increased; whence Cain is punished sevenfold, Lamech seventy times sevenfold. For after a command and an example, the punishment of the sinner is greater, as is the sin. This can also be referred to original sin, whose corruption passed into all; but those who have been freed by grace do not bear the iniquity of the father. For the fathers have sinned, etc. For sin is nothing, and he who sins is nothing, because, leaving true being, he willed not to be, that is, to sin. He did not say: The fathers have sinned, and their sin is not. For when they are dead their sin remains, and the punishment of sin. But after sin has been forgiven in baptism, each one is punished for his own evils or rewarded for his good deeds.
35_interl12073: the demons, or heretics, or wicked prelates
35_interl12074: if God will not, no other can
35_interl12075: but Christ, who gave himself as the price
35_marg2852: Servants have ruled, etc. He weaves and re-weaves the same miseries, always adding something new though turning over the same things, and recounts new torments, that the merciful judge may be moved to mercy. Servants have ruled: as if: Thou didst free us with a stretched-out arm and didst exalt us in a kingdom; now even servants rule over us, and there is none to redeem; as if: Why dost thou forget thy wonted kindnesses? Look on thy works in us, not ours.
35_marg2853: Servants have ruled, etc. The holy nation, the purchased people, weeps that the spiritual wickednesses which destroyed thy freedom rule over us and afflict us with the slavery of sin. Or: the servants of sins, set in the government of the churches, use against those whom the Lord redeemed the fury of wolves, not the defence of dogs. This mourning, then, is that of the penitents, who long to escape the snares of Satan, to whose rule they have been made subject. The heretics too, servants of sins, rule over those whom they have deceived and make them servants of vices; and sometimes there is no one to free those who are caught in the net of their teachings.
35_interl12077: with the desire of souls; as if: how unworthy, how cruel, how pitiable are the things we suffer
35_interl12079: of the Scriptures, of the virtues
35_interl12080: from the assault of the devil lying in wait, who fell from paradise to dwell in the desert
35_marg2854: At the peril of our lives, etc. The harrying of immense toil is described, since both soul and body are shown to labour. For there was the outward toil of getting daily food, the inward toil because of the sword; as if bread was got at the peril of life.
35_marg2855: At the peril of our lives, etc. Happy the soul that so ardently seeks the bread of life, namely of the Scriptures and the virtues, which it gets because of the sword of the wilderness, that is, by fearing and guarding against the snares of the devil, setting against this sword the shield of faith, that it may be saved from the face of the striker, of whom it is said: “The garden of pleasure is before him, and behind him a desolate wilderness”; because before he breaks in upon the faithful soul it flourishes with virtues like a paradise, but by his blast it is dried up and reduced to a desert. For he who is tripped up by the devil is left by God.
35_interl12083: spiritual, which shakes the soul like a whirlwind of storm
35_marg2856: Our skin, etc. Our skin is lamented as burnt like an oven, with which our first parents were clothed when they were cast out of paradise; whence he said “skin” in the singular, not “skins”, we who from them have all contracted one skin of mortality. This is made as a burning oven, that is, the devil, who is the furnace of vices, which he kindles daily with new burnings of lusts. By this burning we are afflicted with the storm of famine, we who are not refreshed with the feasts of eternal life. But another translation has: of the strokes of famine, since there is one stroke or storm of bodily famine, because spiritual famine wounds all the senses of mind and body. Tossed as by the whirlwind of these storms the soul is swept away; whence it follows: They oppressed the women in Sion, etc.
35_interl12086: in their person he wins goodwill for himself
35_interl12087: he brings the adversaries into hatred, whose deed he shows to be foul, proud and cruel
35_marg2857: No one doubts that this happened to the Jews according to the letter, and that the churches of Christ were afflicted with hunger and thirst for the word of God and corrupted by the depravity of the heretics. Whence: “I fear lest your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.” And above: “For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” The prophet rightly mourns that such virgins have been corrupted; who, had they not been women, would not have admitted womanish things, deceived by the frauds of the heretics and humbled in an adulterous wedlock.
35_marg2858: The women, etc. As often as we are weighed down by the foulness of sins and fall from the height of Sion to low things, the women, that is, our souls, raised in Sion, that is, in the summit of the Church, are humbled. But it is one thing to be humbled in Sion, that is, in the Church to confess sins with a contrite and humbled heart and to hope in the mercy of the judge; another thing to have fallen outside, that is, from the height of the virtues, and to have strayed through the lowness of the vices. Whence above: “Teach your daughters wailing, and every one her neighbour mourning.” For he warns us to wash the affections of our souls with tears and to teach them like daughters to mourn as penitents, and to cleanse the workings of our body like neighbours with lamentations. For the minds of the faithful are like virgins dedicated to God. The cities in which they are humbled are called the divers ranks. For the profession of priests is one, of Levites another, of monks another, of virgins another, of widows another, of the married another. In each some are virgins, some, not keeping their resolve, are deflowered. Whence above: “My virgins and my young men are gone into captivity.” For truly all are virgins who serve God with body and spirit uncorrupted; young men, who have put on newness of life and strength; but many have fallen through the snares of the enemies and the disgraces of crimes.
35_interl12092: because the cruelty of the enemies spared neither age nor dignity
35_marg2859: The princes were hanged, etc. That the princes of the Jews were hanged up by their own hands, or by the rack of the enemies or other torments, is plain from other weightier passages. To the old men too, reverend in face and age, no reverence was paid.
35_marg2860: The princes, etc. The teachers of holy Church are hanged up on high by the hands of the enemies when, deserting the intent of good work, they are drawn off to the will of the enemies, and, bound by the works of their own hands, are stretched as on a rack; whence it follows: they did not respect the persons of the ancient. For no age is spared, because the most cunning serpent neither pities children nor reveres young men nor spares the old; he wraps every age and dignity in one storm. But often the princes and elders of the Church, afflicted with insults, have been hanged up by their hands.
35_interl12093: the fourth topic of complaint; for these things are unworthy of their fortune and former honour
35_interl12094: a foul and wicked deed, by which the enemies are brought into hatred
35_interl12095: “men with men working that which is filthy”
35_interl12097: whom not even their age helps
35_marg2861: The young men, etc. Another rendering: The mighty ground at the mills, and the young men were fastened to the wood. According to the history he seems to lament Sedecias, whose eyes the king of Babylon put out and made him grind, and crucified the young men on the wood. But according to our rendering he touches on the disgrace of the Romans, who abused males indecently; whence: “men with men working that which is filthy”. For the children fell under the wood, who would not believe in Christ hanging on the wood; the mighty too were scandalized at the wood like children, and ground at the mills while, turning the law about according to the letter in an endless round, they were condemned to perpetual blindness; as Samson, his eyes put out, drives the mill round, so that he cannot free himself but wanders in the same tracks.
35_marg2862: The young men, etc. There are some mighty in worldly riches and honours, and some in spiritual things. Those are rolled round in the stubbornness and lust of the world; these go over again the mill of Scripture and grind it, turn it and turn it again. With this mill they grind the fine flour of the bread which came down from heaven, and the meal of understandings for the sacrifice of God. These, in the fervour of spiritual youth, conquered in martyrdom, fastened to the wood of the cross by firmness of faith; one of whom says: “God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.”
35_interl12099: a thing unworthy of their age
35_interl12103: “Open ye to me the gates of justice”, etc.
35_interl12104: who say: “I will sing with the spirit, I will sing also with the understanding”
35_marg2863: The ancients have ceased, etc. The aged and those worn out with years were consumed by famine in the very gates, while with trembling and worn-out limbs they strove to go out to seek food; or else the counsellors and judges of the city were scattered by the enemies, so that they did not sit in the gates as was their custom. The young men too, terrified, renouncing their duties, fled from the streets.
35_marg2864: The ancients have ceased from the gates. The ancients, namely, whose senses are grey, gentle and quiet. But if they offend God they fail from the gates, of which it is said: “Open ye to me the gates of justice”, etc. They fail in these when, wearied by scandals, they forsake the right road. The young men cease from the choir of the singers when the spiritual canticle fails in them, and, estranged from the choir of the saints, they forget the canticle of the Lord.
35_interl12107: “To my hearing thou shalt give joy”
35_marg2865: The sixth topic of complaint: for they show that they are in miseries beyond hope, and that when they looked for good they have come into the utmost miseries.
35_marg2866: The joy is ceased, etc. Because the Jews provoked God to anger, all their joy ceased, and the dances which they led at the solemn feasts were turned into mourning.
35_marg2867: The joy is ceased, etc. It is the voice of the penitents, who offer God a contrite and humbled heart, and, because the bridegroom is away, turn all joy into mourning; which David, longing to recover it, says: “To my hearing thou shalt give joy”; “Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation”; because, pricked with spiritual contrition, he prayed with the marrow of his bones in continual weeping. Whence Isaias: “in the day when the Lord shall bind up the wound of his people, and shall heal the stroke of their wound”; in which, namely, are wound and bruise and swelling sore. For as often as the soul is wounded by the arrow of sin its joy is broken up, when it comes back to its conscience. The dance of the virtues is turned into mourning; which is rightly figured in Asael, who was a most swift runner, like a roe; whence, while he pursued the enemy unwarily and headlong, he perished, struck in the groin. So the mind which does not temper its swiftest motions with patience and gravity is often thrown headlong into fornication of mind and body. The dance is turned into mourning when in the penitents the dance of the virtues, as a harmony of mourning, bewails what it has lost, and keeps the intent of penance, so that after laments and tears the same dance may return to joys.
35_interl12111: of honour in the Church, or of brightness, or good will
35_marg2868: The crown is fallen, etc. It marks the overthrow of the kingdom of the Jews, whose honour and glory perished. Whence above: “Say to the king, and to the queen: Humble yourselves, sit down, for the crown of your glory is come down from your head.” But in another rendering it has “is come down”. For the kingdom of the Jews came down little by little until Joachim; in Sedecias it fell altogether. Whence the mournful voice of the captives is added: woe to us, because we have sinned.
35_marg2869: The crown is fallen, etc. The crown of our head is good will, according to that: “Thou hast crowned us as with a shield of thy good will.” Then, therefore, our mind loses its crown; whence it follows: woe to us, because we have sinned. For in vain do we labour at the rest if we have not the crown of will. For so we offend not only by the deed but also by the desire of a most wicked will.
35_marg2870: The crown is fallen. The priests of the Church and the virgins are as a crown of beauty, but these often fall, wasted by vices. Faith too, when it loses its wholeness, falls like a crown from the head. But the Lord himself, according to Isaias, is the crown of the Church; whence: “The Lord of hosts shall be a crown of glory”, etc. This crown the Church loses when the faith of Christ is corrupted in certain members, the crown falling. Woe hangs over sinners, because “where there is no governor, the people shall fall”.
35_interl12117: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise”
35_interl12120: which ought to have looked towards God
35_marg2871: Therefore, etc. It is plain to all that the heart of the Jews was sorrowful in both captivities, and their eyes dimmed with tears and grief.
35_marg2872: Therefore is … sorrowful, etc. It is the voice of the penitents. But there is a twofold kind of sorrow and grief; whence Isaias: “My sorrow upon sorrow”, etc.; because to the sorrow of sins is added the sorrow of compunction. There is a bad sorrow, of which it is said: “In sorrow shalt thou bring forth children.” There is also a good one, according to that: “My sorrow was renewed.” So after sin the heart is humbled with sadness, that by the medicine of this sorrow the sickness may depart. The eyes are dimmed, infected namely and blinded by the malice of sins, so that they cannot see the light of Christ, who is the stone cut out of the mountain without hands and raised into a great mountain. Because it is destroyed: that is, being equal with the Father, he emptied himself, “that they who see not may see, and they who see may become blind”. Therefore with darkened eyes the faithless do not see this mountain, because it is destroyed; foxes have walked upon it, namely the persecutors or the heretics who thought ill of the incarnation of Christ, tearing the Church and fraudulently corrupting the Catholic faith. Therefore “they shall be the portions of foxes”. Herod was a fox, the persecutor of Christ and of John; whence: “Go and tell that fox.” The heretics too are foxes, according to that: “Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vines.”
35_interl12124: emptying himself, taking the form of a servant
35_interl12126: by tearing, by thinking ill of Christ
35_interl12127: in the person of the judge, whose strength and greatness he proclaims without flattery
35_marg2873: The same in David: “But thou, O Lord, endurest for ever”; and elsewhere: “But thou art always the selfsame”, etc. Shalt remain: it is not a remaining in time or in place, nor anything other than himself, but that one, undivided and abiding being; as if: though the Son emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, he remains for ever.
35_marg2874: Thy throne, etc. “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever”; and elsewhere: “Thy kingdom is a kingdom of all ages.” When you hear “throne”, understand the judge and fear; as if: fear God and keep his commandments. Even if he is judged as man, yet his kingdom is for ever.
35_interl12128: “He will not always be angry, nor will he threaten for ever. He hath not dealt with us according to our sins”
35_marg2875: After every kind of lamentation he turns his prayers to him alone who alone can comfort.
35_marg2876: Like this is that: “How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget me unto the end?” Not that “God forgets to show mercy”, but when he delays to help he seems to have forgotten, so as to kindle desire and make the comfort sweeter, and meanwhile he laughs at the pains of the innocent. As the potter tries his vessels, to make vessels unto honour, because “the furnace trieth the potter’s vessels”.
35_marg2877: This we must pray for constantly, that he forget us not, that he forsake us not for ever; which we pray well with words, but better with deeds. Let us then be mindful of him, that he may not forget us, because “God doth not forget to show mercy” unless we forget; and if we have forgotten, he breathes in grace and drives away forgetfulness. Whence: “All the ends of the earth shall remember, and shall be converted to the Lord.”
35_interl12130: he beseeches the judge humbly and suppliantly
35_marg2878: By converting, because conversion is the beginning of restoration; the renewing of the days is the receiving of eternity.
35_interl12131: whence: “his going forth is from the beginning”
35_marg2879: Our turnings away are many; whence elsewhere: “Convert us, O God our saviour.” Convert us by grace, and we shall be converted as far as lies in us by the freedom of choice; whence: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me hath not been void.” For the grace of him who calls goes before and stirs up the freedom of the will. Ours it is that we fall, God’s that we rise again. For men are “flesh, a wind that goeth and returneth not”. “It is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.” Yet it is to be noted that we are not converted by the grace of God unless we are converted by our own will too. But there is a certain veil of our weakness set before our senses, and unless it is removed by the enlightening of God we cannot be converted; freedom, then, is given back by grace. We must always pray, then: Convert us, O Lord.
35_marg2880: Renew, etc. We are called back to this beginning when we are converted; when we have come to it, we shall be renewed. For we have grown old and corrupt and have lost the days of eternity, which we receive back through conversion; whence elsewhere: “Convert me, O Lord, and I shall be converted to thee.”
35_interl12135: be angry as a father, not as a judge
35_marg2881: Thou art angry, etc. The first rejection is that by which we are handed over to the tempter. The second, when, tempted, we yield; but we are rejected to be tempted without the anger of God, of which it is said: “God hath not cast away his people, which he foreknew.” But when we are overcome and afterwards do not repent, God is exceedingly angry; whence: “Who knoweth the power of thy anger?” etc. For sometimes he is angry as a father, when he rebukes the offender with words and makes him penitent. But he is angry as Lord when he chastises like a hard master and at once takes vengeance; whence Moses: “Let not thy indignation be enkindled against thy people.” He will be angry as judge when he says: “Depart, ye cursed”, etc., when there will be no more place for penance or pardon.
35_marg2882: Let these things suffice for the exposition of the Lamentations of Jeremias, which I, Gilbert, deacon of the church of Auxerre, have drawn from the fountains of the fathers.
